"A national conversation about Kenya's development. This conversation must rise above politics, transcend electoral cycles and unite us around a shared destiny."

The President acknowledged that while Vision 2030 had set an ambitious goal of transforming Kenya into an upper-middle-income country by 2030, the country remains off course to achieve that target.

"Vision 2030 set a target of Kenya becoming an upper-middle-income country by 2030. So far, we are off target. This is not a criticism of Vision 2030, nor is it a reason for disappointment; rather, it is an opportunity to learn from our successes proudly, reflect with honesty on where we have fallen short, and define together Kenya's next long-term vision," he said.

At the same time, Ruto announced that the government will formally launch a nationwide conversation on August 12 to develop Kenya's next long-term development blueprint as Vision 2030 nears its end.

"Accordingly, on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, we shall formally launch the National Conversation on Kenya's Future Beyond Vision 2030; the most consequential exercise in national reflection and public participation since the promulgation of our Constitution in 2010," he stated.

Ruto said recent economic reforms had laid a stronger foundation for future growth, citing improvements in key macroeconomic indicators.

"We have stabilized our currency, inflation has fallen, borrowing costs have declined, and investor confidence has returned," he said. "Last year Kenya attracted a record $3.2 billion in foreign direct investment, more than double the amount recorded in 2022."

He added that Kenya's improving investment climate had earned international recognition.

"The 2025 IMD World Competitiveness Ranking placed Kenya as the most competitive economy in Africa, reflecting the confidence our reforms have restored," Ruto said.

At the same time, Ruto also highlighted the establishment of the National Infrastructure Fund and the Sovereign Wealth Fund, saying the two institutions would help finance strategic investments while safeguarding the country's wealth for future generations.

According to Ruto, Kenya must now confront difficult questions about its development path to unlock its full potential.

"The question we must ask ourselves candidly and honestly is why other nations have fulfilled so much of their potential while we have repeatedly fallen short. What must we now do differently to ensure that the next chapter of Kenya's development story is fundamentally different from the last?" he posed.

He urged all Kenyans to help shape a new long-term national vision, saying the country's future depends on collective commitment rather than political divisions.

World.title: Lawyer seeks orders to suspend court boycott
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Advocate Adrian Kamotho argues that LSK's actions create the impression that court orders can be overturned through a boycott. [File, Standard]

A city lawyer has moved to the High Court seeking conservatory orders to suspend the Law Society of Kenya's (LSK) ongoing targeted boycott of judges and judicial officers.

In a petition filed under a certificate of urgency, Advocate Adrian Kamotho has sued LSK led by President Charles Kanjama, over its nationwide and targeted court boycott of Chief Justice Martha Koome, Deputy Chief Justice Philomena Mwilu and other judges, arguing that the action is unconstitutional, undermines judicial independence and denies litigants access to justice.

"The LSK's actions create the impression that lawful court orders can be overturned through a boycott, setting a dangerous precedent to the rule of law and thereby undermining the proper administration of justice," Kamotho states in the petition.

The lawyer has named the Judicial Service Commission (JSC), Chief Justice Martha Koome, Deputy Chief Justice Mwilu, several Supreme Court, High Court and Environment and Land Court judges, Court of Appeal Judge Sankale Ole Kantai, Kibera Chief Magistrate Stella Atambo and the Kenya Magistrates and Judges Association as interested parties in the case.

He is seeking orders to immediately suspend the implementation of the LSK's targeted boycott announced through statements and operational guidelines issued on July 17, July 20 and July 22, 2026, pending the hearing and determination of the petition.

"Pending the hearing and determination of this Petition, the court be pleased to issue a conservatory order restraining the LSK, whether by itself, its Council, officers, agents or any person acting under its authority, from implementing, enforcing or giving effect to the targeted boycott," Kamotho seeks.

According to the petition, the targeted boycott, which commenced on July 23, directs advocates not to participate in fresh hearings, part-heard matters or new applications before judges listed by the LSK.

East Africa Law Society president Ramadhan Abubakar Mukira addresses the media on the court boycott outside the Supreme Court of Kenya in Nairobi on July 22, 2026. [Benard Orwongo, Standard]

Lawyers are also required to seek adjournments, transfers or recusals of matters regardless of their clients' instructions.

"The Respondent has directed advocates not to participate in fresh hearings, part-heard matters or new applications before the listed judges and judicial officers," Kamotho states.

He adds: "Advocates appearing before the targeted judges and judicial officers have been directed to seek the transfer, recusal or adjournment of pending proceedings, irrespective of their clients' instructions, the circumstances of the individual case or the applicable legal principles."

Kamotho further claims the society has threatened disciplinary action against judges, judicial officers and advocates who decline to implement the boycott.

"The LSK has further directed that any judge, judicial officer or advocate who declines to facilitate the boycott be reported to it for 'appropriate action,' including possible complaints before the Judicial Service Commission and such further action as its Council may deem necessary," he says.

According to the petition, every day the boycott remains in force exposes court users to delayed justice and unnecessary hardship.

"Every day that the targeted boycott remains operative exposes litigants and court users to adjournments, disruption of part-heard proceedings, expiry of interim protection measures, prolonged detention, additional expense and denial or delay of access to justice," Kamotho argues.

He also faults the LSK for allegedly including the late Supreme Court Judge Mohammed Ibrahim in its list of judges affected by the boycott.

"The targeted list of judges includes Hon. Justice Mohammed Ibrahim (deceased), demonstrating unconscionable casualness on the part of the LSK and apparent failure to verify elementary material facts before imposing measures of such gravity," the petition states.

Kamotho contends that the boycott creates an unlawful mechanism for exerting pressure on judges outside the constitutional framework.

He argues that the dispute raises fundamental constitutional questions, including whether the LSK has the legal authority to organise an indefinite boycott, compel advocates to withhold legal services from clients and determine which judicial functions judges may perform.

He maintains that the boycott threatens litigants' constitutional rights to equality before the law, access to justice, legal representation and a fair hearing, particularly in urgent and criminal matters.

In his supporting affidavit, Kamotho says advocates have been placed in an impossible position by the LSK's directives.

"The directions therefore place advocates in an immediate and irreconcilable conflict between their lawful professional duties and the Respondent's threatened enforcement measures," he says.

He further says litigants are innocent parties caught in an institutional dispute.

"The practical burden of the boycott consequently falls upon litigants and court users who are strangers to the institutional dispute forming the alleged basis of the boycott," he states.

Kamotho insists the conservatory orders sought are intended only to preserve uninterrupted court operations and judicial independence pending determination of the constitutional petition, arguing that the public interest favours continued access to courts and legal representation rather than disruption of judicial proceedings.

The petition is pending directions and hearing.

World.title: Ruto: Government will deal firmly with criminals
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto arrive for the consecration of Rev. Vitalis Job Ekuru as the fourth Bishop of the ACK Diocese of Katakwa in Busia County on July 26, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has declared war on individuals who involve in violence, destruction of property and political intimidation.

He said people initially participated in anti-government demonstrations have "graduated from protesters to goons."

Speaking on Sunday during the consecration of Rev. Vitalis Job Ekuru as the fourth Bishop of the ACK Diocese of Katakwa in Busia County, the President said the government would no longer tolerate criminality disguised as peaceful protests.

"They have now graduated from protesters to goons. They are bringing chaos everywhere," Ruto said.

President Ruto maintained that safeguarding peace remains the government's top priority while ensuring all leaders have the freedom to campaign without fear of violence or intimidation.

He argued that Kenya had previously experienced a rise in criminal activities, but efforts to deal with those responsible had been complicated by differing opinions over how security agencies should respond.

"We had a small problem earlier when crime issues increased and we did not agree on how to tackle the crime as a nation because sometimes we used to defend those who were hurting people and destroying property. We could say that they should not be touched because they are our children," he said.

"But now we have seen the repercussions because they have now graduated from protesters to goons. They are bringing chaos everywhere."

Ruto said the government had resolved to restore law and order, insisting that criminal gangs would not be allowed to disrupt peace under the cover of political demonstrations.

"We have agreed to discipline all the goons, and no one will be allowed to propagate crime and disrupt peace in our country," he said.

The President also sought to reassure Kenyans that the country would remain peaceful as preparations begin for the 2027 General Election, saying his administration would do everything possible to safeguard stability before, during and after the polls.

"I agree that peace is not negotiable. All of us, irrespective of who we are, our persuasion, our political leaning and whatever it is that we believe in, we must have a peaceful nation," Ruto said.

"I want to assure you as the people of Kenya that we will have peaceful elections next year because elections come and go, but this nation must remain firm, united and stable. We shall do everything possible to ensure that this nation is stable."

At the same time, the Head of State emphasized that every political leader should be free to campaign and present their agenda without intimidation, provided they conduct their activities peacefully.

"Every leader should be given a chance to give their opinion. Those who have an agenda or plan should be given an opportunity to explain it to Kenyans. Even those who have nothing should be given a chance to speak, but all of us must ensure that we are peaceful," he said.

The President's remarks come against the backdrop of heightened political tensions and growing concerns over violent disruptions at political gatherings.

Recent incidents, including the Ol Kalou by-election in Nyandarua County, saw armed gangs disrupt voting and terrorize residents, prompting renewed debate over the role of criminal groups in Kenya's political landscape.

The government has faced criticism from sections of the opposition, who have accused state agencies of sponsoring the gangs.

However, Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has rejected the claims, instead alleging that the groups were mobilized by allies of former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua. Murkomen has pledged decisive action against those behind the violence, regardless of their political affiliation.

World.title: Ruiru 'Vampire' arrested after lodging incident with woman
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The suspect was arrested after an angry mob cornered and assaulted him near the Powerstar area in Ruiru town following weeks of attacks that had spread fear among residents. [Courtesy, X]

Police in Ruiru have arrested a 35-year-old man believed to be behind a series of bizarre and violent attacks in which residents were robbed and bitten, leaving several victims nursing serious injuries.

The suspect, identified as Githaiga from Mugutha, was arrested on Saturday afternoon after an angry mob cornered and assaulted him near the Powerstar area in Ruiru town following weeks of attacks that had spread fear among residents.

Ruiru Sub-County Police Commander Charles Kibathi confirmed the arrest, saying the suspect was heavily intoxicated at the time and had allegedly bitten a woman who was with him, tearing part of her lower lip.

"The suspect and the female victim were taken to hospital for treatment as investigations continue," Kibathi said.

He added that detectives are investigating whether the suspect is linked to the earlier attacks reported in Ruiru and neighbouring Gitothua Ward.

However, some residents defended the suspect, claiming the altercation that led to the woman being bitten stemmed from a disagreement after the two emerged from a room where they had spent the night.

Kibathi assured residents that police are pursuing all leads to establish whether other people may have been involved in the attacks and pledged to intensify security operations in the area.

The arrest follows weeks of panic after several residents reported being attacked by a man who allegedly robbed victims before violently biting them.

Among the latest victims was Daniel Ndegwa, who was attacked on July 11 at about 9 p.m. while walking to a nearby shopping centre. Ndegwa told police he was confronted by a man demanding his mobile phone before a struggle ensued. During the confrontation, the attacker bit his finger and injured his left hand. A friend who was accompanying him was also reportedly bitten.

Residents said the attacks had become increasingly frequent throughout July, forcing many people to avoid walking outside after dark.

In one of the most shocking incidents, another victim reportedly suffered severe facial injuries after the attacker allegedly bit off part of his cheek.

The incidents have disrupted normal life in Ruiru town and Gitothua Ward, with many residents opting to remain indoors in the evenings for fear of being attacked.

Residents, led by Severino Githinji, criticized the security situation, saying families have been living in constant fear and called for increased police patrols and swift action against those responsible.

Police said the first official report of the attacks was made on July 11, and investigations are ongoing to establish whether the arrested suspect is responsible for all the reported incidents.

Kibathi urged members of the public to continue cooperating with investigators as detectives work to unravel the full circumstances surrounding the attacks.

World.title: Murkomen: Police no longer rely on Gachagua's 'gossip'
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Interior CS Kipchumba Murkomen during the official launch of the Multi-biometric Identification System (MBIS) and handover ceremony of ANSI National Accreditation Board Certificate at DCI Headquarters on July 23, 2026. [NPS]

Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has accused former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua of spreading falsehoods, saying technology-driven policing has replaced "gossip-based" investigations.

Speaking during the handover of the ANSI National Accreditation Board certification to the Forensic Evidence Management Unit and the launch of the Multi-Biometric Identification System at the Directorate of Criminal Investigations headquarters on Thursday, Murkomen said the country has shifted from outdated investigative methods to science-based policing.

"We are moving away from gossip-based collection of evidence to science. I saw an impeached former leader claiming he is well connected to police officers and receives gossip every day because he is not busy unlike the President," said Murkomen.

He said the biometric system will strengthen investigations through science and technology, making unofficial information unnecessary.

"That is an old style of collecting evidence. We now have a modern police service driven by science and technology. We do not need his gossip to run the National Police Service," he observed.

Murkomen claimed the technology would make it harder for unsuitable individuals to rise through public office.

"If these systems had been in place many years ago, people like Gachagua would not have survived the system as habitual offenders until he slipped through to become Deputy President. Such things will never happen again with this technological advancement," said Murkomen.

The Interior CS defended Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja, saying he has the government's confidence and has discharged his duties professionally.

"I have full support and faith in the leadership of the Inspector General. He has carried out his duties with dignity, honour and respect for the citizens of Kenya and his office," noted Murkomen.

Murkomen also rejected Gachagua's criticism of police leadership, arguing that Kenya is recording fewer cases of terrorism, banditry, robbery and other crimes.

"There has never been a period when Kenya has recorded fewer incidents of terrorism, banditry, robberies and other crimes. Our security agencies are working together and have improved security," he said.

He also criticised remarks attributed to Gachagua warning tourists against visiting Kenya, saying they damage the country's reputation.

"For anyone to stand out there and say Kenya is not safe and tourists should not come to our country is very embarrassing," explained Murkomen.

Murkomen dismissed claims that 68 women were raped by police officers during the Ol Kalou parliamentary by-election, urging anyone with evidence to report the matter to the Directorate of Criminal Investigations, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority or the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights.

"If those incidents occurred, they should be reported so those responsible can be held accountable. If not, those making such reckless statements must also be held accountable," said Murkomen.

He accused Gachagua of making the allegations out of political desperation.

"I know why Gachagua speaks the way he does. It is because of desperation. Knowing that he cannot hold any office again in Kenya and can never be President of this republic, he wants to take the entire nation, including the economy, down the drain with himself. We will not allow that," he said.

Murkomen also urged media organisations to challenge politicians they host instead of allowing false claims to go unchecked.

"We should not feed Kenyans with lies. I want to tell media houses that when you invite such reckless human beings, please carry with you a lie detector. Otherwise you are going to mislead the people of Kenya and drive bad behaviour in our country," said Murkomen.

He maintained that intelligence gathering within the National Police Service follows lawful procedures and dismissed claims that private individuals receive confidential police briefings outside official channels

World.title: Gachagua: Why Ruto will not steal the 2027 General Election
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

DCP leader Righathi Gachagua during a live interview with KTN at his Karen home, Nairobi. [Kanyiri Wahito, Standard]

Democracy for Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has claimed that President William Ruto will not be able to manipulate the outcome of the 2027 General Election, arguing that Kenyans have become more vigilant in protecting their votes.

Speaking during a live interview with KTN from his Karen residence, the former Deputy President said the recent Ol Kalou by-election had provided opposition supporters with a blueprint on safeguarding the electoral process.

"Voting is not enough; you vote and protect the vote. We now have a template from the Ol Kalou by-election," Gachagua said.

He urged Kenyans to remain vigilant during the next General Election, saying the alleged intimidation witnessed in Ol Kalou had failed to influence voters.

"They tried intimidating the people of Ol Kalou, but they did not succeed. We are celebrating what happened, and people from across the country are calling to benchmark on how it worked," he said.

Gachagua also questioned the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC)'s ability to conduct a free and fair election, accusing the electoral body of failing to condemn alleged voter suppression and bribery during the Ol Kalou by-election.

"IEBC has not even condemned the wrongs that happened during the by-election in Ol Kalou. We lost two people who were actually protecting our votes," he alleged.

The DCP leader further renewed his criticism of President Ruto, accusing him of betraying voters from the Mt Kenya region despite earlier warnings.

According to Gachagua, the outcome of the Ol Kalou by-election should serve as a warning to the Kenya Kwanza administration ahead of the 2027 General Election.

He maintained that the by-election demonstrated that Kenyans could no longer be intimidated by the State and described the result as a preview of what to expect in the next national polls.

Gachagua also revisited the Mbeere North by-election, alleging that DCP lost because of widespread voter bribery, intimidation of elderly voters and failure by the party to adequately protect its votes.

"We lost the Mbeere North by-election because we didn't protect our votes properly. There was also massive voter bribery, and those who participated were allegedly given the balance of their bribe after showing a photo of whom they had voted for," he claimed.

The former Deputy President further argued that DCP would have secured an even larger victory in Ol Kalou were it not for what he described as voter suppression and police intimidation.



More to follow...

World.title: Israeli strike leaves huge crater at Gaza hospital amid uncertainty over Trump plan
World.content:
Israeli strikes on Gaza left a huge crater at a hospital less than 48 hours after US President Donald Trump announced Hamas and Israel had agreed to advance a ceasefire plan, local authorities said.

Gaza’s health ministry said the attack destroyed vital medical supplies.

“When medicines are bombed … illness becomes a weapon of war,” Dr. Munir Al-Bursh, the ministry’s director general, said in a statement.

The strike demolished two medical warehouses at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital and damaged two others, the health ministry said. The director general added a nearby displacement camp was leveled and civilian tents suffered extensive damage.

CNN has reached out to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) for comment.

Footage from the scene shows people sifting through the large cavity, attempting to salvage medical supplies like IV fluids, breathing tubes, surgical masks and cotton balls buried amid the debris.

“Destroying a medical warehouse while Gaza’s health system is already suffering from a 51 percent shortage of essential medicines … is a direct assault on one of the last remaining lifelines of healthcare,” Bursh said.

In the past two days, eight civilians have been killed while a further 76 have sustained injuries, the Palestinian Ministry of Health said on Saturday. More than 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since the announcement of the ceasefire agreement in October last year.

For context: The latest strikes come shortly after Trump announced Thursday evening that Hamas had agreed to “completely disarm” along with an Israeli troop withdrawal. While the move marked progress in the long-stagnant roadmap to peace initiated by Trump’s Board of Peace last year substantial issues need to be resolved first.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is yet to comment on Trump’s announcement but an Israeli official told CNN Israel would not withdraw from Gaza without Hamas disarming first.

World.title: Girl’s undisclosed death in gene-editing trial raises red flags in booming Chinese industry
World.content:
Beijing — A top Chinese medical university is investigating the death of a young girl in an experimental gene-editing trial conducted by a leading expert at its affiliated hospital that has raised serious concerns about ethics in A top Chinese medical university is investigating the death of a young girl in an experimental gene-editing trial conducted by a leading expert at its affiliated hospital that has raised serious concerns about ethics in China’s booming biomedical industry.

Shanghai Jiaotong University School of Medicine said it has established a working group to “conduct a comprehensive investigation” into the clinical trial carried out last year in Xinhua Hospital and a related scientific paper.

The announcement came days after US-based Science magazine and science accountability publication Retraction Watch released a joint report detailing the botched clinical trial that was partially funded by the girl’s parents, who say they paid $860,000 for the development of the treatment.

The girl’s parents told the outlets that doctors didn’t warn them that their daughter could die and had hoped the treatment would correct a gene defect behind developmental delays they worried would affect her in later life.

The hospital’s ethics board concluded the girl’s death was “definitely related” to the treatment, but penalties were minor and the outcome was never made public by the doctors or their institutions, even as results from related research were published in the prestigious science journal Nature, the Science report revealed.

Now in the spotlight, the case has stoked outrage and concern in China especially after a tightening of rules in the wake of another scandal – the revelation in 2018 that babies had been born from embryos gene-edited by Chinese scientist He Jiankui.

The context of the latest clinical trial is vastly different: gene editing is an emerging form of gene therapy that aims to edit DNA or RNA sequences to repair or remove defective genes that cause a range of diseases in children and adults. Unlike gene-editing embryos, these changes aren’t passed to future generations.

Even still, “this case is much more worrying than (that of He Jiankui) … because this case is well-established scientists in one of China’s most prestigious universities,” said Joy Zhang, director of the Centre for Global Science and Epistemic Justice at the University of Kent in the United Kingdom.

Chinese scientist He Jiankui speaks at an international conference in Hong Kong in 2018, when he defended his research. Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images

He, by contrast, was a little-known, entrepreneur scientist working at a recently established institution when he became the first and only known researcher to engineer human embryos for implantation. The move shocked the global scientific community and landed him in jail for three years.

Since then, “there’s been a series of government initiatives and commitment of how they want to strengthen ethics … but obviously this is not the case,” Zhang said.

Global health expert Yanzhong Huang said that seeing the appearance of “similar ethical failures years later suggests persistent gaps in regulation in terms of transparency, safety and accountability.”

“If you look at this case, it’s full of mistakes, loopholes, and irregularities … so in that sense, it is very unique, but in the meantime I’m afraid in this environment of Chinese biomedical boom this may potentially be the tip of the iceberg,” said Huang, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations in the US.

A botched trial

Gene therapy, an umbrella term that includes developing treatments using gene-editing, has become a driver of China’s rapidly expanding biotechnology sector, where researchers are racing with peers in the US and elsewhere for medical breakthroughs.

That research is boosted by the country’s so-called dual-track regulatory system, experts say, which allows for therapies to be tested for the first time in humans through “investigator-initiated trials.”

These small-scale clinical trials generally undergo less oversight than the traditional approval pathway for a green light. Similar models exist in other countries and are seen as important to accelerating breakthroughs and administering life-saving treatments especially for rare diseases, where there is little commercial incentive for research. But they may also come with risks.

It was against this backdrop the Shanghai couple who shared their story with Science undertook a journey to get treatment for their young daughter.

The girl had been diagnosed with a rare gene defect that produces a neurodevelopmental condition known as Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, Science reported.

The disease can cause intellectual deficits as well as severe physical symptoms. While the girl showed symptoms that were milder than others, her parents decided to explore specialized gene therapy, according to Science.

They connected with Qiu Zilong, a prominent neuroscientist at the Shanghai Jiaotong University Medical School’s Songjiang Research Institute. Qiu was known for research working with a cutting-edge technique known as base editing to make custom treatments for children with rare diseases.

Under a treatment plan he developed for the family, the girl would be the first person in the world to receive a gene-editing therapy directed at the brain, according to Science. The family received an assurance from Qiu that there would be “no safety catastrophes,” according to Science, which reviewed recordings of Qiu made by the family.

Children play in at a park in Shanghai in 2022. Qilai Shen/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Preparations included preclinical trials in mice and monkeys, which Qui told the family proved that clinical trials should go ahead, Science reported.

In early 2025, the hospital’s ethics committee approved the clinical trial, before the final results of one of the preclinical studies on monkeys was released, Science reported. Other results were “unconvincing,” according to a scientist who reviewed them for Science.

Several days after the girl’s treatment last March, she developed a high fever and signs of kidney damage, was rushed to the ICU and died. CNN has been unable to independently verify the account.

A clinical trial listing associated with the experimental treatment has not been updated since last year. When reached by phone by CNN, one of the lead doctors for the trial, Yu Yongguo, declined to comment and hung up. Qiu did not respond to an emailed interview request. Repeated calls to the medical university’s publicity department went unanswered.

In September 2025, a Shanghai district health department fined the hospital approximately $3,600 for failing to properly oversee the trial and not registering it as commercially sponsored research on the national database, Science reported, while Yu was required by the hospital to receive verbal counseling, the family said. CNN has also approached the hospital for comment.

It wasn’t until this past February, when the bereaved parents learned that Nature had published a paper from Qiu that they demanded action from the university. The paper described research on the feasibility of using gene-editing to correct the mutation the caused their daughter’s disorder but did not mention a human trial nor their daughter’s death.

The couple called for an investigation and a retraction of the paper, telling Science they were concerned the paper could give other parents false hope. The university denied the request, Science reported.

In a statement to CNN, Nature’s deputy editor Victoria Aranda said the journal was investigating concerns that had been raised around the manuscript, was in touch with the researchers and would take “take editorial action as appropriate” following their probe.

“No information that a human trial was planned or ongoing was ever shared with us, nor was any data related to human therapy shared or mentioned in any version of the submitted study,” Aranda said. “We were shocked to hear of the death of a child in the recent clinical trial and of the circumstances around that trial.”

An editor’s note was added to the Nature paper on July 29. A Chinese-language press announcement for its publication has been removed from the Xinhua Hospital website, CNN found.

‘Safeguards in place’

The scandal comes as Chinese regulators have been scrambling to keep pace with the surge of innovation and investment into advanced therapies.

Since 2015, investigator-initiated trials for cell and gene therapy products have proliferated, enrolling over 30,000 participants in more than a thousand trials, twice the number of participants in investigational drug trials overseen by a national regulatory body, according to a 2025 analysis by Chinese researchers.

Researchers work at a laboratory at the Research Institute of Tsinghua University in Shenzhen, in Shenzhen last summer. Liang Xu/Xinhua/Getty Images

In May, Beijing rolled out new rules specifically for new biomedical technologies, plugging what observers said was a gap in how the development of advanced therapies, including personalized treatments, are controlled.

The new rules establish a national regulatory framework governing such trials, including investigator‑initiated clinical trials like the one carried out at Xinhua Hospital, centralizing oversight and requiring the reporting of adverse reactions. They are also seen as creating a clearer pathway to commercializing these treatments.

“It’s speculation to say if this governance would have made a difference (in this case), but one would hope that … with such safeguards in place … the institution itself might have exercised a lot more care,” said Calvin Ho, an associate professor with Monash Law School in Australia.

Instead, the trial took place at a time when there “wasn’t clear governance regimes in place,” Ho said, adding that balancing innovation and patient protection in these fields is a challenge for governments across the world in this moment.

In China, it’s possible that the case could spark further tightening and oversight in a knee-jerk response that stymies science, observers said. But Beijing is not just balancing innovation and safety, but also global competition – and may not want to slow down.

China’s share of global clinical trial starts grew from 1% in 2009 to 32% in 2025 – nearly matching the US’ 35%, according to a recent survey of US leaders in industry and academia conducted by Cure Innovation Index.

Chinese institutions have the capabilities and are doing cutting edge work, said Huang.

“But at the same time that we are talking about the rise of China as a biotech superpower, we should not forget the other side of the story – the regulatory, ethical challenges that might constitute a serious stumbling block for Chinese science.”

World.title: Zelensky warns air defenses are being overwhelmed as Russia pounds Ukraine, killing 9
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky renewed his plea for Western air defenses following a deadly overnight Russian attack, which saw only one of 27 ballistic missiles shot down.

The attack is the second major Russian aerial assault in two days, with the Kremlin apparently seeking to expose Kyiv’s shortages of key defense systems as it struggles to make advances along the vast front line.

At least nine people were killed and 30 wounded in the latest attack on Ukraine, including four children, with strikes targeting the capital Kyiv and surrounding regions, according to the city’s mayor Vitali Klitschko.

The Ukrainian president has often appealed to Western nations to provide much-needed air defense systems to protect Ukraine’s cities and critical infrastructure from aerial attacks. The country is facing a shortage of US-made Patriot defense interceptor missiles.

Yet the situation has become more desperate in recent weeks, with massive Russian assaults claiming the lives of civilians. Earlier this week, Ukrainian authorities said a ballistic missile slammed into a house in the rural village of Radushne, in the Dnipro Region, killing at least six family members, including four children.

In the aftermath of the overnight strikes on Saturday, Zelensky wrote on Telegram, “We lack missiles for the Patriot systems. And it is precisely this shortage of anti-ballistic interceptors that only encourages Russia to carry out such deadly strikes.”

A CNN team on the ground heard at least three waves of explosions in the capital overnight.

“People are trapped in a five-story residential building due to falling rocket debris in the Solomyanske district,” Klitschko wrote on Telegram. He said a fire had broken out in the courtyard of a residential building and that emergency services are headed to the scene.

While Kyiv took the brunt of the Russian assault, the regions of Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy, Kharkiv and Poltava were also targeted, according to Zelensky.

“Eighteen buildings, a school, the Lithuanian embassy and infrastructure facilities were damaged,” he added.

Russia’s powerful ballistic missiles are incredibly difficult for Ukraine to intercept because they travel at extremely high speeds. Some of the most advanced missiles can only be shot down using the US-made Patriot defense systems.

“It is crucial that our partners understand that these systems are not needed sitting in warehouses for hypothetical scenarios, but here and now,” Zelensky said on Saturday.

“Every anti-ballistic missile package saves the lives of our people. And every night that we lack them results in casualties.”

Overall, at least 14 civilians have been killed and 87 injured across Ukraine over the past 24 hours, data from local authorities shows.

Meanwhile, Russia intercepted and destroyed 274 Ukrainian drones targeting its territory overnight, including over the Moscow region, according to the Russian Ministry of Defense

On Friday, US President Donald Trump said he was hesitant to allow Ukraine to build its own Patriot missile interceptors – an idea he first announced on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Turkey last month.

“We’re talking about it, but it’s a hard thing to give away that kind of technology,” Trump said during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David. “We have to be very careful.” He voiced particular concerns about the risk that Ukraine could someday use the Patriot missile interceptors against the US, even though he acknowledged that it’s unlikely to happen.

The deliberations mark a turnaround from earlier this month, when Trump suggested during the NATO summit that he would aid Ukraine’s fight against Russia by permitting them to build the Patriot systems.

World.title: Palestinian Christians call on American evangelicals to stop ignoring their plight
World.content:
Bethlehem, West Bank — Father Munther Isaac can lean on a 2,000-year history of Christian faith and practice as he studies and promotes the teachings of Jesus Christ.

But he fears the places where Christ was born and was killed could face a harder future, not only because of the ongoing strife between Israelis and Palestinians but because of actions by some of his fellow Christians.

While Christians come under verbal and physical attack almost daily in Jerusalem, Isaac argues that the existence and experiences of the Palestinian faithful are almost invisible to American evangelicals who support returning the Holy Land to the Jews.

“Come and see,” is the call from Isaac, the director of the Bethlehem Institute for Peace and Justice, from Father Bashar Fawadleh of the last entirely Christian town in the occupied West Bank, and other clergy.

“Our experience has been when pastors and lay people come to Palestine, see the walls, see the settlements, meet with families struggling just to survive in their land — that’s when their eyes are opened,” Isaac said.

Isaac and Fawadleh want to reach evangelicals following the broad movement known as Christian Zionism, which sees the modern state of Israel as the fulfilment of biblical prophecy.

But they argue that ignores the communities of Palestinian Christians and goes against the Christian ethos of loving your neighbor.

“Theology has been weaponized,” Isaac said. “These are Christians who are funding and supporting the major threat on our existence in the land today.”

Ancient communities under new threats

Father Munther Isaac says a lot of the land around Beit Sahour where he played as a boy has been taken over for settlements. Scott McWhinnie/CNN

Isaac, 47, was born in the Christian town of Beit Sahour, near Bethlehem. Jewish settlements have spread over much of the land where he played as a child and he can no longer walk the couple of miles to the ancient churches, temples and mosques in Jerusalem from his home in Bethlehem. The West Bank town is encircled by Israel’s separation wall that rises to 26 feet high and was introduced to stop suicide bombers during the Second Intifada from easily reaching Jerusalem.

Israel has been ramping up its support for building on Palestinian land in the last year. That’s forced many Muslims to move and further splintered the 50,000 or so Christians who live in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.

Fawadleh said more than 90 people had left Taybeh, known as Ephraim in the Gospel of John, over the last three years. Now the last fully Christian town in the West Bank has about 1,200 residents, and that number threatens to dwindle further.

Fawadleh said his parishioners are afraid to get the harvest from their olive groves, and Roland Bassir said his cement factory just outside Taybeh comes under attack from settlers most days. “If I have the opportunity to leave, I would leave and not stay in this town, because there is no future for me or my children,” he said.

The view from St. George’s Church in Taybeh include the outskirts of the town and, on the hillside in the distance, settlement building. Scott McWhinnie/CNN Roland Bassir says he and his cement factory come under nearly daily harassment and attack. Scott McWhinnie/CNN

Troubling to the Christian leaders is that moral and financial support for the settlement growth is coming from many individuals faithful to “Christian Zionism.” In January, the Patriarchs and Heads of the Churches in Jerusalem issued a statement calling it a “damaging” ideology.

Christian Zionists see Scripture as telling them to support Jews living across the Holy Land to hasten a Second Coming of Christ, the end of the world, and transition to an eternal afterlife for Christians.

Among the most prominent faith-centered organizations supporting Israeli settlements are US-based evangelical groups Christians United for Israel (CUFI), and Christian Friends of Israeli Communities (CFOIC), both of which highlight Bible verses for their missions.

CFOIC says it supports 80 Israeli “communities” in the occupied West Bank, which it calls by the Biblical names of Judea and Samaria. On its website, it urges supporters to “give generously, so that the communities of Biblical Israel may flourish.”

Kimberly Troup, director of the US office for CFOIC, told CNN she was friends with a pastor in Bethlehem and understood that Palestinian Christians had left Bethlehem because of Muslim persecution, not the actions of Israel.

Armenian Christians process through the streets of the Old City, Jerusalem. Scott McWhinnie/CNN

In an email she wrote: “Christian Zionism is an authentic expression of Biblical beliefs grounded in the Bible, which, as Christians, we believe is the word of God. Being a Christian Zionist means following God’s word as stated in the Bible that He gave the Land of Israel to the Jewish people.”

Isaac argues that this does not consider the reality of life on the ground, that the land in question is already home to Christians and Muslims.

“Given the threat of settlers over our lives these days — an actual threat against our lives as Palestinian Christians — these are Christians who are funding and supporting the major threat on our existence in the land today,” Isaac said. “What this shows is, again, that we are not in their plan. They don’t think of us. They don’t see us.”

CUFI said in an emailed statement that it supported the Israeli government and declined to respond to Isaac.

The sun rises over Jerusalem. Scott McWhinnie/CNN Father Munther Isaac lights a candle and prays inside the Bethlehem Christmas Lutheran Church Scott McWhinnie/CNN

Isaac jokes that it is as if evangelicals including US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, himself a Baptist minister, are living in the 7th Century BCE.

In a statement to CNN, Huckabee rejected Isaac’s criticism, and said he personally knew Palestinian Christians who were themselves Christian Zionists.

“No one overlooks the experiences of Palestinian Christians in the Holy Land. But Evangelicals believe the Bible — ALL of it,” Huckabee continued. “It’s not a cafeteria where we pick and choose what fits our own prejudices and desires. There is nothing ‘racist’ about believing what the Bible clearly says about God’s promises to the Jews, and the Jewish faith is the foundation of the Christian faith. I hope Rev. Isaac joins evangelicals in calling for an adherence to the authority of Scripture.”

Younger evangelicals have different views

A shrine inside the 5th Century St. George’s Church in Taybeh. Scott McWhinnie/CNN

Isaac proselytizes through social media, doing interviews and traveling to the US for conferences where he can appeal for people to learn about the Palestinian Christian existence.

“I think many evangelicals are warming up to our perspective,” he said.

“We’re not coming into this discussion by saying, ‘Forget the Bible. Let’s talk about politics.’ It’s not our approach. Our approach is ‘Let’s read the Bible together,’ but let’s also read it with Palestinian Christians and connect it to the reality on the ground.”

Last year, Isaac spoke at Wheaton College, one of America’s best-known evangelical institutions, while touring his book “Christ in the Rubble.” For him, invitations from traditionally conservative evangelical spaces suggest younger Christians are increasingly willing to question long-held assumptions.

Polling appears to reflect that shift. A 2025 University of Maryland study found that 51% of older evangelical Americans sympathized more with Israelis than Palestinians, compared with 24% of younger evangelicals.

Isaac is now supported by some converts, including Ben Norquist, who said he accepted Christian Zionism as a legitimate narrative while growing up in Minnesota, and never really thinking of who could be negatively affected.

“Palestinians were invisible to me,” he recalled to CNN, saying his viewpoint only changed in his 20s when he began engaging with the stories of Palestinians and eventually travelled to the Holy Land for his PhD focusing on higher education in the Palestinian territories.

“Something that’s important about what happened for me is that that process didn’t make me less Christian, so to speak. I didn’t ever question the foundations of my faith. What it felt like was I was actually discovering a truer version of what Jesus calling us to all along, and that’s how I feel even today.”

Father Bashar Fawadleh has seen many parishioners leave the Christian town of Taybeh. Scott McWhinnie/CNN

Both Isaac and Fawadleh believe they have a special role to play as Christians in the Holy Land.

Fawadleh welcomes all to visit. “As Jesus invited the two disciples of John the Baptist, come and see. Hear our stories,” he said.

Isaac echoed the peaceful call. “We feel the weight of history upon our shoulders to continue the Christian presence and message from the place where it all started, and that message has to be one of love your neighbor, justice, and peacemaking.”

World.title: Tomorrow is here
World.content:
I’ve been concerned for some time now about the pace of global change.

​

This pace continues to accelerate and, frankly, under the general human radar, confronting humanity with unprecedented challenges.

​

So how do we manage what we don’t know?

My simple answer is to continue to dig, research, engage, and have significant persistence to connect the dots.

I continue searching answers as the majority of humanity sleepwalks to its fate.

​

Many ask me why I invest time, energy, and resources in this task, and my only answer is that it is my genes that guide me and primarily my fate.

​

Seated by and gazing at the powerful flow of the Chao Phraya River in Bangkok, I had a feeling of serenity engulfed by the river’s ceaseless ongoing in all directions.

​

My thoughts took me to the eight developments seriously underway, to which we are not paying enough attention to the impact.

​

I feel we are at the stage Alvin Toffler described in his book Future Shock back in 1970, when the idea of a smart cell phone was bubbling under the surface but had yet to emerge, and how that instrument has impacted human beings across the globe.

​

The eight underway developments I have recognized are, in no specific order:

Artificial Intelligence

Biotechnology

Cloning

Fact versus Fiction

Humanoid robots

Autonomous Intelligence

Space

Quantum Computing

In a general sense, everyone believes that they understand “AI”. That it may take some jobs away, accelerate efficiency, reduce costs, etc. But there is a much more sinister aspect of AI that has already been reached, which is still not in the public domain.

​

Insofar as “biotech” is concerned, all you have to do is research Jennifer Doudna, an American biochemist who pioneered CRISPR gene editing and a 2020 Nobel Prize winner who can alter the genes of human beings.

Tiffany Vora on the other hand, has immense knowledge of the microbiome, space biology, the impact of viruses that are significantly worse than COVID and biohacking, which can be devastating.

​

As for cloning, advances in this field remain largely undercover to date. However, circumstances allowed me to experience what a friend has done and how a clone is not only physically the same but has the same character.

​

Over 15 years ago, I wrote about the threat of being incapable of differentiating fact from fiction. Just as I wrote before about the need to authenticate the use of the internet. Both to avoid the damaging use of fiction dressed in real facts.

The faking of voice and physical imaging have reached a stage of serious danger and complexity which will only become more difficult to see through.

​

Last month at a board meeting, there were nine human beings and one humanoid robot (a machine with an appearance, form, and characteristics that resemble a human being) that was six feet tall and quite dominating in a polite way. It corrected facts, brought forward research and global statistics, provided background, and took notes.

I say no more to the impact of this humanoid presence.

​

It is a fact that autonomous intelligence is already with us, and its system can set goals, make decisions, and take action without human supervision. Unlike traditional generative AI, which suggests or creates content, autonomous intelligence can execute multi-step tasks on its own.

It has already reached levels of learning, reasoning, and independent action.

Today, autonomous intelligence is used by the military in many areas, such as selecting targets for bombing, global markets, trading in milliseconds, etc.

​

Space is a frontier we are already a part of in a big way, but which is still not generally recognized. It has significant roles to play in communication, transportation, the military, and much more.

Recognition and regulation of space is a dream that is still far away.

​

Quantum computing is the one development that, when it emerges, will impact the other seven underway developments in a big way, as well as turn upside down all the ongoing activity in cyber, privacy, blockchain, security, crypto, and much more.

​

Having outlined the eight underway developments as I was gazing at the river, I paused, wondering about their impact in today’s world, where the old order that emerged after World War II has disappeared but no new order has emerged, and we live under constant chaos.

​

A sharp knock on the door of my room in the Four Seasons brought my thoughts back to Bangkok. It was three close friends who were coming for a coffee before we went to dinner:

​

Steve Tan is a professor of computer science living and teaching in Singapore. Young, active, and a global traveler.

​

Jacqueline Cavory, an entrepreneur and very successful businesswoman and investor in global companies in Asia, Europe, and the US.

​

Larry O’Callaghan, an Irish American who over the years has innovated, created, and patented multiple manufacturing processes in the aerospace, transportation, and industrial sectors.

​

After ordering coffee and exchanging pleasantries since we had not met in person since 2023, we discussed the state of the world.

Globalization, fragmentation, multilateralism, multipolarity, international security architecture, up to 50 global conflicts, lack of effective global institutions and law, disappearance of soft power and moral compass as well as significant global income inequality and corruption.

​

The conversation got heated at times but was always constructive. Larry remained positive that such challenges would find processes to resolve them. Jacqueline was convinced that this volatility galore was useful for business opportunities but harmful for humanity at large.

Steve, quite cautious, remained worried about any black swan episodes.

We all agreed that the world was moving towards a clear differentiation. Winners, Navigators (middle powers), and Losers.

​

The winner, in spite of all its issues, was America at the top (see my article titled ‘The Lamborghini Theory’), followed by China.

​

The navigators are the middle powers in their regions that will navigate at a cost as these challenges manifest themselves.

These include Russia, India, the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Singapore, and others.

​

The losers we decided not to name.

​

We also agreed that global instability will continue and increase, there will be higher governmental intervention in economics, a less benign environment, no more free markets, anemic growth and economic fragmentation, but no World War III.

​

Jacqueline looked at her watch and declared she was hungry. It was eight pm, and our booking was at 7:30 pm at an Italian restaurant.

We got up and exited towards the elevators.

​

As we were walking down the corridor to the elevators, Jacqueline, Steve, and Larry were discussing their flights tomorrow and their different destinations.

​

I was thinking that human beings have been given everything on this earth. Yet, frankly, we have failed to make this world better for all of us.

Thus, I thought, a future shock awaits us as machines may emerge and become a major player in our world.

That is why I am convinced business and governments must work together seriously to wake up to this reality before our sleepwalking has us facing this development unprepared.

About the author

M. Shafik Gabr is a renowned leader in international business, innovation, investment and one of the world’s premier collectors of Orientalist art, and an accomplished philanthropist.

During his career, Gabr established over 25 companies plus three investment holding companies including ARTOC Group for Investment and Development which, established in 1971, is a multi-disciplined investment holding company with businesses in infrastructure, automotive, engineering, construction and real estate, over the past three years focusing on investment in technology and artificial intelligence.

Gabr is the Chairman and a founding member of Egypt’s International Economic Forum, a member of the International Business Council of the World Economic Forum, a Board Member of Stanhope Capital, an International Chairman of the Sadat Congressional Gold Medal Committee, and a Member of the Parliamentary Intelligence Security Forum.

Gabr is a Member of the Metropolitan Museum’s International Council and serves on the Advisory Board of the Center for Financial Stability, the Advisory Board of The Middle East Institute, and the Global Advisory Council of the Mayo Clinic.

Through the Shafik Gabr Social Development Foundation, Gabr is helping to improve elementary-school education in Egypt, introducing students to arts and culture and promoting sports and physical fitness for youth. The Foundation has its first Medical and Social Development Center in Mokattam, Cairo, offering free medical and health services.

In 2012 Gabr established in the US the Shafik Gabr Foundation which supports educational and medical initiatives plus launched in November 2012 the ‘East-West: The Art of Dialogue initiative promoting exchanges between the US and Egypt with the purpose of cultural dialogue and bridge-building.

Gabr holds a BA in Economics and Management from the American University in Cairo and an MA in Economics from the University of London.

World.title: FM: Egypt backs regional, international efforts to consolidate Somalia’s security, stability
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty reiterated, Egypt’s full support for all regional and international efforts aimed at consolidating Somalia’s security and stability.

He said Egypt is committed to backing Somali state institutions and preserving the country’s unity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, especially as Somalia’s stability represents a key pillar of security and stability in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region, as well as of regional and international peace and security.

Abdelatty made the remarks during his meeting on Friday, July 31, 2026, with Qurat-ul-Ain Sadozai, Acting Assistant Secretary General and Head of the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), on the sidelines of the Second Extraordinary Summit of Troop-Contributing Countries to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), held in the Ugandan capital, Kampala.

The foreign minister stressed the importance of securing sustainable funding for the African Union mission, voicing deep concern over the financial challenges facing the force.

He called on international partners and members of the UN Security Council to continue supporting the mission and ensure it has the logistical and financial resources needed to carry out its mandate effectively.

Abdelatty also underlined the need to maintain both AUSSOM and UNSOS, ensuring their continuity and adequate funding to help preserve Somalia’s security, stability, and unity.

He reaffirmed Egypt’s readiness to continue providing support to Somalia, whether through the African Union mission or bilateral cooperation, drawing on Egypt’s extensive expertise in counterterrorism, border security, and institutional capacity-building to enhance stability in Somalia and the wider region.

World.title: Egyptian, Ugandan FMs discuss bilateral ties, regional issues
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty and his Ugandan counterpart, Haruna Kasolo, discussed on Friday, July 31, 2026, ways to strengthen bilateral ties and coordinate positions on issues of common concern during a meeting held on the sidelines of the Second Extraordinary Summit of Troop-Contributing Countries to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM).

Abdelatty lauded the growing momentum in relations between the two countries and stressed the importance of expanding trade, economic and investment cooperation, particularly in infrastructure, energy, mining, agriculture, aquaculture, water resources management and the pharmaceutical industry.

He also underscored the need to continue efforts to expand the Egyptian medical center in Jinja, while supporting Egyptian companies operating in Uganda and increasing access for Egyptian exports to the Ugandan market.

The foreign minister underlined the significance of swiftly establishing the Egyptian-Ugandan business council as a key step towards boosting bilateral trade and enhancing the economic partnership.

He also expressed Egypt’s interest in expanding cultural and educational cooperation through scholarships, stronger partnerships between universities, and capacity-building programs offered by the Egyptian Agency of Partnership for Development, the Cairo International Center for Conflict Resolution, Peacekeeping and Peacebuilding, and Al-Azhar.

Abdelatty stressed the importance of cooperation and integration among Nile Basin countries to achieve mutual benefit and shared interests, calling for preserving the spirit of consensus and solidarity among the countries of the southern Nile Basin.

He reiterated Egypt’s rejection of unilateral measures in the Eastern Nile Basin and praised Uganda’s efforts during its chairmanship of the Nile Basin Initiative (NBI) consultative process to restore inclusivity and consensus, advance development projects that serve shared interests in line with international law, and safeguard the interests of all Nile Basin states.

The two ministers also exchanged views on regional issues, including developments in Sudan, Somalia and eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, and agreed to strengthen bilateral and multilateral coordination to support peace, stability and development across Africa.

World.title: Egypt wins chairmanship of AI governance, quantum computing working groups at Arab AI Committee
World.content:
Egypt won on Friday, July 31, 2026, the presidency of the AI Governance Working Group and the Quantum Computing Working Group under the Arab Permanent Committee for AI and Emerging Technologies, affiliated with the Arab Ministers of Council for Communications and Information, reflecting Arab trust in Egypt’s growing role in future technologies.

The committee aims to enhance Arab integration in AI and emerging technologies while supporting digital transformation efforts to build an innovation-based knowledge economy and present a unified Arab position in international forums.

Egypt’s election took place during the committee’s second founding meeting in Tunisia, attended by representatives of Arab states alongside regional and international organizations serving as observers.

The committee’s formation implements a resolution issued by the Council of Arab Ministers of Communication and Information during its 29th session hosted by Egypt in January 2026.

The committee is tasked with developing regional policies for AI, supporting digital transformation across sectors, enhancing human capacity building, exchanging expertise, monitoring global technological developments, and periodically evaluating recommendations.

It also prepares strategic frameworks for adopting modern technologies, proposes regional and international agreements, establishes specialized working groups, and coordinates between member states in international arenas.

Comprising six specialized working groups, the committee includes representatives from Arab nations and observer entities, with each working group electing a chair and two deputies from member states.

Egypt previously hosted the committee’s first founding meeting at the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology headquarters last May.

The AI Governance Working Group develops a guidance framework for AI governance, technical tools, and mechanisms for activating the Arab Charter for AI Ethics.

Meanwhile, the Quantum Computing Working Group focuses on drafting an Arab strategy for quantum computing, developing applications, tracking global research, and exploring quantum cybersecurity deployment.

World.title: Inclusive electoral process, flourishes democracy-ECZ
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) says it recognises that an inclusive electoral process is the cornerstone of a thriving democracy.

Speaking during the ECZ Women’s Conference held at Ndola Skills Training Centre in Ndola today, Copperbelt Provincial Electoral Officer, Shaft Musaka, said women are not just participants in elections, but decision-makers, advocates and architects of a brighter future.

Mr Musaka said the Commission has deliberately implemented policies aimed at empowering women at every stage of the electoral process.

“We have strengthened voter education programmes specifically tailored to address barriers that hinder women’s full participation in elections,” he said.

Mr Musaka said the Commission is also actively promoting women’s representation in electoral administration to ensure their voices are heard, valued and integrated into decision-making structures.

He added that the ECZ continues to champion safe, peaceful and fair elections that are free from intimidation and discrimination, enabling women to vote and contest leadership positions with confidence.

Mr Musaka explained that empowering women requires collective action and collaboration, adding that the Commission is working with communities, organisations and other stakeholders to amplify women’s voices, promote civic engagement, and encourage more women to stand as candidates, election observers and advocates for peaceful and credible elections.

“As we embrace this commitment, let us remind ourselves that peace is not just the absence of conflict; it is the presence of justice, equity and opportunity,” he said.

Mr Musaka urged women in Ndola and across the country to actively participate in shaping Zambia’s democratic future.

“Let this Women’s Conference be a call to action for every woman in Ndola and beyond to rise, participate and shape the future of Zambia’s democracy,” he said.

World.title: Hichilema completes ten-province tour amid Kaingu row
World.content:
Hichilema completes ten-province tour with Western Province pledges as independent candidate Kaingu accuses him of overreach

President Hakainde Hichilema has concluded a nationwide community outreach campaign by pledging a sweep of infrastructure and economic projects for Western Province, becoming the first presidential candidate in the 2026 general election to campaign in all ten provinces. But the closing leg of his tour has also drawn sharp criticism after he urged voters in Mwandi not to support independent parliamentary candidate Iris Kaingu, prompting accusations that he overstepped his role as head of state.

Speaking during engagements in Shang’ombo, Nalolo, Limulunga and Senanga, President Hichilema said his government’s focus for Western Province would be on infrastructure and economic projects that create jobs, improve livelihoods and strengthen cross-border trade with Angola. He told supporters in Shang’ombo that the district’s strategic location and natural resources gave it the potential to become one of Zambia’s most prosperous border towns.

“I see the potential of developing Shang’ombo into a very successful town. We are going to improve the border post so that people trade well with Angola and some of you will be employed there,” he said.

He announced plans to establish an abattoir in the district to allow livestock farmers to process beef locally for export, expand agricultural production to boost food security, improve telecommunications through additional mobile towers, modernise the Shang’ombo airstrip, construct a new market with reliable water supply, establish more boarding secondary schools and build a skills training centre for young people. He also pledged to rehabilitate the Shang’ombo-Rivungo canal through construction of a harbour and related facilities.

The President said the creation of a second constituency in Shang’ombo had already increased Constituency Development Fund allocations from K40 million to K80 million, allowing for faster investment in schools, health facilities, feeder roads and water projects. He said upgrading the Sioma-Shang’ombo road remained a priority.

In Nalolo, he said economic growth would be driven by expanded agricultural productivity, timely Farmer Input Support Programme payments through mobile money platforms, and improved road networks. He pledged to improve mobile network coverage, construct a district hospital, complete government offices and staff houses, and recruit more teachers and health workers.

In Limulunga, President Hichilema said Western Province had enormous untapped potential and announced plans to establish a milk-processing plant, expand fisheries into a commercial enterprise, complete Lewanika University, upgrade Mongu Airport into an international facility, and advance plans for the proposed Sioma Hydro-power Station.

“The upgrading of the Mongu airport is starting soon and we will continue to develop for our people. Running a country is not a joke, one must have the love for the people,” he said.

UPND Liuwa parliamentary candidate and former Finance and National Planning Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane said President Hichilema had demonstrated commitment to Western Province through continued investment in infrastructure and social programmes, and urged residents to support UPND to ensure development programmes continue.

In Senanga, the President apologised for arriving late due to a demanding schedule and appealed to voters to support UPND, saying this would ensure continuity of programmes including free education. He said upgrading the Senanga-Maata road remained a key priority.

The engagements marked the conclusion of the President’s nationwide community outreach programme, which he began earlier in the campaign season and which took him to all ten provinces ahead of the 13 August vote.

However, the tour’s final stretch has been overshadowed by controversy following remarks President Hichilema made in Mwandi on Thursday, where he urged residents not to vote for Iris Kaingu, an aspiring independent parliamentary candidate, because she defied his advice not to contest outside the UPND.

Kaingu, reacting to the remarks, said Zambians have the right to choose the person they want to vote for and should not be forced to support a candidate they do not want. She said she was shocked that the Head of State would attack her in such a manner when she was merely exercising her democratic right to contest as an independent.

“I cannot believe the president came all the way to de-campaign me even when the people of Mwandi have clearly indicated that they do not want the UPND candidate,” she said.

Kaingu also pushed back on the suggestion that Western Province remains loyal UPND territory, arguing that the party’s traditional support base in the province has been eroded by continued underdevelopment.

“If Western Province is UPND’s bedroom, then it is a dirty bedroom, because the people in the province are now suffering, as infrastructure is in a deplorable state,” she said.

Movement for Multi-Party Democracy national secretary Lumba Kalumba condemned the President’s remarks as an affront to democracy, saying that calling an adult woman a “difficult child” and labelling her difficult for refusing to obey was not mere rhetoric but language of subordination.

“It frames her as disrespectful for making independent choices. It reinforces the idea that women in politics must be compliant, not assertive; obedient, not ambitious. A democratic President does not dictate who may or may not stand. He does not use state and party platforms to bully opponents, especially women. He competes on issues, not on intimidation,” Kalumba said in a statement.

She said labelling a woman a “difficult child” set a dangerous precedent for Zambian democracy. “This is not strong leadership. It is an infringement on women’s rights, democratic rights, and the basic principles of a free and fair election,” Kalumba said.

The controversy has also drawn editorial criticism. An opinion piece published this week argued that the remarks in Mwandi sit uneasily alongside the President’s repeated declarations of commitment to increasing women’s participation in leadership, noting that the Constitution expressly recognises independent candidates as a legitimate category of contestant, not a violation of party loyalty.

President Hichilema‘s tour of Western Province, and the broader ten-province outreach it capped, has been framed by his campaign as evidence of a leader personally engaged with every corner of the country ahead of polling day. But the Mwandi remarks have instead become the dominant talking point in the campaign’s closing fortnight, with critics arguing that a sitting president using his platform to campaign against an independent candidate raises questions about the boundaries between incumbency and electoral fairness that voters will now weigh alongside the infrastructure pledges themselves

World.title: Two funerals, two flashpoints: politics intrudes on mourning
World.content:
“No life is worth losing for power,” Chief Chisunka warns as funerals become flashpoints and party accuses police of standing by

Traditional leaders, a Catholic priest and an opposition party chairman have issued pointed warnings against rising political violence ahead of the 13 August general election.

Their intervention comes after two funerals in Eastern and Southern provinces this week descended into standoffs over party politics.

Chief Chisunka of the Ushi people of Luapula said no life is worth losing for the sake of power. He called on politicians to rein in their cadres before the country is set alight.

“We don’t have to lose lives just for certain people to cling to power. Peace needs to prevail because the country has been a beacon of hope,” the chief told The Mast.

He said it was unfortunate that parts of the nation were experiencing bloodshed in what he described as a Christian country. Politicians, he said, needed to sober up and tame their cadres before Zambia is drawn into wider conflict.

The Ushi traditional leader called on chiefs countrywide to rise to the occasion and denounce political violence wherever it occurs.

Catholic priest Father Gladson Phiri echoed the call. He said the church and traditional leaders are best placed to lead the fight against political violence because they deal directly with the citizens who go on to engage in political activity.

“The church and traditional leaders are the ones that should champion the fight against political violence because they usually deal with the masses who in turn engage in various political activities,” Fr Phiri said.

He said clergy and chiefs needed to engage both politicians and the electorate on the dangers of violence, warning that the country risked being set ablaze if the trend continues unchecked.

The warnings came in the same week that two funerals turned into flashpoints, illustrating how deeply campaign season has begun to intrude on ordinary community life.

In Aslot Township, Chipata District, mourners stormed out of Mgwelo Maplot Cemetery on Wednesday. The walkout came the moment a UPND official was called upon to address the gathering.

Both the ruling party and the opposition National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity had contributed toward funeral arrangements for the deceased. UPND gave K400; NRPUP reportedly covered other costs, including transport.

The solemn atmosphere shattered when director of ceremony Goldwin Soko announced that the UPND representative would give remarks. Without warning, a section of mourners rose and left the graveyard in a show of disapproval.

“When funerals are politicised and become battlegrounds, then we have a problem,” Alakwisa Jere, a Chipata-based mourner who witnessed the scene, told The Mast.

The Chipata walkout came barely a day after a similar episode in Mazabuka.

There, District Commissioner Oliver Mulomba was booed by angry residents on Tuesday and forced to abandon his speech. The crowd accused him of campaigning for President Hakainde Hichilema and the UPND at a funeral.

Mr Mulomba had to leave the scene to avoid possible harm.

Jere warned that the Chipata and Mazabuka incidents were a sign of what could unfold as campaigning intensifies in the final stretch before polling day. Leaders from both UPND and opposition parties have since appealed for calm, urging cadres and officials to keep politics out of funerals and other community gatherings.

Separately, Leadership Movement national chairperson David Kalumba accused the Zambia Police Service of failing to act against known perpetrators of political violence.

“Police officers have become spectators of violence,” he said in a statement.

He said his party had campaigned throughout the country encouraging people to reject violence and demand accountability, but that police had “betrayed people it is supposed to protect by failing to stop violence.”

Kalumba said no one should celebrate the destruction of public and private property currently taking place in parts of the country at the hands of political cadres. Zambians, he warned, must reject political violence at all costs, because the aftermath would be difficult to rebuild from.

He stressed that his own party was not a violent movement but a pro-poor organisation focused on building a Zambia with equal job and business opportunities for all.

“Our people have told us that all they want is peace, unity and development, and that is the message we are preaching,” he said.

The Leadership Movement chairman said his party had learnt a great deal on the 2026 campaign trail. Poverty, underdevelopment and lack of opportunity, he said, remain a disease afflicting many communities, particularly in rural areas he accused previous leadership of excluding from the national development agenda.

“Our people in rural areas need development but they cannot see it because previous leadership have excluded them from national development agenda,” Kalumba said.

He pledged that, if voted into office, his party would open access to rural development, working toward better roads, schools, markets, hospitals and clinics for rural communities.

Kalumba said the rural population should remain the main focus for the next five years, noting that the rural vote is larger than the urban vote on the current voter register.

Taken together, the warnings from traditional and religious leaders and the accusations levelled by the Leadership Movement chairman paint a picture of mounting anxiety over the tone of the campaign’s final fortnight. Community leaders are now openly worried that political competition could spill into the kind of bloodshed Zambia has largely avoided in recent electoral cycles.
