World.title: More for MSMEs
World.content:
WILLIAMS... it is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica.

ONLY about one per cent of the Government’s annual procurement spending currently reaches micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), a disparity Finance Minister Fayval Williams says the upgraded Government of Jamaica Electronic Procurement portal (GOJEP 2.0) is intended to address. The platform will increase MSME access to public contracts.

Speaking during Thursday’s launch of the updated digital procurement portal, Williams said the modernised system eliminates outdated technical requirements, and creates more opportunities for local businesses to access a share of the Government’s roughly $470-billion annual procurement spend.

“Let me put the scale in perspective. Each year, the Government of Jamaica spends roughly US$3 billion — translated into Jamaican dollars, that’s about $470 billion, depending on the currency at any point in time – and this procures goods, services, and works from the private sector. This is close to, I think, about 13 per cent of our GDP (gross domestic product). And yet, of that enormous sum, only about one per cent reaches our micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises,” the minister pointed out.

“That imbalance is exactly what we are determined to correct so that more Jamaican businesses can share in the billions that Government spends each year, particularly as we rebuild in the wake of Hurricane Melissa. So every procurement decision carries real responsibility. It must inspire public confidence, deliver value for money, create economic opportunity, and make certain that every dollar entrusted to Government works harder for the people we serve,” she said during the event held at AC Hotel Kingston.

According to Williams, GOJEP 2.0 is an upgraded version of the Government’s online system for buying goods, works and services from the private sector. She explained that the remodelling of the digital portal will see the removal of outdated barriers, put in place stronger record keeping aimed at making the process faster and more transparent.

“It’s easier to use. You no longer need to install extra software just to submit a bid. You log in from any ordinary web browser on any device, including your phone. It’s better connected. The system now talks to other government systems, so the same information doesn’t have to be entered twice, it keeps a proper record digitally,” explained the minister.

“Every key decision made during evaluation is captured and tracked automatically instead of living in a paper file or in someone’s memory. It cuts duplicate paperwork for government staff, and it collects far better data on how long procurements take, how much competition is there, and how well our small business set-asides are working,” Williams added.

She also pointed out that bidders and buyers will now be able to follow opportunities that the government brings to market, and see who ultimately wins the work. Furthermore, she assured that GOJEP 2.0 was not the finished product, noting that upgrades will continue overtime.

“It is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica. And, over the next years, we will build a fully integrated end-to-end digital procurement system, one that connects planning, tendering, evaluation, contract management, supplier performance, and payment.

“Imagine in a year or two being able to open GOJEP and see the goods, works, and services that government intends to buy over the coming years. A business could then prepare, assess its capacity, build partnerships, secure certification, arrange financing, and position itself to compete. For our MSMEs especially, that advanced visibility can be the difference between watching from the sidelines and winning the work,” said the finance minister.

Meanwhile, Chief Public Procurement Policy Officer Jovell Barrett also highlighted the gap that exists for MSMEs, pointing out that of the 300,000 active businesses registered with the Companies Office of Jamaica, less than 10,000 unique people and entities are awarded government contracts each year.

“Government is one of the largest purchasers of goods, works and services. And so, the question that we have asked ourselves at the Office of Public Procurement Policy is how many Jamaican businesses see government as a potential customer? How many entrepreneurs look to the public procurement system as an opportunity? And perhaps most importantly, how many do not see public procurement as an opportunity — and if they don’t, why?” said Barrett.

He hailed Thursday’s launch of GOJEP 2.0 as an opportunity to ensure that every taxpaying Jamaican has a fair chance to participate in the public procurement process.

“That’s the vision that I have and that’s what I want to see as a Jamaican. Why? I want to see more Jamaicans participating in public procurement. When public procurement operates as I want to see it happen… small businesses, hundreds and thousands of them in each community, [will] become a mechanism through which public procurement will work best and will be able to develop our economy more. It becomes the instrument of change that Government really wants it to be. That is the power of public procurement,” he said.

World.title: Dexta Daps stays true
World.content:
Dexta Daps.

As thousands of patrons prepare to descend on Montego Bay for Dream Wknd, few performers arrive with the kind of anticipation that surrounds Dexta Daps.

Over the past decade the dancehall star has built one of the genre’s most devoted followings by staying true to the soulful, emotionally driven sound that first set him apart.

“Staying true to the vibe that started my career and keeping the music honest and relatable,” he says when asked about the secret to his longevity. “I evolve with the production sounds, but I don’t chase trends; solid melodies, real emotion, and a performance that connects with the audience is always the goal.”

In a genre that constantly reinvents itself, Dexta Daps has remained relevant by refining his craft rather than reinventing his identity. As production styles and audience tastes have evolved, he has focused on strengthening the qualities that first resonated with listeners.

His creative process, however, has never stood still.

“It’s ever-evolving,” he explains. “I’ve continued to sharpen my sense of arrangement and storytelling while balancing intimate, soulful moments with the dancehall energy.”

That balance has become one of his defining trademarks. Whether delivering emotionally charged ballads or high-energy dancehall records, he has demonstrated an ability to connect with audiences on multiple levels, creating music that feels both deeply personal and widely relatable.

As with any artiste whose career has spanned several years, thoughts inevitably turn to legacy. For Dexta Daps, the impact he leaves extends far beyond chart success or hit records.

“If fans only remembered one thing about my career years from now,” he says, “I’d want it to be that I gave people real, heartfelt music that resonated beyond the dance songs, music that felt honest and performances that stayed with them.”

That same commitment to delivering memorable performances is what fans can expect when he takes the stage at Dream Wknd, one of the Caribbean’s premier entertainment festivals, which runs from July 30-August 3 this year.

Sharing the stage with Dexta Daps at Dream’s Montego Bay debut are some of the biggest names in dancehall, including Alkaline, Tommy Lee, Govana, Shaneil Muir, Tifa, Elephant Man, General B, Jamal, Skeng, and Armanii, alongside a number of international acts.

“It’s always great to share the stage with so much talent,” he says. “It’s about representing the culture well and keeping the energy high for the crowd. I don’t take that for granted.”

While he remains tight-lipped about exactly what fans can expect, he hints that patrons should be prepared for something special.

“Always a few surprises,” he says with a laugh. “However, I can’t reveal them because then it wouldn’t be a surprise.”

Looking beyond the summer, Dexta Daps’s focus remains firmly on creating new music while continuing to expand his reach internationally.

“More music, working on an album,” he responds.

So, with new music, an album in the works, and another Dream Wknd appearance on the horizon, Dexta Daps is continuing to build a career rooted in authenticity, one heartfelt performance at a time.

World.title: DOLPHIN COVE’S US$2.5-M LIFT
World.content:
Visitors interact with dolphins at one of Dolphin Cove Limited’s Jamaican attractions. The company has added approximately US$2.53 million to its net book value following a revaluation of its Jamaican properties

DOLPHIN Cove Limited has added approximately US$2.533 million to its net book value after revaluing its Jamaican properties, an adjustment disclosed while its majority shareholder has agreed to sell its controlling stake and is seeking to add four directors.

Property Consultants Limited valued the group’s Jamaican land and buildings as at March 31, but its report reached Dolphin Cove’s board after the company had published its first-quarter financial statements.

The appraisal increases the carrying value of property, plant and equipment by approximately US$2.576 million. After adjustments to deferred taxation, the net increase in Dolphin Cove’s book value is approximately US$2.533 million.

Applied to the previously reported March figures, the adjustment would lift property, plant and equipment from approximately US$26.65 million to US$29.23 million and shareholders’ equity from US$27.39 million to approximately US$29.92 million, before any other second-quarter movements.

The increase is equivalent to approximately nine per cent of the equity Dolphin Cove reported at the end of March.

It is an accounting adjustment rather than new income or cash. Dolphin Cove said the revaluation has no effect on revenue, operating results or cash flow for the period.

The revised values will be reflected in the company’s financial statements for the six months ended June 30.

Dolphin Cove did not identify the individual Jamaican properties covered by the appraisal, disclose their separate values or say whether the updated figures were considered in the proposed sale of the company’s controlling stake.

The transaction under way is a sale of shares in Dolphin Cove rather than a direct sale of the properties.

World of Dolphins Inc agreed on July 9 to sell all 313,901,858 Dolphin Cove shares it owns to Global Attractions Limited, a Saint Lucia company incorporated in March. The shares represent 79.99 per cent of Dolphin Cove.

Neither the purchase price nor the expected completion date has been disclosed. Completion is subject to conditions, including arrangements for the refinancing and discharge of Dolphin Cove’s existing credit facility with Sagicor Bank Jamaica Limited. The beneficial owners of Global Attractions, its financing arrangements and its plans for Dolphin Cove also remain unknown.

The property adjustment has now been announced as World of Dolphins seeks to add four directors to the listed company’s board.

The majority shareholder has nominated Colin Kerr, Darys Estrella, Alberto Bergés González and Sylvain Dominici for election, according to a notice signed by World of Dolphins representative and Dolphin Cove director Steven Strom.

Dolphin Cove has not published biographies of the nominees, explained their connections to World of Dolphins or said whether any of them is associated with Global Attractions.

It also has not explained why the selling shareholder is seeking to expand the board before the ownership transaction is completed.

The nominations were scheduled for consideration at Dolphin Cove’s annual general meeting on Thursday, July 30, at The Courtleigh Hotel & Suites.

However, the chairman was expected to seek shareholders’ consent to adjourn the meeting to allow investors at least 14 days’ notice of the proposed appointments. The outcome was unavailable at press time.

If shareholders approve the adjournment, the resumed meeting would be held between August 13 and August 28. The exact date has not been announced.

Based on Dolphin Cove’s latest public disclosures, electing all four nominees would expand its five-member board to nine if the present directors remain in office.

World of Dolphins currently holds enough shares to determine the outcome of the elections if it votes its 79.99 per cent stake. That could change if the sale is completed or the voting rights are transferred before the adjourned meeting.

Once completed, the acquisition will trigger a mandatory offer allowing minority shareholders to sell their shares to the new controlling owner. The price and other terms have not been published.

Dolphin Cove said its properties in Saint Lucia and the Turks and Caicos Islands will also be revalued. It did not say when those appraisals would be completed or whether it expects them to increase or reduce the assets’ carrying values.

World.title: ‘He who has the gold’
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (centre) addresses a round table press briefing at the end of the FIFA Executive Summit at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James in January 2018. Also pictured are Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts (left) and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani.

Veteran administrator Tony James says FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s proposal to privatise world football is “underhanded”, but cautions that developing nations under severe financial stress will find the promised US$40-million payout nearly impossible to resist.

James, who led the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) from 1985 to 1992 and has spent over 50 years working in football, offered a sharp critique of Infantino’s proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). Under the plan, FIFA aims to create a private commercial entity valued at US$20 billion (over $3 billion) to handle broadcasting, ticketing, sponsorship, and hospitality rights for competitions like the World Cup. Developed alongside JP Morgan, the strategy involves selling up to 21 per cent to private equity investors — led by Joshua Kushner’s firm, Thrive Eternal — to raise US$4.2 billion (roughly $665 billion) in upfront capital. Kushner is the brother of US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

To win over member nations, FIFA offered a substantial payout of increasing baseline development funding from US$10 million (over $1.5 billion) to US$20 million (over $3 billion) per nation for the 2027-2030 cycle. Associations could also access an additional US$20 million upfront through a new FIFA Fast Forward Programme for infrastructure, putting up to US$40 million on the table per country ahead of a September 19 deadline. Infantino, however, warned that member nations declining support would continue to receive the baseline.

While continental governing bodies have moved to block the move, James says that for smaller member associations, the financial reality takes precedence.

“It is underhanded, and the cynical view is being reinforced by the way it is being proposed now,” James told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday. “He who has the gold makes the rule. That’s how people perceive of it; that it’s the current way of the world. You’re trumping (pardon the pun) institutionalised good governance structures, integrity, etcetera. That’s what’s being put out in the public now.”

Despite the governance concerns, James says smaller associations operate in a vastly different financial reality than European giants.

“This US$40 million for each affiliate will have traction in all the poorer and developing countries,” he said. “The focus will be on CAF [Confederation of African Football], and Concacaf, which includes the Caribbean, but it’s also the poorer countries in Asia and UEFA.

“UEFA’s principled position is understandable, but it’s fortunate in having three financial platforms. One is the World Cup, like everybody else, and their teams are the top of the heap. Let us call them Category A teams because they’re the ones who are going to get most of the money. All of the rest of us are Category B and C teams that should get money, but not like the A teams.”

James’s comments come as global opposition to Infantino’s scheme reaches a boiling point. After an emergency meeting, Concacaf — the governing body for North America, Central America, and the Caribbean — unanimously voted down the proposed enterprise plan, joining European governing body UEFA in open revolt. Concacaf made its announcement moments after the Observer’s interview with James.

In its official statement, Concacaf mentioned severe procedural failures surrounding the proposal.

“During the meeting, the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies,” Concacaf said on its website. “In addition, the need for private equity investment to fund new and existing FIFA Forward programmes following the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history was questioned.”

Concacaf confirmed all 41 member associations rejected the deal after UEFA’s warning that it would pull its teams from FIFA competitions entirely.

“As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” UEFA said on its website on Thursday.

Despite Concacaf’s joint rejection, local sentiments reflect exactly what James described.

JFF President Michael Ricketts rejected all of the Observer’s calls to him seeking a comment, and declined to respond to questions posed on WhatsApp.

However, while speaking to Nationwide Sports, he struck a far more open tone regarding the commercial structure.

“I have not discussed it with my directors, but my personal feeling is that, on the face of it, I really don’t think that anything is wrong with it,” Ricketts said. “It’s workable. But the big problem I’m having is the — for want of a better word — non-transparent way in which it was done. We would’ve spent so much time together with the leadership of FIFA before, during, and after the World Cup, and we were never apprised of these discussions, and this would bring to the fore some level of non-transparency.”

Ricketts’s pragmatic view is tied directly to local circumstances. He told the Observer in an interview on July 14 that the JFF is strapped for cash after a costly, unsuccessful World Cup qualifying campaign. He also said in that interview that he would fully support Infantino’s plan to expand the World Cup to 64 teams as early as the 2030 tournament as it would provide a greater chance of qualification for Jamaica.

A US$40-million windfall would completely alter local operations. Furthermore, with Jamaica actively bidding to co-host the 2031 Women’s World Cup with the US, Mexico, and Costa Rica, maintaining good relations with FIFA ahead of Infantino’s re-election bid in March remains a practical priority.

While acknowledging the lifelines that FIFA funds provide, James warned that dumping millions into unprepared administrative set-ups brings serious risks.

“Regrettably, I don’t think most developing countries have an administrative structure to deal with this kind of money. They don’t,” he said. “You also have to ask, given our system, how much of this US$40 million would actually reach football development, because human nature says when you have money, it’s about a source of power, greed, corruption, football politics, and that syphons off the money.”

And on whether Infantino’s tactics amount to using FIFA’s massive wealth to secure political survival ahead of the upcoming presidential vote, James gave a blunt assessment of how the global game operates.

“He has been a disgrace,” James said. “But in a new world where the golden rule applies, when he hits FIFA and hits the politics, what do you think they’re going to say to him? When he tells them how much he has earned off this World Cup, that the vision was his, the planning was his, what he has had to do, ‘Listen, we had problems here and there, but at the end of the day, look at what I have done for you. Look at what FIFA has done for you. Who are you going to vote for?’ What do you think is going to be the response? It’s all about performance. Let’s face it, he has performed.”

World.title: 2026 Isuzu D-MAX: Built to last
World.content:
The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the Isuzu D-MAX pickup continues in 2026. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Isuzu has long been one of the darlings of the commercial vehicle sector, having built a reputation for durability, reliability, and longevity over its long history.

The D-MAX pickup is endowed with these characteristics, and for 2026 continues to be so.

EXTERIOR

The four-door cab pickup is based mostly on function rather than form. Redesigned from the ground up, Isuzu calls it their ‘Spirit of Truck’ DNA, giving the D-MAX a masculine and no-nonsense look from its wide stance and wedge-shaped body lines. However, function over form still rules, and the D-MAX uses aerodynamic integration of the lower body to boost fuel efficiency and reduce wind noise. For those wanting style, up to 18-inch wheels can be had.

INTERIOR

Inside the new spacious cabin it reflects the working nature of the D-MAX. There’s a quality impression and the presence of durability to the cabin. There’s a mixture of hard-wearing plastics, with soft-touch materials at the main points of user contact. Ergonomics is a key word, with simple large buttons for the main functions to be accessed with ease under all conditions, and feel like they’ll be working for years to come.

Storage is plentiful for those who have to work. The deep centre console will swallow important gear, as will the dual gloveboxes. Cup holders and door pockets that all can hold a 1.5-litre bottle further contribute to the ability to hold personal cargo. The D-MAX has redesigned seats with improved internal materials for higher comfort, and better lateral support to increase occupant, especially driver, comfort.

The infotainment is similarly focused, using USB-C for smartphone-run connectivity and services.

ON THE ROAD

Powered by a 3-litre turbodiesel, the D-MAX is not lacking in this area. With 190bhp and 332lb/ft of torque, it manages to be both frugal and powerful. This is because there is tons of low-end torque to effortlessly pull the D-MAX along in the situations it’s built to operate in.

Boost response is good, and it rarely has to be taken into the higher rpms for more power. On road, this keeps engine noise and vibration low so as not to upset passengers in the cabin, meaning a strong case for prolonged on-road use.

But the D-MAX didn’t get its reputation for its on-road manners. Off-road, it has the ability to match the class leaders, because it’s all under the skin with a chassis boasting greater torsional and longitudinal rigidity. The same suspension that smooths out rough roads and can deal with highway travel can easily handle tough terrain with or without payload.

Rookie or professional, the D-MAX gives confidence in challenging situations, delivering up to 800 millimetres of wading depth, 30 degrees of approach angle, 22.9 degrees of breakover, and 24.2 degrees of departure angle. Being equipped with 2WD, 4WD, and 4WD Low, plus a rear differential, few things can slow, even stop, the D-MAX on a trail.

VERDICT

The D-MAX retains the ethos of the Isuzu brand. There’s a reason the company is a commercial equipment manufacturing powerhouse, and that all is installed into their flagship pickup. The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the D-MAX pickup continue without question. 2026 adds some key updates and refinements to keep it a top contender.

World.title: Ceuta crisis: 22 EU leaders gang up against Spain’s Sánchez over his migration policy
World.content:
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the 22 leaders made direct reference to the need for EU-level cooperation on policies such as Madrid’s migrant regularization scheme.

“We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration, by coordinating our action, strengthening our external borders and addressing all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularization of [a] very large number of irregular migrants,” the leaders wrote.

Madrid has pushed back against the claim that the country’s regularization scheme triggered the crisis in Ceuta, and has pointed out that none of the people who illegally entered the exclave would be eligible to benefit from the measure.

“This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said a spokesperson for the Spanish foreign ministry. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June.

But those explanations have not appeared to sway the EU leaders who signed the letter to Costa, Von der Leyen and Martin.

“We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” they went on.

World.title: Labour holds Greater Manchester mayoralty after counting goes to second round
World.content:
Speaking at the Co-Op Live arena to the east of the city, Craig said she stands “ready to serve” her 3 million constituents.

“Every single decision I take as your mayor of Greater Manchester will pass the test of making your life better,” Craig pledged.

The vote was triggered after three-time mayoral contest winner Burnham resigned the job in June to return to Westminster, where he swiftly claimed leadership of the governing Labour Party and became prime minister. There had been concern that Burnham’s move would allow Reform UK — which performed strongly in local elections in England earlier this year — to seize the mayoralty.

Craig will now be have to deal directly with Burnham, who has promised to devolve more powers to England’s mayors as a part of a devolution package. The post currently comes with powers over transport, policing, and housing.

Turnout for the special election was noticeably lower than when Burnham last ran back in 2024, with only 25 per cent of voters heading to the polls this time, compared to 32 per cent at the last vote. POLITICO witnessed some voters on doorsteps Thursday evening learning of the election for the first time.

Counting continued late into the night as the re-instated supplementary voting system took the contest to a second round for the first time ever.

World.title: Almost all of Ceuta migrants have returned to Morocco, Spain says
World.content:
People gather on a hilltop near Bab Sebta on the Morocco-Spain border, near Ceuta and the Moroccan town of Fnideq on July 30, 2026. | Abdelmajid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” an official said.

BRUSSELS — More than 48,300 of the approximately 50,000 people who entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta from Morocco have returned, a Spanish government official told POLITICO.

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, adding that the situation was “on the path back to normality.”

The influx of migrants could be linked to a recent Spanish court ruling that limited the use of the country’s immediate-return procedure for migrants, the official added.

The European Commission said “there are no onward movements towards the European continent or other member states” by the migrants.

World.title: Trump administration slams Spain’s Sánchez for migrant ‘invasion’ of Ceuta
World.content:
“This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe. We are considering actions to defend Americans at home and abroad from this threat and stand ready to assist other European allies considering similar options,” wrote the department.

Sánchez will hardly be surprised by the scathing American reaction, having emerged as the fiercest Trump critic among EU leaders, slamming U.S. military action in the Middle East and barring U.S. military planes from using Spanish air bases.

“Thank God POTUS was elected and our country’s border no longer looks like this. These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West,” wrote U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security made the same argument, saying: “If Spain had their own President Trump, this wouldn’t be an issue.”

The U.S. criticism came as the situation in Ceuta escalated into a Europe-wide political flashpoint in little more than a day. Neighboring governments moved to tighten their response on Friday, with France restoring border checks and Italy calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area, exposing divisions over the bloc’s migration policy.

Former Trump adviser and world’s first trillionaire Elon Musk initially shared a video comparing footage from the Ceuta migrant crisis with scenes from the 2013 zombie film “World War Z.” “Wow, the situation in Spain looks crazy!” he posted.

Clarifying the comparison was a joke, he then shared footage from 2023, showing hundreds of Venezuelan migrants attempting to cross into the U.S., captioning it: “This is what America looked like under Biden.”

World.title: Northern Ireland misses a deadline to fix its budget crisis
World.content:
Bryant, a former Anglican priest who’s never held a Cabinet post before, held his first press conference as Northern Ireland secretary shortly before meeting delegations from the region’s two main government parties, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionists.

Bryant emphasized that the U.K. government expects Stormont to get more bang for its buck by reforming the delivery of local services, most crucially hospital care, where Northern Ireland suffers the worst waiting lists in the entire National Health Service.

“Look, we need to get to a budget,” Bryant said. “And I understand the financial pressures. I know everybody expects me to come with a checkbook. I’m actually coming with a checklist of things that I want to get sorted.”

Sinn Féin, which holds the key finance and economy ministries, has shied from taking any significant decisions on raising local taxes—not that the DUP wouldn’t immediately veto such moves. Nothing much can happen in Northern Ireland’s system of cross-community government unless the largest parties on each side of the divide can agree.

The two parties blame each other for delivering so little and agree that it’s up to the U.K. Treasury to break the budgetary impasse by providing them much more annually to spend. An independent budgetary watchdog, the Northern Ireland Fiscal Council, recently concluded that the region wasn’t being subsidized by English taxpayers to the same levels as in Scotland and Wales — and if it was, Northern Ireland could gain an extra £1 billion to £3.5 billion annually.

While few expect the Burnham administration to come anywhere close to that, both sides in Belfast do expect Bryant to take charge of key budget decisions — which is what his predecessors did when the Northern Ireland Executive collapsed in 2017 from a Sinn Féin walkout, and again in 2022 from a Democratic Unionist walkout.

World.title: London mayor Sadiq Khan accuses Palantir of bypassing procurement rules
World.content:
Palantir claims that Khan’s office blocked the contract unlawfully and “irrationally,” citing comments attributed to the mayor’s spokesperson which referred to the company’s unspecified “values and ethics.”

Louis Mosley, Palantir’s U.K. CEO, has argued that Khan’s decision puts politics above Londoners’ safety, while Met Police Commissioner Mark Rowley has said that the force’s inability to access Palantir’s technology would worsen the impact of cuts to the force’s budget.

In a pre-trial defense statement filed last Thursday and seen by POLITICO, lawyers for MOPAC said Palantir’s claim is “without merit and should be dismissed,” stating that the Met Police “conducted an award process that was unlawful.”

It says the Met Police and Palantir designed a pilot of the technology in 2025 so that the value remained below a £500,000 threshold at which it would have required MOPAC approval. MOPAC, led by Khan’s deputy mayor for policing and crime, oversees the Met Police.

Prior to the conclusion of that pilot in April 2026, the Met Police and Palantir started discussions on directly awarding Palantir a much larger contract to extend the pilot, according to the statement.

The Met Police intended “at each stage” to award the larger contract to Palantir, the statement says, adding that the approach that was “supported/encouraged/assisted” by the company.

World.title: UK to hold budget on Oct. 28, chancellor announces
World.content:
“Fiscal credibility is the bedrock of economic stability and national security,” said the chancellor in the letter. “That is why we will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East.”

Healey also pledged the budget will move “money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.”

Burnham announced today that local English mayors will be given powers to retain and spend business rate taxes to boost growth in their regions.

The prime minister said mayors will soon have power over income taxes, but Healey will unveil a whitepaper and a “roadmap” on the topic at the autumn budget.

World.title: Germany's small islands: nature and slow living almost on your doorstep
World.content:
Germany's lesser-known islands offer exactly what many people are looking for today: less hustle and bustle, more nature and authentic experiences. Whether it's the Wadden Sea on the North Sea coast, a Baltic Sea beach or quiet countryside, for a short break it is often the smaller islands that provide the greatest relaxation.

 

Hiddensee: Baltic Sea island made for slowing down

Hiddensee in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may no longer be a real insider tip among island lovers, but it is still far less well known to many travellers than Rügen or Usedom. The island in the Baltic Sea is only about 17 kilometres long, car-free and best explored by bicycle, horse-drawn carriage or on foot.

The long sandy beaches, dune landscapes and the Dornbusch in the north with its lighthouse are particularly appealing.

The west coast of Hiddensee Sebastian Negraszus, Wikimedia Commons

Ummanz: Island feeling without the island stress

Ummanz lies to the west of Rügen, also in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and is one of the quietest islands in the German Baltic Sea. It is linked to Rügen by a bridge, which makes it especially easy to visit for a short stay.

The flat landscape of meadows, salt marshes and small villages is a paradise for nature lovers and photographers. In autumn, thousands of cranes stop here to rest – a spectacular natural spectacle.

Poel: Baltic Sea holiday without mass tourism

Poel lies between Wismar and the island of Rügen and is often underestimated. This Baltic Sea island offers wide beaches, small villages and a laid-back atmosphere.

Cycle tours along the coast, walks along the cliffs and visits to the historic lighthouse in Timmendorf are particularly popular. Poel is a good alternative for anyone wanting the Baltic Sea experience while avoiding the hustle and bustle of larger resorts.

Timmendorf on the island of Poel at sunset. Daniela Kloth, Wikimedia Commons

Vilm: Germany's little nature island

Vilm, off the coast of Rügen, is one of Germany's most strictly protected islands. Only a limited number of visitors are allowed ashore each day. The island is known for its ancient beech forest, untouched nature and its status as a nature reserve. Visits are only possible on guided tours.

Vilm Island nature reserve M. Anarbaev - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php

Neuwerk: Island holiday in the middle of the Wadden Sea

The small island of Neuwerk belongs politically to Hamburg, but lies around 100 kilometres away in the Wadden Sea off the coast of Lower Saxony. It forms part of the Hamburg Wadden Sea National Park.

At low tide, the island can be reached on foot or by horse-drawn wagon across the mudflats. The historic lighthouse dating back to the 14th century is Neuwerk's landmark. Anyone staying overnight experiences something special: almost complete silence at night and a spectacular starry sky.

East Frisia: A nature paradise with plenty of peace

Baltrum is the smallest of the inhabited East Frisian islands and is often referred to as the "Sleeping Beauty of the North Sea". With an area of less than seven square kilometres, it is easy to explore entirely on foot.

Palisade wall as coastal protection on the East Frisian island of Baltrum. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/

There are no cars here; instead, bicycles, horse-drawn carts and the sound of the sea set the pace. Walks across the mudflats, long strolls along the beach and sweeping views over the North Sea make Baltrum an ideal destination for a short escape.

Langeoog is one of the better-known East Frisian islands, but still feels much quieter than the big North Sea hotspots. The car-free island offers endless sandy beaches, dunes and a rich birdlife.

A short trip to Langeoog is particularly worthwhile in spring or autumn, when there are fewer visitors and walks by the sea are especially impressive.

Spiekeroog is one of the quietest of the East Frisian islands. The car-free island is known for its unspoilt dunes, old lime-tree avenues and its kilometre-long sandy beach. Unlike some of its neighbours, Spiekeroog relies less on large holiday complexes and more on nature, peace and relaxation. Walks through the dunes, mudflat excursions and bike rides are especially popular.

Wangerooge is the easternmost of the inhabited East Frisian islands and is ideal for a long weekend. The island is car-free and, alongside its beaches, offers protected natural areas where you can see seabirds and seals. A particular highlight is the journey on the island railway from the harbour to the village.

Juist, at around 17 kilometres long, is one of the longest East Frisian islands but only a few kilometres wide. With horse-drawn carriages instead of cars, it is wonderfully quiet. Its wide sandbank, the Wadden Sea and endless horizons make Juist a favourite with nature lovers.

The Foto Fitti, Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported license.

Arngast is no longer a classic holiday island, but it is an intriguing destination for outings. The former island in the Jade Bay near Wilhelmshaven is best known for the Arngast lighthouse, which stands in the middle of the Wadden Sea. At low tide, you can discover this unique landscape on guided mudflat walks.

Islands in southern Germany: Time out on Lake Chiemsee

It's not only the North Sea and Baltic Sea that offer island experiences. Southern Germany also has some remarkable islands – right in the foothills of the Bavarian Alps. The Chiemsee islands show that you don't necessarily have to head to the sea for an island escape.

Fraueninsel: Monastery, gardens and Bavarian island charm

Fraueninsel is probably the best-known island on Lake Chiemsee and also one of the most atmospheric. Covering just 15 hectares or so, the island is car-free and easy to explore on foot. Its centrepiece is the historic Benedictine convent Frauenwörth, usually called Frauenchiemsee Abbey, which is still home to nuns today. Founded in 782 by Bavarian Duke Tassilo III, it is one of the oldest surviving convents for women in Germany.

Frauenchiemsee Abbey Allie Caulfield, Chiemsee, Schliersee 025, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php

Alongside the convent, small gardens, old fishermen's houses, narrow paths and numerous arts and crafts shops shape the island's appearance. The combination of lake, mountains and historic architecture gives Fraueninsel its very special atmosphere.

Krautinsel: The quiet nature haven on Lake Chiemsee

Krautinsel is the smallest and at the same time the most original of the three main Chiemsee islands. It is uninhabited and serves primarily as a natural habitat. Its name goes back to its former use: vegetables – especially cabbage – were once grown here to supply the inhabitants of the neighbouring islands.

Today, Krautinsel is above all a retreat for plants and wildlife. The flat, green island with its meadows and reed beds offers a glimpse of how pristine the Chiemsee landscape once was. Landing on the island is not possible – the best way to see it is from a boat or by circling it during a trip on the lake.

It shows that island experiences do not always have to be about beaches and swimming.

Herreninsel: Royal history and nature trails

Herreninsel, at around 230 hectares, is the largest of the Chiemsee islands and is famous for Herrenchiemsee Palace. The Bavarian King Ludwig II began building the palace in 1878, modelled on Versailles – a homage to the French King Louis XIV.

Ferry landing stage on Herrenchiemsee Island By Jannis Raabe - Own work, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=64923231

Away from this main tourist attraction, large parts of Herreninsel are covered by forests and meadows, criss-crossed by quiet walking paths. Anyone who leaves the main routes behind will find peaceful spots with views over the lake and towards the Alps.

World.title: Hamburg celebrates Pride with increased security one week after deadly Berlin attack
World.content:
Hamburg celebrated its annual Pride event, one of Germany's biggest, with increased security on Saturday, one week after a deadly attack near Berlin's pride parade that shocked the country.

 

Organisers expected around 250,000 people to attend the parade, which this year has the motto "Queer in solidarity. Take a stand — for a future without fear."

A late addition to the trucks taking part was one representing the Berlin Pride event — or Christopher Street Day, CSD for short, as the parades are known in Germany. People on that truck were asked to wear dark clothing as a sign of respect for the victims of last week's attack, where one person was killed and 29 others injured.

A reveller holds a placard during the Hamburg Pride 2026, the Christopher Street Day (CSD) parade, in Hamburg, Germany, Saturday Aug. 1, 2026. Georg Wendt/dpa via AP

Late on July 25, a man plowed a van into people a few hundred metres from the closing party of the Berlin Pride event before cutting others with what appears to have been a machete.

The 21-year-old suspect, Abdul Ballout, was killed in a confrontation with police on Sunday. Investigators later found a video in which a person believed to be the suspect claimed responsibility and pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group.

Prosecutors have said Ballout, who was born in Germany and has Lebanese roots, travelled to Lebanon in 2025 with the goal of going to Syria to join IS. He made contact with several people who were presumed members.

Hamburg's police chief said earlier this week that roughly twice as many officers as last year would protect the Hamburg event.

A police officer stands on Steindamm at the edge of Hamburg Pride 2026, the Christopher Street Day (CSD) parade, in Hamburg, Germany, Saturday Aug. 1, 2026. Georg Wendt/dpa via AP

“After the brutal attack on the CSD in Berlin, many are unsure in the queer community but also in society whether here and today is the right place,” Hamburg's deputy mayor, Katharina Fegebank, told RTL television.

“I say, now more than ever, let’s all take to the streets, stand up for diversity, for freedom, for an open society, and above all, in full solidarity with and for the queer community," she added.

"Well, when something like that happens, we all have to show that we’re not afraid, that we won’t let it get us down," said Petra Schwab, who was attending Saturday's Pride in Hamburg.

World.title: Wildfires in Europe: blazes continue to spread in France and Greece
World.content:
A wildfire in France's Provence region continued spreading on Saturday as overnight efforts successfully stopped the blazes from reaching the nearby towns of Correns and Montfort-sur-Argens.

 

Some 1,300 firefighters have been deployed to tackle the blaze, which has flared up again in the Gros Bessillon area, burning approximately 1,250 more hectares since Friday. By the end of the week, authorities said a total of 4,500 hectares had been burnt.

Despite the difficulties, 2,500 people were still unable to return home.

Meanwhile, authorities say France's largest wildfire in 70 years has been brought under control near the southwestern city of Bordeaux.

The Gironde fire has burned 420 square kilometres of pine forest west of the city, an area four times the size of Paris.

Firefighters said it remained contained within that perimeter Saturday, meaning flames had not broken beyond its existing boundaries. But it had not been declared “fixed” — the point at which crews determine that a fire is no longer advancing — and active sectors and buried hot spots persisted.

Twenty French departments were under an orange heat warning Saturday, mostly in the east and southeast. Temperatures of 35 to 39 degree celsius were forecast around the Mediterranean, while eight departments faced a high forest-fire risk.

Residents evacuated in Greece

In Greece, hundreds of firefighters on Saturday were battling to save a popular coastal resort northwest of Athens as violent winds lashed the country, hampering operations.

More than 400 firefighters, backed by several dozen specialised aircraft, were battling blazes in the area of Porto Germeno, the country's fire department said.

According to meteo.gr, the weather service of the National Observatory of Athens, winds up to 130 kilometres per hour were recorded Saturday.

The fire broke out Friday near the neighbouring coastal village of Agios Vasileios. Residents initially ignored a civil protection call to evacuate, and some 300 people had to be rescued by sea.

Wildfires have flared in several parts of the country this week, including on the popular island of Crete, and three firefighters have so far lost their lives.

World.title: Find in German cave: 40,000-year-old mammoth ivory bird figures discovered
World.content:
The two figurines, discovered by a team from the University of Tübingen in the lower layers of the cave, are thought to have been made by people of the Aurignacian culture, who lived in the region during the Upper Palaeolithic.

 

The better preserved of the two carvings depicts a bird at rest, possibly brooding. The other shows a bird with outstretched wings, although the left wing has broken off. Archaeologists found the two figurines only about a metre and a half apart.

Miniature carvings made from mammoth ivory

Both sculptures are so small they would fit on a fingernail and weigh just 1.3 and 0.7 grams respectively. One of them – a bird with outspread wings and a length of only two centimetres – is currently regarded as the smallest known Ice Age artwork ever discovered in the region.

One of the bird figures bears parallel lines on its wing, which are thought to represent feathers. Ralf Ehmann, Universität Tübingen

"Mammoth ivory was not simply used here to create a simplified form of a bird's body," explains Nicholas Conard, an archaeologist at the University of Tübingen and head of the excavations, in a statement. "Detailed observations of nature were translated into figurines whose richness of detail even allows us to investigate which bird species is depicted and what it is doing."

The resting bird, shown stretched out and lying flat, may depict a bird brooding or sitting on a nest of eggs. The second figurine, with its wings spread and neck extended, could show a bird in courtship display, taking off or landing on water.

Ptarmigan or capercaillie?

Archaeologists are still not entirely certain either about the exact species of bird or the behaviours portrayed. One possibility is that the figurines show ptarmigan – a cold-adapted species whose bones are frequently found at prehistoric sites in the region.

However, they might also represent larger, pheasant-like birds such as the capercaillie, a woodland species known for its striking appearance and elaborate courtship rituals. The detailed carvings allow comparisons of body shape, posture and the depiction of plumage, but the tiny dimensions and stylised execution of the figurines make a definitive identification difficult.

What is clear is that both species were already present in Europe during the Ice Age.

Hohle Fels cave (often also called Hohler Fels) was inhabited during the Aurignacian period (around 43,000 to 28,000 years ago) by early Homo sapiens, at a time when Neanderthals had already disappeared from Europe.

In this period, humans experienced a remarkable cultural and artistic flowering and created some of the oldest known musical instruments, items of jewellery and figurative artworks. Among the cave's most famous finds is the "Venus of Hohle Fels", a roughly 41,000-year-old ivory figure of a woman with accentuated breasts and hips, regarded as one of the oldest examples of figurative art in Europe.

Hohle Fels is one of six caves in the Swabian Jura that enjoy special protection as part of a UNESCO World Heritage site. The region is considered one of the most important archaeological landscapes for studying the beginnings of human art in Europe.

Since archaeological excavations began there in the 1860s, numerous finds dating from between 33,000 and 43,000 years ago have been uncovered, including some of the earliest known musical instruments.

The figurines will remain on display at the Museum of Prehistory and Ice Age Art in Blaubeuren until 4 April 2027.

World.title: Situation in Ceuta 'almost entirely reversed' as death toll climbs to 67, Spain says
World.content:
Almost all of the estimated 60,000 migrants who entered Spain's Ceuta enclave have returned to Morocco, Spanish officials said on Saturday.

 

"The situation has been almost entirely reversed," Spain's interior minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told reporters.

Under the watch of Spanish soldiers and police, the last remaining young migrants continued crossing back over the border to Morocco on Saturday morning.

To cross into Ceuta, many swam around a small border barrier that juts out into the Mediterranean.

Spanish army soldiers stand next to migrants who swam from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere

At least 67 people died in the attempt, Grande-Marlaska said, including some who drowned and others who were killed in a stampede to cross a breakwater barrier.

A handful of exhausted migrants who swam to Ceuta's urban Tarajal beach Saturday morning were met by soldiers who escorted them back across the border.

“The events require an evaluation by Spain and Morocco,” Grande-Marlaska added. But it was the cooperation with its neighbours that allowed Spain “to revert the situation in 24 hours.”

“Morocco is not a threat to Ceuta, or to the rest of Spain. It is a reliable partner,” Marlaska emphasised.

Spanish army soldiers and Red Cross workers assist a migrant who swam from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere

Spain announced it was installing a 500-metre-long containment barrier on the sea border between Ceuta and Morocco.

Ceuta, a territory of 18.5 square kilometres, and the nearby exclave of Melilla are Europe's only two land borders with Africa. It sits around 25 kilometres from the coastline of mainland Spain.

It isn’t clear what triggered the influx, but social media was awash with posts encouraging Moroccans to try to enter Ceuta days before it began, said Myriam Cherti, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford’s Centre on Migration, Policy and Society.

The posts included practical information on how to cross the border and what migrants should say to increase their chances of being allowed to stay.

Cherti said some of the migrants she interviewed over the past year had lost count of the number of times they had tried to cross the border.

Migrants return to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Friday, July 31, 2026. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere

“They’re doing it out of despair, they’re doing it because they’ve tried other ways to build a life and failed, they’re doing it because they feel the obligation that they want to help their families and support them,” she said. “And that’s possible if they make it to Spain and not necessarily possible if they stay” in Morocco.

Soufian, 42, was one of these hopefuls that attempted to cross the border. He explained he was motivated by the potential to visit his mother, who is ill and lives in Madrid.

"Even though there's no food, nothing at all, I'll endure anything to see my mother," Soufian said, adding he makes just 10 euros a day working 12-hour shifts as a security guard.

As for the others who crossed, he said, "everyone wants to move up, wants a good future, something that doesn't exist in Morocco".

Previous migrant surges have occurred during tensions between Spain and Morocco, including in 2021 which led more than 10,000 migrants to enter Ceuta in just two days.

World.title: Lithuania moves to tighten curbs on pro-Kremlin Russian and Belarusian figures
World.content:
Lithuania is proposing to tighten restrictions on Russian and Belarusian nationals by barring pro-Kremlin figures from carrying out public activities in the Baltic country and further limiting their ability to acquire property near strategically important sites.

 

The measures (link in Lithuanian) put forward by the Foreign ministry as amendments to Lithuania's Law on Restrictive Measures in Response to Military Aggression against Ukraine, would prohibit individuals and legal entities from Russia and Belarus from conducting public activities in the fields of education, science, culture, sport, the arts and entertainment if they have supported Russia's war against Ukraine, worked in occupied Ukrainian territories, backed repression in Russia or Belarus, or refuse to sign a declaration condemning Moscow's invasion.

According to the ministry, the changes are intended to prevent Moscow and Minsk from using cultural, educational and sporting activities as instruments of "soft power" to spread propaganda and influence public opinion.

"Establishing these restrictions would prevent situations where cooperation in the fields of education, science and studies, culture, art, and entertainment could be exploited to foster a favorable view of ongoing aggression, disseminate the ideology of aggressor states, and legitimize the politicized and manipulative activities of the Kremlin and Minsk regimes,” the Foreign ministry spokesperson told Euronews. The measures would also "enhance the resilience of Lithuanian society against information threats," the spokesperson added.

The ministry says the legislation would provide authorities with a clearer legal basis for taking consistent decisions based on objective criteria rather than ad hoc assessments.

The proposals also tighten existing restrictions on property ownership. Under current Lithuanian law, Russian citizens without a permanent or temporary residence permit are already barred from purchasing real estate. The amendments would extend the restrictions to Russian citizens who do hold residence permits, but only for properties located near facilities deemed critical to national security or close to military training areas. The same restrictions would apply to Belarusian citizens.

According to Vilnius, the objective is to “significantly” reduce the risk that property near sensitive sites could be used for intelligence gathering, surveillance or other hostile activities.

Lithuania would thus join several neighbouring countries that have introduced similar restrictions.

Estonia already restricts third-country nationals, including Russians and Belarusians, from acquiring property in certain areas important for national security. Latvia has adopted a prohibition on Russian and Belarusian citizens purchasing real estate anywhere in the country, while Finland has, since 2025, prohibited Russian and Belarusian citizens from obtaining permission to acquire property.

If approved by Lithuania's parliament, the Seimas, and signed by President Gitanas Nausėda, the amendments would enter into force on 1 January 2027.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: 25 years after civil partnerships, how far has Germany come on LGBTQ+ rights?
World.content:
In 2001, same-sex couples in Germany were able to register a civil partnership for the first time. The Civil Partnership Act was a crucial step toward "marriage for all," which was introduced in 2017.

August 1, 2001, marked a turning point: with the Civil Partnership Act, same-sex couples in Germany gained a legal framework for the registration of their partnerships. However, another 16 years would pass before marriage itself became an option.

"The Civil Partnership Act was a milestone for the legal recognition of same-sex couples in Germany and laid the foundation for opening up marriage," Alexander Vogt of the national board of "Queere Vielfalt e.V. " (Queer diversity) told DW.

"It introduced a legally secure partnership with rights similar to those of marriage — such as inheritance, maintenance, and residency rights — though it remained discriminatory in many areas – like adoption or tax law. Nevertheless, it gave us a foot in the door — a solid base from which further rights could be secured, usually by appealing to the Federal Constitutional Court."

Reinhard Lüschow (r) and Heinz-Friedrich Harre were the first same-sex couple in Germany to register under the new Civil Partnership Act Image: picture alliance/dpa

Public opinion was ahead of the political establishment

The legislation was preceded by a fierce political debate. The opposition bloc of conservative parties, the Christian Democratic Union and the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), denounced it as an "unconstitutional attack on marriage and the family." Lawmakers from the ruling center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, described the law as "a long-overdue act of redress."

"There was strong conservative opposition, for instance from churches and civic groups," Alexander Vogt noted. "The debate reflected the classic culture war between traditional and progressive values."

Backed by the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens, the majority of Bundestag lawmakers voted in favor of the Civil Partnership Act in November 2000, despite opposition from the CDU/CSU and the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP).

German public opinion was already a step ahead: A 1999 survey showed that 55% of respondents were already in favor of the Civil Partnership Act.

However, Germany was by no means a pioneer. Denmark was the first country in the world to introduce civil partnerships for same-sex couples, doing so as early as 1989. Norway, Sweden, and Iceland followed in the mid-1990s, with France following in 1999.

Two fathers, two babies To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'We simply wanted equal treatment'

Twenty-five years ago, Reinhard Lüschow and his husband Heinz-Friedrich Harre — who has since passed away — became the first same-sex couple in Germany to tie the knot at a registry office under the new Civil Partnership Act. They had spent the preceding decade fighting for legal recognition as a couple.

As early as 1992, they had made a public statement by applying to register their marriage — in a coordinated move by 250 male and female same-sex couples across Germany. When their application was rejected, they took the case all the way to the Federal Constitutional Court. "We simply wanted to be treated equally," Lüschow recently told the Protestant Press Service (epd).

Although the court ruled at the time that marriage was a union between a man and a woman, it also mandated that the legislature ensure same-sex partnerships were not discriminated against. When the Bundestag implemented this requirement through the Civil Partnership Act, Lüschow and Harre reacted immediately.

Hard-won changes

The Civil Partnership Act regulates matters such as the use of surnames, mutual financial support, and inheritance rights. In the years that followed, the scope of civil partnerships was gradually expanded — first in 2004 to include stepchild adoption, and later to achieve tax equality following several rulings by the Federal Constitutional Court.

What do weddings look like in Germany? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Civil Partnership Act was merely the first step toward equality. The decisive step did not come until October 1, 2017, with legislation that introduced so-called "marriage for all."

This, too, was a hard-won victory. The conservative parties had come to power again in 2005. They blocked the legislation until Chancellor Angela Merkel authorized a vote free from party-line constraints, meaning lawmakers were to follow only their consciences; this is how the majority was secured in 2017. Angela Merkel and current Chancellor Friedrich Merz voted against the legislation.

Bodo Mende and Karl Kreile were the first same-sex couple to marry. Reflecting on the 2001 Civil Partnership Act, Mende later told DW: "It was a second-class partnership." Although there were few legal restrictions, the status lacked the standing of a conventional marriage.

Married partners enjoy more rights — for instance, regarding naming laws, child adoption, and the equalization of pension rights. Marriage also carries greater recognition internationally.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 108,000 couples had availed themselves of this new option by 2025. At the same time, approximately 24,000 registered civil partnerships remain in existence; these can be converted into marriages upon application.

Bodo Mende and Karl Kreile (r) were the first same-sex couple to marry in Germany in 2017 Image: Britta Pedersen/dpa-Zentralbild/ZB/picture alliance

'Marriage for all' does not amount to full equality

Differences remain between same-sex and opposite-sex couples. Alexander Vogt of the association Queere Vielfalt cites an example regarding the law of parentage: "If a child is born into a family with two mothers, the non-biological mother must first go through an adoption process to establish legal parenthood. This is not the case for heterosexual couples."

Reflecting on societal developments, Vogt observes: "Acceptance of same-sex marriage has clearly increased."

However, he adds: "We have become more visible in recent years, but not safer; violence and hate crimes — particularly against queer people — have risen sharply. The figures have increased tenfold since 2010! The attack in Berlin represents a tragic peak in this trend, one that has garnered significant public attention."

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan
World.content:
Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. Faridoon Tofan, who is currently in deportation detention, fears the same fate.

Things would likely have turned out very differently had Faridoon Tofan not taken the bus to Italy. He had intended to go on a short trip to Rome. The 46-year-old — who had fled the Taliban to Germany just under four years ago and had since been working and learning the language — was detained during a border check in mid-April and taken directly to a deportation detention center in Munich.

The reason: Tofan did not have the legal right to leave Germany. His asylum application had been rejected; he held only a temporary residence permit, which does not protect against deportation. He could now be sent back to Kabul, even though he is neither a convicted criminal nor has he been classified as a security threat. His asylum application appeal was definitively rejected in July, and he is now to be deported.

Faridoon Tofan fled to Germany from Afghanistan four years ago Image: privat

Tofan's wife and six children are still living in Kabul. They were recently paid a visit by Taliban officials and say they've been living in constant fear ever since and the sons no longer dare attend school, Nina Alizadeh Marandi told DW. She is an asylum law expert at the human rights organization Amnesty International in Germany and in close contact with Tofan's lawyer.

The Taliban officials' interest in the Tofan family in Kabul came after Faridoon Tofan's meeting with Afghan consulate staff in Berlin. Both the embassy in the German capital and the Afghan Consulate General in Bonn are now under Taliban control — a state of affairs for which the German government has faced heavy criticism from the opposition and human rights organizations.

While the German government does not officially recognize the Taliban administration as the legitimate government of Afghanistan, it points to contacts maintained at a purely "technical level."

Deportation precedent

This week, another Afghan national with no criminal record was deported.

The flight — operated by Freebird Airlines using an Airbus A320-214 — departed Leipzig/Halle Airport in Eastern Germany at 1:43 a.m. on Tuesday, bound for Trabzon, Turkey, before continuing to Kabul, Afghanistan. The Afghan national with no criminal record was on the plane alongside 30 convicted offenders.

This set a precedent that sparked vociferous protests: 260 people heeded the call of an anti-racism alliance and came to demonstrate inside the airport's departure hall, accompanied by a police escort.

The complicated matter of deportation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Luca Müller, spokesperson for the anti-racism group, also referenced the deadly terror attack on the Pride event in Berlin over the weekend: "While Islamist violence targeting Berlin's Pride celebration is being condemned from all sides, the federal government is supporting the Islamist Taliban through its deals," Müller said.

By "deals," Müller is referring to accusations leveled by many human rights organizations and the political opposition that the German government is de facto legitimizing the Taliban regime in Afghanistan in order to facilitate more deportations.

Interior Minister justifies the tough approach

What critics view as a breach of fundamental taboo, others see as nothing more than the swift enforcement of existing law. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt again told journalists this week, that anyone who has gone through an asylum process resulting in a rejection is therefore required to leave the country and must expect deportation if they do not depart voluntarily. Dobrindt, who is a member of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), stated that the federal government is simply pursuing its goals in migration policy, driving forward this "shift in migration policy" with "control, a clear course, and a firm stance," Dobrindt added.

Improved security situation in Afghanistan?

Since the resumption of deportations to Afghanistan in 2024, Germany has returned more than 200 individuals. According to Amnesty International, at least one of them was killed following his arrival in Kabul.

However, the German government points to assessments by the UN migration agency (IOM) , which considers the return of men to Afghanistan to be feasible again — in principle.

"The security situation in Afghanistan has improved significantly; that is simply an objective fact," Mihyung Park, the IOM's country chief in Kabul, told the media outlet Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland. Park added one caveat: "Under current circumstances, we would strongly advise women against returning to Afghanistan."

In general, however, UN agencies warn against involuntary returns, noting that the returnees heavily depend on support to settle again in their country of origin.

Amnesty International condemns the German government for increasingly toughening its deportation practices without regard for the catastrophic human rights situation in Afghanistan. Nina Alizadeh Marandi pointed out that the very day of this week's historical deportation happened to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the adoption of the Geneva Refugee Convention .

"Human rights standards must not be eroded simply because upholding them is politically inconvenient," Alizadeh Marandi said. "Amnesty calls on the federal government to refrain from further deportations and to monitor whether Afghans who have already been deported are able to live in Afghanistan without persecution or danger to life and limb," she added.

Under Taliban shadow, Afghans in Pakistan look to Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Opposition speaks of a 'dangerous wrong turn'

Germany's political opposition has also sharply criticized the first deportation of an Afghan national with no criminal record. "It is irresponsible that Alexander Dobrindt is now deporting people to Afghanistan who have done absolutely nothing wrong here," said Marcel Emmerich, the Green Party's parliamentary spokesperson on interior policy.

Emmerich said that Dobrindt's "dirty deal" regarding deportations strengthens the Taliban, "makes us vulnerable to blackmail, and undermines Germany's own security." He added that the federal government is taking a "dangerous wrong turn" with this Afghanistan policy.

Juliane Nagel, a lawmaker for the socialist Left Party in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony, called the flight "shameful" and demanded that Saxony's Leipzig/Halle Airport — which is largely state-owned — no longer be used for deportations to Afghanistan.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Famed climber Nirmal Purja among 10 killed in avalanche
World.content:
A major search was launched after an avalanche struck the expedition high on Pakistan's Broad Peak. The confirmation ended hopes of a rescue and marked the loss of one of the world's best-known high-altitude climbers.

Celebrated climber Nirmal Purja and nine other mountaineers have been confirmed dead after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak, his expedition company said on Saturday.

The confirmation came a day after rescuers located four bodies while searching for the 10-member expedition.

How did Purja and the other mountaineers die?

"It is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak," Purja's company Elite Expeditions said in a social media post.

"We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive."

The climbers had been missing since Thursday, when an avalanche struck the expedition at around 6,600 meters (21,650 feet) on Broad Peak. The party is believed to have been swept away.

Two Pakistan Army Aviation helicopters joined the operation on Friday, while an experienced ground team was deployed to the area where the group was last believed to have been.

Pakistani security sources said four bodies had been located that day, although they had not yet been recovered.

The mountain is the 12th highest in the world and lies near Pakistan's border with China (file photo) Image: Photoshot/picture alliance

At the time, rescuers were still searching for the remaining members of the group.

The deaths of all 10 climbers were confirmed on Saturday.

The expedition included Purja and five other Nepalese climbers, including several Sherpa guides, as well as mountaineers from four other countries.

They were Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi, Omani climber Nathira Ahmed, US climber Mallory Geis and China's Wang Zhong.

Who was Nirmal Purja?

Nirmal Purja, widely known as Nims Dai, was a British-Nepali mountaineer who became one of the best-known high-altitude climbers of his generation.

The 43-year-old served with Britain's Brigade of Gurkhas and later the elite Special Boat Service before leaving the military to become a full-time mountaineer and guide.

Purja shot to international fame in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains above 8,000 meters in just over six months, dramatically beating the previous record of nearly eight years.

His feat was chronicled in the 2021 Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible," which helped bring him a global following.

In 2021, Purja was also part of the 10-member Nepali team that completed the first winter ascent of K2, the world's second-highest mountain.

Before the latest ascent, Purja had posted his hopes for the expedition on X, asking the mountain for safe passage.

What is Broad Peak?

Broad Peak stands at just over 8,000 meters in Pakistan's Karakoram range, close to the border with China. It is the world's 12th-highest mountain and lies only a few kilometers from the better-known K2.

Originally designated K3 during the surveying of the Karakoram, its more modern name refers to its unusually wide summit ridge, which stretches for roughly 1.5 kilometers (just under a mile).

The region contains five of the world's 14 peaks above 8,000 meters and attracts climbers from across the globe, although avalanches and rapidly changing weather make expeditions particularly dangerous.
