World.title: Croatia Plans Taxi Fare Caps to End Excessive Charges
World.content:
July the 31st, 2026 – Croatia is planning to finally deal with the taxi fare issue with caps and a hope to end excessive charges and frequent tourist rip-offs during summer.

Croatia is preparing to introduce a new set of rules for the taxi industry that will allow the government to cap fares, aiming to protect passengers from excessive prices while ensuring drivers can continue operating sustainably. Poslovni reports that the measures form part of amendments to the Road Transport Act, which have already been approved by Parliament and are expected to reshape the country’s taxi market.

Under the new legislation, the Minister of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure will be authorised to set maximum fares for all key components of a taxi ride, including the starting fare, per-kilometre rate, waiting time, and per-minute charges. The goal is to prevent extreme price spikes that have generated negative publicity, particularly in tourist destinations.

The reform follows several high-profile incidents in which passengers, including foreign tourists, were charged hundreds or even thousands of euros for relatively short journeys. Those cases prompted calls for stronger consumer protection and greater transparency across the industry.

The government says the new framework is intended to strike a balance between protecting customers and ensuring taxi drivers receive fair compensation. Officials have been working with representatives of the taxi sector, digital ride-hailing platforms and consumer groups to develop a pricing model that avoids both unreasonably low fares and excessive charges.

The legislation also introduces several additional changes designed to improve oversight of the sector. Every taxi vehicle will require its own operating permit, while specially designated TX licence plates will make licensed taxis easier to identify. Authorities are also strengthening checks on drivers and expanding enforcement powers to police, customs officers and municipal inspectors.

Digital ride-hailing platforms will face tighter regulation as well. They will be required to work only with properly licensed operators and maintain records that allow authorities to verify compliance with Croatian transport regulations.

The government believes the reforms will create a more transparent, competitive and reliable taxi market, improving confidence among both residents and the millions of visitors who use taxi services each year. The new rules are expected to take effect following the implementation of the amended Road Transport Act.

World.title: €20 Million Investment Aims to Transform Continental Croatian Tourism
World.content:
July the 31st, 2026 – A massive investment is aiming to totally transform continental Croatian tourism, with the majority of the focus on the overlooked Daruvar Spa.

Croatia has officially unveiled the fully renovated and expanded Daruvar Spa, a €20 million project that the government says marks a major step in strengthening the country’s continental tourism and positioning it as a leading European destination for health and wellness travel.

Poslovni reports that Prime Minister Andrej Plenković attended the opening ceremony, describing the project as one of 15 major investments designed to reshape Croatia’s tourism offer beyond the Adriatic coast. He noted that €13.2 million of the investment was financed through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), while the overall goal is to create a year-round tourism industry with high-quality facilities that attract visitors throughout all seasons, not just the summer months.

The renovation has transformed one of Croatia’s oldest spa resorts, whose history stretches back nearly 2,000 years, into a modern wellness and rehabilitation destination. The project included the complete reconstruction of 77 existing accommodation units and the construction of 13 new rooms at the Hotel Termal.

Guests can now enjoy newly renovated thermal pools featuring massage zones, an expanded sun deck, and a modern pool bar. The investment also introduced a new recreational and tourism centre with a multifunctional sports hall that will be used by both spa visitors and Croatian war veterans staying at the nearby Veterans’ Centre.

Among the new wellness facilities are beer baths, oak baths, salt rooms, cryotherapy chambers, and hyperbaric chambers. Spa director Ratko Vuković described the beer and oak baths as unique products that reflect Daruvar’s local identity and wellness tradition.

Local officials called the redevelopment a turning point for the region. Daruvar Mayor Damir Lneniček said it is the city’s largest investment in the past 45 years, adding that it will stimulate not only tourism but the broader local economy. Bjelovar-Bilogora County Prefect Marko Marušić said the upgraded spa has the potential to become the “locomotive” of Croatia’s health tourism sector by setting new standards in quality and visitor experience.

The project also focused on sustainability and digitalisation. Alongside modernising the facilities, the investment included a digital transformation of operations, the installation of photovoltaic power systems, and electric vehicle charging stations to improve energy efficiency and reduce environmental impact.

According to Plenković, the Daruvar project is part of a broader national strategy involving 15 spa and health tourism developments, with 10 located in continental Croatia and five along the coast. The wider programme is backed by a €356 million tourism investment package, of which €320 million comes from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan.

Other destinations included in the programme are Veli Lošinj, Stubičke Toplice, Lipik, Varaždinske Toplice, Topusko, Terme Bjelovar, Biograd na Moru, Makarska, Crikvenica, and the island of Korčula. The government says the investments are intended to diversify Croatia’s tourism offer, reduce seasonal dependence, and strengthen the country’s position in the growing European health and wellness tourism market.

Although continental Croatia currently accounts for less than five percent of the country’s total tourism traffic, officials believe projects such as the redevelopment of Daruvar Spa will help unlock its significant growth potential by attracting domestic and international visitors throughout the year while creating new economic opportunities for local communities.

World.title: Schengen Area must be preserved, says Estonia's PM
World.content:
Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) has said the European Union must jointly act on migration after the crisis in Spain this week and that the Schengen free movement area must be preserved.

Approximately 60,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco this week. As of Friday evening, more than 48,000 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco, Spanish officials said.

The influx comes after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla, another Spanish enclave, cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.

Michal signed a joint letter with 21 other member states addressed to the EU's top leaders on Saturday calling for "an immediate and coordinated European response."

"We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant's illegal entry can turn into legal stay," the statement says.

It added that ministers should consider enhanced support from the EU's border force, Frontex, and "the effectiveness of EU cooperation with Morocco."

Estonia, together with 21 other Member States, calls on @eucopresident, @vonderleyen, and @MichealMartinTD to take immediate action to jointly support Spain in restoring effective control of the EU's external border.



Europe must respond with unity to uncontrolled mass crossings,… pic.twitter.com/RxMdi8zBKh — Kristen Michal (@KristenMichalPM) August 1, 2026

The letter was signed by representatives from Italy, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Sweden.

Schengen Area 'must be preserved'

He also responded to comments from the chairman of the opposition party Isamaa, Urmas Reinsalu, who said suspending the Schengen free movement zone would be justified in such a critical situation, as Italy temporarily did with Spain earlier this week.

Writing on social media, Michal said: "The creation of new internal borders within the Schengen Area is in no way in the interests of Estonia or Estonians. None of us wants to return to a time when travelling overland to Central Europe meant passing through more than five cumbersome border checks."

Michal stressed that Estonia treats every illegal border crossing with the "utmost seriousness" and is already helping other countries, such as Latvia, with their border issues.

"Those who organize such migration will be punished, and those who arrive in Estonia illegally will be detained and sent back to the countries they came from," he wrote.

"The Schengen Area is a great value that must be preserved."

'Full solidarity with Spain'

Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200). Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

While other countries took to social media to criticize Spain on Friday, Estonia's Minister of Foreign Affairs sent a message of solidarity.

"The developments in Ceuta are deeply concerning. Estonia stands in full solidarity with Spain as it faces unprecedented migration pressure," Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) wrote on social media.

"Spain has both the right and the responsibility to protect its borders – and the European Union's external border. No one has the right to enter the European Union without abiding by our common rules. Respect for those rules is essential to safeguarding the integrity of the Schengen Area," he continued.

The developments in Ceuta are deeply concerning.

World.title: Police will not control queue 'place buying' at Narva border
World.content:
The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) and the Ministry of Interior are not planning to crack down on people selling places in the queue at the Narva border crossing as wait times increase due to summer tourism to Russia.

The Ministry of the Interior and the PPA said they are aware that places in the queue are being sold around the Narva border crossing, Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) acknowledged in response to a question submitted by MP Aleksandr Tsaplõgin (Centre Party).

Queues at Estonia's land borders increase considerably in the summer as Russians living abroad and international tourists visit Russia. Flights from Europe were suspended following the start of the full-scale invasion, and Finland closed its borders after migration pressure several years ago. Estonia has also reduced the operational hours at the border to 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Taro noted that the queue forms in a public space and that there are no regulations governing the line. "The PPA monitors the situation from the perspective of public order and safety. If violations or conflicts arise, the police intervene," he said.

The minister confirmed that the police assess every report indicating possible organized crime. "If specific cases contain indications of threats, extortion or other criminal activity, they are investigated and, if necessary, proceedings are initiated. It has not been confirmed that this involves a criminal group," he noted.

Minister of the Interior Igor Taro. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

The police have received reports concerning the area around the Narva border crossing, but they do not amount statistically to the volume or pattern that would indicate a widespread, systematic wave of violence or extortion.

"Reports involving threats, the risk of violence or damage to property are reviewed and, where necessary, misdemeanor or criminal proceedings are initiated if the legal grounds are met," Taro said.

In 2025, the police received 46 reports that places in the queue were being sold at Peetri Square in Narva. This year, they have received 16 such reports. Last year, there were 62 reports of public order violations, while this year the number stands at 17," the minister said.

"At the same time, it cannot be said that all of these reports are related to the border queue. Over the past two years, seven offense reports have been filed. In two cases, criminal offenses involving either theft or causing bodily injury were reported, while the remaining five involved misdemeanors, including damaging another person's property, consuming alcohol in a public place, or disobeying or insulting officials."

No proceedings have been initiated on the basis of reports about selling places in the queue. The situations have been resolved by Narva police officers, and those selling places in the queue have been removed from the line, Taro added.

Peetri plats in 2024. Source: Jenny Va / ERR

'Avoid travelling to Russia'

Asked why, despite the well-known problem, there is no permanent police presence or regular patrols near the border crossing to prevent unlawful activity, Taro replied that the law does not assign the police the task of organizing the queue of pedestrians crossing the border in a public space.

"However, the police are responsible for maintaining public order. Around the Narva border crossing, patrols and police presence are deployed on a risk-based basis where there is a greater threat to public order or security. Maintaining a permanent stationary police presence wherever a queue forms is neither practical nor proportionate. If conflicts or the threat of violence arise, people can call 112, and the police will respond," the minister said.

Tsaplõgin also asked what specific measures the Ministry of the Interior intends to take to stop the illegal sale of queue places.

"The PPA will continue to maintain public order through risk-based patrols and by responding to specific incidents. People are continually reminded of the complexity of crossing the border and the need to take into account long waiting times, restrictions and unexpected changes to border crossing procedures," Taro said.

Adding: "As a representative of the government, I support the recommendation of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and likewise advise people to avoid travelling to Russia altogether!"

World.title: Raul Meel's anniversary exhibition on display at the Poco Ajamaja gallery
World.content:
Dedicated to Raul Meel's 85th birthday, the exhibition "Concret" is open at the Poco Ajamaja gallery. It traces the artist's journey from his first groundbreaking experiments in the late 1960s to the present day.

Exhibition curator Jaan Heinsoo says the exhibition focuses on concrete poetry – works that combine poetry and visual art. In concrete poetry, meaning is not only derived from words but also from visual experience, the rhythmic structure of words and signs, the interplay of colors, repetition, and silence.

"The exhibition is a retrospective of the artist's life's work spanning more than fifty years, presenting a cross-section of the various eras, facets, and techniques of Raul Meel's creative journey from 1970s typewriter drawings to a painting from the "Epic of Bristles" series created this year," Heinsoo explained.

"A large portion of the works were produced over the past year, yet the ideas and motifs largely originate from earlier creative periods."

Meel (b. 1941) is one of Estonia's best-known avant-garde artists and among Europe's leading practitioners of conceptual art and concrete poetry. He has participated in more than 600 group exhibitions and over 100 solo exhibitions, and remains the only Estonian artist to have received a prize at a major international biennial.

World.title: Teachers, NGO call for more emphasis on global education in school curricula
World.content:
NGO Mondo has said Estonia's education system should place greater emphasis on global citizenship, and the chair of the Estonian History and Civics Teachers' Association agrees. The Ministry of Education says that global education competencies are already included in the current curricula.

Global education, knowledge of how global issues affect the daily lives of individuals, communities and society, and how everyone can influence the world, has been promoted in Estonia for 15 years.

Schools can choose elective courses, take part in themed weeks and projects, and such content has been integrated into various subjects, but according to those involved, this has been done in a fragmented way.

Meelis Niine, project manager at the non-profit organization Mondo, told ERR that in the future global education could be described more clearly in the general sections of the national curricula and in subject syllabi, and that global citizenship competencies could also be set out more specifically.

"If there were a separate emphasis specifically on global citizenship competencies, it would help make global education a clearer and more integral part of formal education. What do I mean by global citizenship competencies? On the one hand, it means that young people should understand different global challenges, their local dimension, and how global challenges are reflected locally. At the same time, it is also important to care about these issues and to take active action," he said.

Niine thinks this is a weak point because many young people in Estonia may be fairly well informed about global issues, but they make relatively few active choices in their daily lives or engage in civic activism.

Madli-Maria Naulainen, chair of the Estonian History and Civics Teachers' Association, said that global education is certainly already part of civics classes, but that does not mean it could not receive greater emphasis.

"At the moment, a great deal depends on the individual teacher – some choose to address these topics more, others less," Naulainen explained. "I very much agree that the topic of global education should be highlighted more and should not depend solely on teachers' individual choices."

According to the chair, the association has worked closely with Mondo all along and has helped distribute the educational materials created by Mondo for use in civics lessons.

"That line of cooperation certainly exists now, but in a situation where teachers can choose which topics they use to achieve particular learning outcomes, a specific section in the curriculum would provide a better guarantee that everyone has gained some knowledge in this area," Naulainen argued.

Ministry: Schools have a lot of autonomy

Adviser on general education policy at the Ministry of Education and Research, Mare Oja, said there is no contradiction in the current situation. The principles of global education are already included in the national curriculum's general competencies and core values.

"We have universal human and social values, which include both solidarity, civic engagement and seeing oneself as a citizen of the world. In Estonia, the national curriculum is a general document on the basis of which schools develop their own curricula, and our schools have a great deal of autonomy," she said.

She added that in upper secondary school, 63 of the 96 courses are determined by the national curriculum, while schools design the remaining third themselves, creating their own profile and deciding what they want to explore in greater depth. Some focus on economics education, others on financial literacy, and some on global education. As a result, the situation is diverse.

"In fact, all these principles are already included. Specific topics are covered in geography and civics. For example, when we talk about cultural diversity, foreign languages, language and literature, and certainly history all support that," Oja said.

Teachers: Schools may lack broader perspective

Madli-Maria Naulainen of the History and Civics Teachers' Association noted that although several school subjects touch on global education, what may be lacking is a broader perspective that would help students understand globalization and give them an idea of what development cooperation is and why it is necessary.

"In today's globalized world, it is inevitable that we must keep up with these issues. Understanding and solidarity toward others are also areas that could certainly be better addressed through these topics," Naulainen said.

Maari Ross, adviser at the Humanitarian Aid Bureau of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said some European countries also look to Estonia's education system for inspiration, but at the same time, the issue of fragmentation still needs to be addressed.

"One important area is regional support and cooperation networks. In Estonia, we actually have several very strong schools and competence centers working on global education. The question is how to ensure and improve the sharing of their experience with others. Another important area is research and evaluating the impact of global education – how to increase the interest of Estonian researchers in studying global education," Ross said.

According to Naulainen, civics is expected to provide good citizenship education, while in reality the subject has a fairly limited place in schools.

"Civics as a subject is taught only in the sixth, ninth and 12th grades. We have discussed whether the volume of civics education should perhaps be expanded, because expectations have increased and there are visible signs of polarization and extremism in society," the association's chair said.

At the end of last year, stakeholders in the field produced a vision document, and on that basis they are now moving toward drafting an action plan.

World.title: PPA: Nõmme migrant case is not an isolated incident
World.content:
The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) detained 15 suspected illegal migrants on Thursday in a Tallinn suburb, but said similar incidents have occurred elsewhere. The agency asked the public to be vigilant but "reasonable," stressing "not everyone with a different skin color is problematic."

The PPA has said the migrants have likely entered the European Union after illegally crossing the Latvian-Belarus border. Politicians and the security services say the route is part of a "hybrid attack" by the Minsk authorities with Russian support.

The uptick in migrants in Estonia is likely caused by additional checks on Poland's northern and western borders to stop people smugglers traveling to Germany. The destination has now changed to Finland and Scandinavia, the PPA has said. Over 80 have been caught in the last two weeks, compared to 39 last year.

When police arrived at the scene in a suburb in the south of the capital, they initially detained 12 people. Three others had already left the area, but authorities caught them a few hours later.

Neighbors alerted the police after noticing people whose appearance and behavior stood out in the neighborhood.

The migrants were detained outside the guesthouse. The building's owner told ERR that he had not been aware of them staying at the property, although the house was later found in disarray. The owner said they had no security camera footage or other evidence confirming that the people had stayed at their accommodation.

Police operation on Tallinn's Nõmme district on Thursday. Source: Private collection

Local residents told ERR that even late in the evening, after 11 p.m., plainclothes police officers could be seen around the house. Dogs were used in the search early in the evening, and drones were also deployed. Searches were also carried out in a nearby forest.

Indrek Aru, head of the Border Guard Bureau of the North Prefecture, said on Friday that no additional people were found during the late-night searches.

"If there is reason to believe that there may be people somewhere who have no legal basis to stay in Estonia, then naturally we verify such information. That is what we did yesterday in Nõmme. When we detained a larger group of people in the area who presumably had no legal basis to stay here, we naturally looked around more broadly, and that is how those operations were carried out," he said.

However, the police are not certain that all 15 people detained on Thursday belonged to the same group.

"There is obviously reason to look for those connections, and that work is still ongoing," Aru added.

The PPA has not disclosed its communication with the property owner. However, Aru stressed that accommodation providers are obliged to verify whether third-country nationals arriving to use their services have a legal basis to stay in the country by checking their documents.

"Naturally, verifying and complying with those requirements is more complicated in the case of guest apartments offered for short-term rental," Aru acknowledged.

Fifteen suspected illegal migrants were arrested in Tallinn's Nõmme district on July 30. It is assumed they were trying to travel on to Finland. Source: Helen Wright/ OSM/ Datawrapper

He urged owners of rental properties to notify the police if a large number of people arrive at their guest apartment who may not have a legal basis to stay, or if they appear exhausted and as though they have arrived from difficult conditions.

Although the group of migrants detained in Nõmme attracted considerable attention, it was not an exceptional case for the PPA.

"We have also discovered groups of foreign nationals who presumably do not have a valid legal basis to stay at other accommodation establishments and in other districts," Aru said. "What happened in Nõmme is not an isolated case; we have had a couple of similar incidents. The Nõmme case simply attracted greater public attention this time because a significantly larger police response was involved."

Police have received unfounded reports based on skin color

Minister of Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) has also urged people to report suspicious individuals.

However, the Police have already received unfounded reports about people based solely on their skin color.

"I have heard about a few cases where people drew our attention to someone and even approached us on the street, saying they had seen someone who was probably staying in the country illegally or without a legal basis. It later turned out that the person had all the necessary documents, was completely law-abiding, and even spoke Estonian," Aru said.

"I would certainly recommend maintaining a reasonable approach," the PPA representative stressed. "Even today we are seeing well-intentioned reports, but it is important to remain reasonable when making notifications. Not everyone with a different skin color is problematic. This should be viewed in a balanced way."

A police van at the Port of Tallinn. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

The PPA is also carrying out additional checks across the country, not only Tallinn and Harju County where the main ports and airports are located.

Aru said police resources have not been exhausted.

"There is no reason for people in Estonia to worry. If you call 112, the police will come, and they do so quite quickly. Estonia has a very good emergency response time. When migration pressure increases, cooperation between countries also increases," he said.

Aru explained that this type of illegal migration is being facilitated by the authorities in Russia and Belarus.

"Naturally, people in the countries of origin of migration are looking for a better life or have other reasons for setting out. But the fact that they have chosen such a route and end up entering our visa area illegally clearly shows that this is a hybrid attack by Belarus," he said.

Migrants have been crossing the Belarusian border into Latvia, Lithuania and Poland since 2021, in what European officials say is a manufactured hybrid attack orchestrated by the Belarusian regime. The issues started after the EU sanctioned Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko.

Migrants cross the border and then try to travel onto western or northern Europe. Last year, Germany and Poland introduced checks on their borders in an attempt to stop people smugglers. Over the past year, several drivers transporting migrants have been stopped at the Polish-Lithuanian border, and now the flow has redirected northwards, the PPA said on Wednesday.

World.title: Aimar Ventsel: In Moldova, Kazakhstan and Georgia, Russia is 'one of us'
World.content:
In Estonia there is a clear distance toward Russia; for many Georgians, Kazakhs and Moldovans, by contrast, Russia occupies the same space and world, writes Aimar Ventsel.

I was recently in Georgia. To be honest, I didn't just visit — I stayed for about a month. I must say I chose the worst possible time to be in Georgia. Late June and July are the hottest period, and I often suffered in temperatures reaching 37 degrees.

I spent time in several parts of Georgia, from Adjara to Kakheti, and in some places in between. In plain language, I was in the far south near the Turkish border and then a bit in central Georgia. In April I was in Kazakhstan, mainly in the northern part, around the city of Karaganda. And a few years ago I spent several months in Moldova.

Sometimes it is useful to spend longer periods in different former Soviet republics. It gives reason to reflect on quite a few things.

As many surely know, economically and institutionally the Baltic states are the most developed among the fragments of the former Soviet Union. It is hard to say who holds the leading position; Estonians would of course like to think it is the Republic of Estonia. The same claim cannot be denied to Lithuania or Latvia.

But there is one thing in which Estonia stands out most: here the Soviet Union is the least important reference point. By that I mean that although the Soviet past is mentioned fairly often, compared with the post‑Soviet countries I have visited, it is still pleasantly rare. One could say Estonia has left the Soviet past behind and looks forward.

Georgia is a complete catastrophe in this regard. It is very hard to find anyone over forty who does not sooner or later start talking about the Soviet Union, comparing life "under the communists." And "communist" is not always a swear word in Georgia.

I have of course met people, mainly entrepreneurs, who say things are better now, that they can run their business without restrictions and success depends mainly on willingness and skills.

In many cases the comparison with today's Georgia is that "it was better under the communists." There are entire regions where the collapse of the Soviet Union meant not only the disappearance of jobs but also electricity, gas and cheap subsidised food. I have met people who say things are better now, but many do not.

"In many cases the comparison with today's Georgia is that 'it was better under the communists.'"

In Kazakhstan, comparisons with Soviet times also come up constantly, though not in a positive way. Kazakhs still remember how they were not only a minority in their own homeland but second‑class citizens. Russians, Ukrainians and even a few Estonians who had arrived from across the Soviet Union constantly reminded Kazakhs that they should be grateful for being brought "civilisation" and "culture," turning nomadic herders into "civilised" people.

All this came with the suppression of Kazakh culture and language. Islam, central to Kazakh identity to the point where it is sometimes hard to draw a line between being Muslim and being Kazakh, was pushed underground.

Kazakhs themselves say that Kazakh sufism saved Islam and thus Kazakh identity. Since nomadic herders could not regularly attend mosques, a tradition developed where the local religious authority was the oldest man in the family, the aksakal. Thus mosques, mullahs and imams were not critical for being Muslim. Prayer and Islamic customs survived the Soviet era among Kazakhs.

In Moldova, emphasising Soviet heritage is highly political and characteristic of pro‑Russian politicians and their supporters. Moldova shows clearly where cultivating Soviet heritage leads: it brings Russia increasingly into the life of the state and its people.

About half the population of Moldova believes the country has only one path of development — together with Russia, through difficulties toward the stars. There is also an economic reason: Russia is an important market for Moldovan goods, more important than the European Union.

It should also be mentioned that in all the countries above, Russian is the first language used to communicate with foreigners. It is ironic that Georgians like to say Russian is disappearing and English is taking over, but in practice it is very hard to manage outside central Tbilisi and Batumi's tourist areas without Russian.

All this leads to an interesting mental geography. For Estonia and most Estonians, Russia is clearly "the other" country, somewhere beyond the border, with which nothing much connects us anymore and about which we do not know much.

"I would dare say that while Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have mentally turned their backs on Russia, most former Soviet republics have not."

In Moldova, Kazakhstan and Georgia, Russia is "one of us," a foreign country in the same way Estonians tend to view Latvia. As a colleague once told me years ago in Kazakhstan: "For us, the Soviet Union is the Homeland." With a capital letter. In the shadow of that Great Homeland, Russia slips ever deeper into these countries, and the boundary between the Soviet Union and Russia fades — in a positive sense.

A Russian tends to be a different kind of foreigner in these countries than a citizen of any random European state. Georgians, Kazakhs and Moldovans share music with Russians, from Kino to Soviet‑era pop, jokes that everyone understands, well‑known films and even shared terminology — the word "comrade" still appears in Russian conversation, and various coins are still called kopecks.

I would dare say that while Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have mentally turned their backs on Russia, most former Soviet republics have not. Yes, propaganda seeps through every crack here too, and there are those who idealise Russia, but in Estonia there is a clear distance toward Russia. For many Georgians, Kazakhs and Moldovans, by contrast, Russia occupies the same space and world.

And that world shines through everywhere in Georgia, Moldova or Kazakhstan. Russian pop music plays in every second taxi, Soviet pioneer songs sound in children's playgrounds, walls are plastered with posters for concerts by Russian artists, and many people eagerly watch Russian television. Still one of us.

World.title: Turkish Air Force takes over NATO's newly upgraded Baltic air defense mission in Estonia
World.content:
Turkey's air force has been deployed to Estonia for the first time to participate in NATO's newly transformed Baltic air defense mission and will patrol the airspace for the next four months.

At last month's NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, it was decided that the two-decade-old Baltic air policing monitoring mission in Estonia and Lithuania would evolve into an air defense mission from August 1.

The new mission makes it possible to counter aerial attacks by employing NATO's integrated air defense system.

"This should ensure that if, for example, the threat picture changes and there is a need to rapidly bring in additional forces, that will be done. Likewise, all the necessary pre-authorizations for making all possible decisions have already been completed as far in advance as possible," Minister of Defense Hanno Pevkur (Reform) said on Friday.

The four-month rotation timetable for NATO allies has already been agreed upon for the next three years. The minister said air forces are unlikely to get bored, as few regions have similar conditions.

The Turkish Air force will lead the first rotation of the Baltic Air Defense Mission in Estonia from August 1, 2026. Source: EDF/ Siim Verner Teder

"Under previous practice, once, twice, even three times a week they have to go and identify aircraft from a country that is not friendly toward us. In their home countries, as a rule, and if we are talking primarily about, for example, Portugal or Spain, which have served here, or Germany as well, they do not have to constantly identify Russian reconnaissance aircraft or Russian fighter jets flying nearby. The visual contact you get with a Russian fighter jet is not something you can experience in Portugal. Therefore, every country that comes here is certainly in a somewhat special situation," Pevkur told ERR.

The Turkish Air Force contingent at Ämari consists of nearly 80 personnel, including 10 pilots. Five F-16 fighter jets are on round-the-clock standby for takeoff.

"Of course, we are proud to be here under NATO. Our aim and goal is to protect NATO airspace, identify threats in this region, and maintain strong air deterrence," Turkish Air Force pilot Lieutenant Atila Özdemir said.

On Friday, mission medals were awarded to the Portuguese Air Force personnel who flew the last air policing mission in Baltic airspace. Lt. Col. Katrin Tõugjas, commander of the Ämari Air Base, thanked the Portuguese for their "outstanding cooperation" and welcomed the new Turkish contingent.

The Turkish Air Force's deployment will end in November. The Italians took over the mission in Lithuania.

The Turkish Air force will lead the first rotation of the Baltic Air Defense Mission in Estonia from August 1, 2026. Source: EDF/ Siim Verner Teder

World.title: Chevron CFO bullish on Iraq after West Qurna 2, Nassiriya agreements
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Chevron boasts “significant potential” to expand its activities in Iraq over the next decade, according to Chief Financial Officer Eimear Bonner, highlighting the US oil company’s increasing trust in the country’s energy sector after recent deals with Baghdad.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Bonner said that Iraq remained one of Chevron’s top priority markets for future production expansion after the signing of preliminary agreements to pursue negotiations on the massive West Qurna 2 and Nassiriya oil fields.

She added that Chevron has been encouraged by its interaction with Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi and Iraq’s Ministry of Oil while discussions continue and that the corporation is also collaborating with Baghdad on diverse crude export routes to boost Iraq’s long-term energy security.

The statements bolster rising trust among foreign energy corporations after Al-Zaidi’s visit to the United States earlier this month, during which Iraq inked more than $60 billion in investment deals covering energy, infrastructure, banking, and technology.

World.title: Syria joins Saudi Arabia, Jordan in warning Iraq over Iran-backed militias
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Syria has joined Saudi Arabia and Jordan in warning Baghdad that strikes conducted from Iraqi soil against neighboring nations may result in military strikes against the armed groups responsible, according to Syrian military officials cited by regional media.

According to Al Jazeera and the US-funded Al Hurra, a senior Syrian military source said that Damascus will react to any strikes from Iraq by attacking the “terrorist militias” involved inside Iraqi territory.

The purported warning comes amid a steep increase in regional tensions after US-Saudi bombings against Iran-backed militias in Iraq in retaliation for drone assaults on Saudi oil installations, which Riyadh said were conducted from Iraqi territory.

The Iraqi government has frequently said that it would not allow Iraqi land to be used as a launchpad for attacks on neighboring nations.

Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi recently issued an order establishing a comprehensive security strategy aimed at enhancing state authority and preventing armed organizations from endangering regional security.

The new threat puts further pressure on Baghdad, as more neighboring nations indicate they may take direct action if cross-border assaults continue.

Iraqi authorities have attempted to prevent such a situation, claiming that security activities should be overseen by the Iraqi government rather than foreign forces.

Several Iran-backed organizations operating inside Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) are at the heart of the conflict, including Kataib Hezbollah, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, Harakat al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada.

While the PMF is technically part of Iraq’s security system, some of its sections have strong links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and have been accused by regional governments of carrying out strikes outside of Baghdad’s jurisdiction.

For Iraq, the diplomatic stakes go beyond security.

Baghdad has been attempting to reestablish ties with Syria as part of greater regional economic integration, including talks on resurrecting the old Iraq-Syria oil pipeline to the Mediterranean, which is considered strategically crucial for diversifying Iraq’s export routes outside the Gulf.

The purported Syrian warning comes at a critical moment for Al-Zaidi’s administration, which has spent recent months bolstering relations with Washington, Ankara, Riyadh, and Damascus while portraying Iraq as a secure destination for global investment.

The mounting threats from neighboring Arab governments highlight the importance of Baghdad demonstrating its ability to prevent armed groups from conducting strikes independent of the state.

Failure to do so risks increasing regional military tensions and jeopardizing Iraq’s aspirations to boost commerce, energy cooperation, and infrastructure projects with its neighbors.

The Syrian government has not issued an official warning, and IraqiNews.com has not independently confirmed the statements ascribed to the Syrian military source.

However, the claims reflect rising regional worry that strikes by Iran-backed militias operating from Iraqi soil could further destabilize the area and hamper Iraq’s diplomatic and economic goals.

World.title: Iran-backed militias threaten Iraq’s ties with US and Gulf
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Escalating tensions between Iran-backed militias are providing one of the most serious hurdles yet to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s ambitions to deepen ties with the United States and Gulf states while luring billions of dollars in international investment.

The most recent crisis followed US-Saudi airstrikes on Iran-aligned armed groups in Iraq, when Saudi Arabia accused militias operating from Iraqi territory of firing drones at oil installations in the kingdom’s Eastern Province.

Riyadh claimed that the operation targeted the militias responsible for the assaults rather than the Iraqi state or its military forces, but Baghdad denounced the strikes as a breach of national sovereignty.

The recent tensions are being fueled by numerous prominent Iran-aligned organizations operating inside Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), notably Kataib Hezbollah, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, Harakat al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada.

While the PMF is technically part of Iraq’s security apparatus, many of its groups have strong links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and have occasionally conducted operations outside of Baghdad’s chain of command.

Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi responded by calling an emergency meeting of the Ministerial Council for National Security, canceling a planned trip to Saudi Arabia, and announcing a comprehensive security strategy to prevent Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks on neighboring countries.

The administration also reiterated its resolve to keep all weapons entirely under state control.

That vow has gained importance after Al-Zaidi’s visit to Washington earlier this month, during which Iraq and the United States reiterated their commitment to completing the US-led coalition operation by the end of September 2026.

During the visit, Al-Zaidi pledged to ensure that all weapons eventually come into the control of the Iraqi state, citing it as a cornerstone of his government’s security strategy and a crucial step toward bolstering Iraq’s sovereignty and stability.

Since entering office, Al-Zaidi has maintained a policy of balancing Iraq’s ties with rival regional and international forces.

During recent travels to Washington, Ankara, and Tehran, he achieved huge investment and cooperation deals totaling tens of billions of dollars in the energy, banking, technology, infrastructure, and industrial sectors.

His administration has also attempted to strengthen connections with Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Turkey, and other Gulf nations via new transportation corridors, energy alliances, and trade agreements aimed at diversifying Iraq’s economy beyond oil and positioning the country as a regional center linking the Gulf to Europe.

According to analysts, Baghdad’s approach is highly dependent on proving that the Iraqi state, rather than armed groups, controls the country’s security and foreign policy.

Continued strikes from Iraqi territory risk eroding the country’s reputation with major regional allies and international investors, at a time when foreign investment has risen after years of turmoil.

The stakes rose when US President Donald Trump said that recent US-Saudi operations against Iran-backed militias were coordinated with the Iraqi government, a claim Baghdad has denied.

Observers believe it reflects rising discontent among Iraq’s leadership with armed groups accused of dragging the nation into regional conflicts that contradict Baghdad’s diplomatic and economic interests.

Al-Zaidi is currently facing the most significant test of his leadership.

Delivering on his promise to place all weapons under state control will be critical not only for Iraq’s internal security but also for maintaining trust with the United States, Gulf Arab states, and international investors, many of whom support many of the country’s largest economic projects.

Baghdad’s dilemma now extends beyond managing ties between Washington and Tehran.

It demonstrates that the Iraqi state possesses both the authority and the political will to prevent Iran-backed militias from using Iraqi territory to launch attacks that risk isolating the country, harming relations with Arab neighbors and the United States, and jeopardizing Iraq’s long-term economic recovery and investment goals.

World.title: Iraq faces growing fiscal strain
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is under increasing financial strain as plummeting oil earnings tighten government budgets, with Health Minister Abdul Hussein al-Mousawi saying that ensuring monthly public-sector wages has become the government’s top priority.

Speaking at a public meeting, al-Mousawi stated that the government requires approximately 10.8 trillion Iraqi dinars ($8.2 billion) per month to pay public-sector salaries, while current monthly oil revenues have fallen to approximately 2.5 trillion dinars, highlighting the growing gap between government obligations and income.

The statements are one of the most direct public acknowledgements by a top Iraqi official of the government’s financial challenges after months of decreased oil prices and fewer export profits.

Iraq’s government finances remain very vulnerable to variations in global energy markets because the vast bulk of public revenue comes from crude oil.

Official figures published this week indicated that oil accounted for over 84% of federal income in the first five months of 2026, but collections decreased by more than one-third compared to the same time the previous year as oil prices and export profits plummeted.

The health minister also warned of financing restrictions in the healthcare sector, citing worries about the supply of medications and the government’s capacity to sustain public services if financial pressures continue.

The fresh warnings follow weeks of increased regional tensions, which disrupted oil markets and added uncertainty to Iraq’s economic prospects.

As OPEC’s second-largest producer, Iraq relies on oil exports to fund wages, pensions, social welfare, and the majority of government expenditure, making the budget susceptible to long-term reductions in crude prices.

Economists have long cautioned that Iraq’s reliance on oil income makes the nation susceptible to external shocks, while a hefty public-sector pay bill constrains the government’s budgetary flexibility.

Previous administrations attempted to diversify income streams via tax changes and non-oil investments, but hydrocarbons remain the economy’s backbone.

The financial pressure comes at a critical time for Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s government, which has been promoting Iraq as a destination for billions of dollars in foreign investment following agreements signed with US, Turkish, and international companies in energy, banking, technology, and infrastructure.

Continued budgetary strain may make it more urgent to accelerate economic reforms, raise non-oil income, and improve public financial management to lessen Iraq’s reliance on petroleum exports.

They also emphasize that preserving investor trust will be contingent on the government’s ability to maintain macroeconomic stability while continuing to fund big development projects.

Despite the present issues, Iraq has large foreign currency reserves, which act as a financial cushion for the government.

However, experts warn that while reserves might help absorb short-term shocks, they are not a substitute for the fundamental changes needed to diversify the economy and reduce its dependence on unpredictable oil earnings.

World.title: Iraq expects record 22 million pilgrims for Arbaeen
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is prepared to welcome around 22 million pilgrims for this year’s Arbaeen pilgrimage, including up to 5 million overseas tourists, in what officials believe to be one of the country’s greatest religious gatherings and a significant boost to tourism and the local economy.

According to Iraqi official data, well over 22 million people are anticipated to attend the annual pilgrimage to the holy city of Karbala, with 4.5 million to 5 million pilgrims coming from outside Iraq.

The government has announced that tens of thousands of volunteers would be deployed to assist pilgrims, and Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has urged officials to boost the number of buses and other transport services to facilitate travel during the festival.

The surge of foreign tourists is projected to have a substantial impact on Iraq’s tourism, hospitality, transportation, and retail industries, with hotels, restaurants, transit operators, and local businesses benefitting from increased demand during the pilgrimage season.

Officials have extended transportation networks in preparation for this year’s pilgrimage, including more rail services, buses, and logistical assistance, as part of larger measures to boost connectivity and promote Iraq’s tourist industry.

The government has increasingly highlighted religious tourism as a crucial pillar of economic diversification, with millions of people visiting the country’s holy sites at Karbala, Najaf, Kadhimiya, and Samarra each year.

According to officials, continuing investment in infrastructure and tourist services will help Iraq become one of the Middle East’s major religious tourism destinations, while also creating jobs and helping local economies around the country.

World.title: Reports: Iraq PM threatened to resign over militia disarmament
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi has threatened to resign if Iran-aligned armed groups do not cooperate with his government’s efforts to bring all weapons under state control, according to reports citing political sources, highlighting the growing pressure on Baghdad to address one of its most difficult security challenges.

According to sources, Al-Zaidi warned leaders of Iraq’s Shi’ite Coordination Framework that if armed groups did not react to government efforts to disarm and completely submit to state authority, he would stand down.

IraqiNews.com was unable to independently verify the claims, and the Prime Minister’s office had no immediate response.

According to the sources, Al-Zaidi has been more dissatisfied by what he sees as a lack of cooperation on one of his administration’s fundamental commitments: guaranteeing that all weapons stay solely under the control of the Iraqi government.

The claims came days after US-Saudi airstrikes struck Iran-backed groups in Iraq in response to drone assaults on Saudi oil installations, which Riyadh said were launched from Iraqi territory.

The bombings forced Al-Zaidi to call an emergency security conference, cancel a planned trip to Saudi Arabia, and unveil a new security strategy aimed at preventing Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks on neighboring nations.

Armed organizations have emerged as one of Al-Zaidi’s most pressing problems.

Since entering office, he has attempted to solicit billions of dollars in foreign investment with trips to Washington, Tehran, and Ankara, while portraying Iraq as a stable location for oil, infrastructure, and technological projects.

Analysts believe Baghdad’s economic objectives are strongly dependent on its ability to show that the state, not armed groups, controls Iraq’s security strategy.

Repeated strikes conducted from Iraqi territory have strained ties with regional allies and risk weakening investor trust.

According to Western diplomatic sources published by Asharq Al-Awsat, key Iraqi officials, including Al-Zaidi and members of Iraq’s security apparatus, have received threats in connection with the government’s attempts to restrict weaponry outside of state control.

Unlike many regional leaders, Iraq’s prime minister leads by wide political agreement rather than a legislative majority, restricting his power to make unilateral choices.

Major security and political changes usually need agreement among Iraq’s different political blocs.

Al-Zaidi’s biggest power may not be the threat of resignation, but rather the international backing his administration has garnered as a result of recent accords with the United States, Turkey, and other allies.

These agreements, which span energy, finance, technology, and infrastructure, have boosted hopes that Iraq will attract tens of billions of dollars in investment if security improves.

Whether Al-Zaidi can translate that international momentum into domestic reforms will ultimately depend on gaining broader political support for his pledge to keep all weapons under Iraqi state control, which has become one of his government’s most closely watched tests.

World.title: Iraq denies launching strikes from its territory against neighboring nations
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The military spokesperson for the Iraqi commander-in-chief, Sabah al-Numan, confirmed on Thursday that neither a foreign nor local body has presented proof that recent regional drone attacks were launched from Iraqi territory.

In a statement to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA), al-Numan urged accusing parties to submit reliable proof, saying that Baghdad has yet to receive such data.

The development comes following statements made by the Saudi Ministry of Defense, alleging that drone attacks targeting key oil infrastructure in the past few days originated in Iraq.

The Iraqi official indicated that the government will neither tolerate unilateral military acts from within its borders nor accept foreign violations of its territorial sovereignty.

Al-Numan’s remarks come a day after the United States and Saudi Arabia launched coordinated airstrikes targeting several bases of Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), killing and injuring many fighters.

The joint operation targeted several logistical and weapons storage locations in different provinces in Iraq, escalating the current regional battle.

The PMF described the joint US-Saudi strike as a dangerous escalation and a clear breach of Iraqi sovereignty.

World.title: Iraqi oil flows to continue via Turkey’s Ceyhan as renewal deal is discussed
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Turkish sources told Reuters that crude oil shipments from northern Iraq to the Turkish port of Ceyhan will continue while the two countries seek an arrangement to extend the pipeline’s operation for another 12 months.

On July 27, a bilateral agreement that had been in place for decades ended. Despite expectations, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi did not sign a 12-month renewal deal during his meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara on Tuesday.

According to a Turkish official, oil flows via the Iraq-Turkey pipeline, which is Baghdad’s only operational export pipeline, will continue while negotiations for a renewal deal are still in progress.

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar recently announced a 12-month extension agreement between the two countries.

During a joint press conference in Ankara, Erdogan stated on Tuesday that Turkey hopes to finalize a comprehensive energy cooperation agreement as soon as possible.

An extension is intended to provide additional time for discussions on a complete accord. Turkey aims to fully utilize the 1.5 million barrels per day pipeline and consider expanding it to oil fields in southern Iraq.

Turkish data suggests that the pipeline currently transports approximately 170,000 barrels per day.

World.title: NEET-PG 2026 gets major overhaul: Centres closer to home, single-shift exam, fewer questions with no change in test duration
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Centre has announced a series of changes for the NEET-PG exam to be held later in the month, including expanding the choice of test locations, giving candidates more time to plan travel, and increasing the time available per question.

The reforms are aimed at making the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for Postgraduate (NEET-PG) process more convenient and secure, according to the Union health ministry.

Under the revised system, candidates will have to provide preferences for three states for their examination centre. Their correspondence state will be the mandatory first preference, allowing allotment of centres closer to their place of residence.

Earlier, examination centres were allotted on a first-come, first-served basis, prompting candidates to submit applications immediately after registrations opened. Those who delayed often found nearby centres unavailable and had to travel to other states.

Candidates will now be informed of their allotted test city nearly three weeks before the August 30 examination, giving them more time to arrange travel and accommodation.





The National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) has also revised the exam pattern, reducing the number of questions from 200 to 180 while keeping the total duration unchanged at 210 minutes. The move will provide candidates with more time per question.

The exam was earlier conducted with 200 multiple-choice questions carrying a maximum of 800 marks.

The ministry said the question paper preparation and delivery process has been strengthened through multiple layers of encryption, secure offline preparation, time-bound finalisation of papers shortly before the examination, and controlled digital decryption at the start of the test.

To further strengthen security, Aadhaar-based authentication has been introduced during registration and on the examination day. Iris-based biometric verification will be used where fingerprint authentication fails.

NBEMS has also introduced a dedicated email address for reporting impersonation, touting and other unfair practices, while issuing advisories to candidates to improve awareness and vigilance.

NEET-PG 2026 will be conducted in a single shift to ensure uniformity in difficulty level and assessment. In recent years, the exam was conducted in multiple shifts due to emergencies or postponements.

Union health minister JP Nadda on Saturday reviewed preparations for the examination and directed agencies to ensure a smooth, secure, transparent and technology-enabled process. He assessed the readiness of NBEMS, technology partners and other stakeholders, and stressed the need for a fair and candidate-friendly examination.

A total of 2,73,183 candidates have registered for the medical entrance test, an increase of over 12.5% from last year. The exam will be held in a single shift across around 340 cities and more than 1,300 centres.

Security measures include advance sealing and verification of centres, CCTV surveillance, biometric authentication, candidate frisking, deployment of signal jammers, live monitoring through central and regional command centres, and supervision by independent observers and appraisers.

More than 60,000 examination functionaries will be deployed for the smooth conduct of the examination, the ministry said.

World.title: Army's intelligence units, Rajasthan police bust counterfeit combat uniform racket in Sriganganagar
World.content:
The action followed a seizure of similar counterfeit combat cloth in Bareilly in June this year

NEW DELHI: Busting a big racket on counterfeit military uniforms, a joint operation by Indian Armyâs intelligence units and Rajasthan police has led to the seizure of nearly 1,000 metres of unauthorised army-pattern combat cloth from shops across the stateâs Sriganganagar district.Acting on a lead, intelligence personnel of the Indian Army carried out a discrete investigation in the city, which pointed to a local firm, as a key link in the supply chain allegedly distributing counterfeit army-pattern combat cloth to shops in Sriganganagar town as well as Lalgarh Jattan, Suratgarh and other nearby markets, the Indian Army said.An interim investigation report was shared with Rajasthan police in mid-July, leading to a coordinated operation on July 30 in which security personnel and police searched multiple shops across the district. The raids yielded approximately 1,000 metres of unauthorised, new-pattern counterfeit combat cloth, exposing a wider network allegedly supplying counterfeit military uniforms to vendors in the region, the Army said.The action followed a seizure of similar counterfeit combat cloth in Bareilly in June this year, which was traced back to a manufacturing source in Sriganganagar.Radical elements and terrorists had in the past exploited open-market military fatigues to infiltrate high-security zones or stage attacks such as in Pathankot and J&K.In India, unauthorised sale, production or storage of official military-pattern camouflage cloth is heavily restricted and banned by local civil administrations in many sensitive regions. Section 168 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 punishes any civilian who unlawfully wears military uniforms or carries tokens of the Indian armed forces with the intent to trick others into believing they are a soldier, sailor or airman.Furthermore, the Indian Army holds exclusive Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) over its digital camouflage pattern design, making commercial reproduction by open-market vendors illegal.

World.title: 'You should've apologized': Congress targets PM Modi over his 'forgive you' remark in Insta video
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress leader Supriya Shrinate on Saturday launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi, demanding that he apologise to the country instead of "forgiving" people, while accusing the Centre of using excessive force against students protesting over the alleged NEET-UG 2026 examination irregularities.

In a post on X, Shrinate described the Prime Minister as a "drama king" and questioned his remarks, saying he should instead apologise to the country's youth.

"What a drama king Narendra Modi is. You should have been the one to apologize, Modi ji, and instead you're forgiving the country!" she wrote.

Shrinate accused the government of allowing brutality against student protesters and listed several allegations in her post.

She demanded an apology for the alleged use of force against students, including pellet firing, lathi-charge, use of spiked batons, electrocuting protesters, injuries to a young girl, and the alleged mistreatment of women protesters.

World.title: ‘My return to Kolkata proves injustice cannot be permanent’: Taslima Nasreen
World.content:
Exiled Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasreen in Kolkata. (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Exiled Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasreen on Saturday described her return to India after nearly two decades as proof that âinjustice can be long but cannot be permanent. âShe made the remarks at an event in Kolkata, nearly two decades after she was forced to leave the city in 2007. The 63-year-old writer had been living in Kolkata since leaving Bangladesh in 1994 amid alleged death threats from radical groups over her writings and views on religion.Nasreen, who has been living in Europe since leaving Kolkata, also clarified that her return to the city was not linked to any "political agenda.""Today, the opening of this door proves that injustice can be long, but it cannot be permanent. History remembers who closed the doors and who opened them...I am not here to speak for any political party, or against any party. I am here to speak in favour of women's rights," PTI quoted her as saying.She also expressed concern over what she described as a "rise" in religious extremism in Bangladesh."I am against all forms of fundamentalism, but I have spoken against Islamic fundamentalists because I have seen it from close quarters since childhood.The rise of fundamentalism in Bangladesh is at an alarming stage. Freedom of speech is being curtailed," Nasreen said.Visibly emotional, Nasreen called her return a "fulfilment of a long-awaited moment.""It took me 19 years to say these words: 'I have returned to Kolkata.' I felt the pain of losing an address every single day. On August 8, 1994, the then government forced me to leave Bangladesh. The state may have removed me from my country, but it could never remove my country from within me," she added.Lamenting that she could not find a permanent home in either Bangladesh or West Bengal, Nasreen highlighted that Europe had provided her security but not a sense of belonging."Europe has given me citizenship and a place to live, but unfortunately, I couldn't get a small place to stay in the two Bengals. Europe gave me security, but it could not give me a sense of belonging. A home is not built by security alone; it is built by language, memory and culture," Nasreen remarked.Nasreen maintained that she had never been convicted by any court but had faced restrictions because of opposition from fundamentalist groups."I committed no crime. No court has ever punished me. It is a painful truth of our times that a writer needs police protection to visit the city of her own language."Rejecting allegations that her writings were offensive, she emphasised that her advocacy had focused on equality and human rights."I only spoke about equal rights for women and men, and about human rights irrespective of religion or caste. I said that any rule or doctrine that takes away equality and human dignity must be changed."She also criticised what she described as the unequal treatment of women in the name of religion and backed a Uniform Civil Code across South Asia, arguing that religion-based personal laws discriminate against women."The real conflict is between secularism and fundamentalism, between the rational mind and irrationality, between innovation and tradition, and between people who value freedom and those who do not."

World.title: DMK moves SC seeking immediate release of Cauvery water from Karnataka to Tamil Nadu
World.content:
Responding to the growing protests in Karnataka, chief minister DK Shivakumar appealed on Saturday to organisations opposing the release of water to withdraw their proposed agitation.

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) on Saturday moved the Supreme Court seeking directions to the Karnataka government to immediately release Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu, arguing that Karnataka must comply with the apex court's 2018 verdict and the recent directions issued by the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA).The plea seeks an order directing Karnataka to implement the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee's recommendation, upheld by the CWMA on Thursday, to release 3,500 cusecs of water per day for 15 days to Tamil Nadu at the inter-state border point of Biligundlu."Direct the State of Karnataka / Respondent No. 1 to forthwith and fully implement the direction of the CWRC dated July 28, 2026, as affirmed by the CWMA on July 30, 2026, by ensuring a flow of 3,500 cusecs per day at Biligundlu for the period of 15 days commencing from date of the order passed by this Hon'ble Court, and to make good the shortfall in compliance from July 29, 2026 onwards," the DMK said in its plea.The party also sought a direction to Karnataka to clear the accumulated shortfall in water releases. It asked the court to direct the state to "make good the accumulated backlog of about 9.46 TMC due at Biligundlu as on July 26, 2026, computed on the pro-rata/distress-sharing basis, by ensuring releases such that about 7,000 cusecs per day is realised at Biligundlu over a period of 15 days".In addition, the DMK urged the Supreme Court to direct the CWMA to monitor reservoir releases in Karnataka and the flows realised at Biligundlu on a day-to-day basis and submit compliance reports.The move comes amid renewed tensions between the two southern states over the sharing of Cauvery waters during the current monsoon season. On Thursday, the CWMA upheld the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee's recommendation that Karnataka release 3,500 cusecs of water daily for the next 15 days to Tamil Nadu.Responding to the growing protests in Karnataka, chief minister DK Shivakumar appealed on Saturday to organisations opposing the release of water to withdraw their proposed agitation. The farmer groups and pro-Kannada organisations staged demonstrations across the Cauvery basin, arguing that the state could not spare even a drop of water for Tamil Nadu because major reservoirs did not have enough water even for drinking.Shivakumar said the Kabini reservoir was rapidly filling up and warned that water could not be retained once the reservoir reached full capacity."Kabini reservoir is filling up. Once a dam is full, water has to be released. It is impossible to hold it back. I humbly appeal to those planning to agitate against the release of water to withdraw their decision," he said.Shivakumar also cautioned protesters against approaching water release points, saying, "Even if we decide not to release water, once the reservoir is full, it is impossible to hold it back. Protesters should not go near the points where water is being released. The force of the water can sweep you away. No one should lie down in the path of flowing water."The Karnataka CM said the state would protect the interests of its farmers while respecting judicial orders. "There is an order to release 177 TMC of water to Tamil Nadu, and the Supreme Court has upheld it. We must respect the court's order while also protecting the interests of our farmers. Our government is committed to safeguarding the welfare of Karnataka's farmers," he said.He also accused the BJP of "politicising" the issue and said an all-party meeting would be held to consult former chief ministers, political leaders and legal experts before deciding the state's next course of action. According to Shivakumar, Tamil Nadu had sought 9,000 cusecs, but the Authority had directed Karnataka to release only 3,500 cusecs.The Cauvery Water Management Authority was constituted by the Centre in 2018 following the Supreme Court's final verdict on the decades-old Cauvery river water dispute among Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and Puducherry. The Authority includes representatives of the riparian states as well as a nominee of the central government and is responsible for overseeing implementation of the court-mandated water-sharing arrangement.

World.title: ‘Egg-therapy could turn on its head’: Bengal BJP chief Samik Bhattacharya cautions party workers
World.content:
NEW DELHI: BJP's West Bengal unit president Samik Bhattacharya on Saturday cautioned party workers against becoming arrogant, warning that the infamous "egg therapy" could otherwise "turn on its head.

"

"No system can function or be made to live for long by quashing protests. All autocracies across the world inevitably fall. If someone from our side sports a body language of having 207 MLAs and hits the road, then the consequence will be disastrous," he said at event in Kolkata, referring to the number seats the BJP won in the assembly elections in April to form its first government in the state.

âThe unwarranted egg therapy we see now can turn on its head and start falling on the other side as well. Everyone, including those in my party, must understand that. Those âSanatanisâ who have suddenly found a place in our party and are harbouring aspirations for influence and advantage must also remain careful because the trajectory of those eggs can change in no time,â the Rajya Sabha MP remarked, apparently referring to leaders who joined the BJP from the

(TMC), which lost power in West Bengal after 15 years.

The âegg therapyâ Bhattacharya mentioned alluded to incidents of egg-pelting targeting TMC leaders after the party's defeat.

He also acknowledged that despite having assumed political power in West Bengal, the BJP has not yet been entirely successful in eradicating the "culture of extortion."

"Our government has come to power only two months ago. We have not been able to solve all problems. If I say that we have been able to eradicate extortion from everywhere, then I will be making a false claim.





There are deviations. People had become accustomed to passing through a system of making easy money through syndicates. Not everything has changed with the change in state power," Bhattacharya told the audience.

"Some joined the ruling party (BJP) within four hours, others had dormant wishes that have now surfaced. We are trying to control such tendencies within the party. Our CM Suvendu Adhikari is also trying to apply strict brakes on such tendencies."

Emphasising the need to free the business ecosystem from "partisan politics," the BJP leader argued that West Bengal stood at the "cusp of breaking with its chequered industrial past."

"We must keep partisan politics out of this system. We have become residents of a political society in West Bengal. We need freedom from it. Till such time Bengal is able to come out of the culture of infiltration of politics in every sphere of life, no government can bring about its effective change and attract investment."

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Fantastic five as Indian boxers put on a show
World.content:
To have 10 boxers — six women and four men — reach the finals across 14 weight categories is no mean feat and a testament to India’s commanding performance at the Commonwealth Games at the Scottish Event Campus here on Saturday (August 1, 2026).

India capped its finest-ever boxing campaigns at the Games, with five pugilists winning gold medals so far.

Preeti Pawar opened the floodgates for India. Facing a relentless Scarlett Delgado, Preeti absorbed the pressure with calm defence and struck effectively when opportunities came her way, earning a 5-0 win over the Canadian in the women’s 54kg title clash.

It was then Jaismine Lamboria’s turn to showcase her technical brilliance against Northern Ireland’s Michaela Walsh in the women’s 57kg final, and the reigning World champion did so in emphatic fashion, cruising to a 5-0 victory.

Jaismine was near-flawless in execution, repeatedly outboxing her experienced opponent. Walsh, conceding both height and reach, struggled to land clean punches as the Indian controlled the distance with ease.

Whenever her opponent tried to close in, Jaismine either slipped away with swift footwork or stood her ground to unleash sharp right-left combinations that consistently found the target.

Jadumani Singh, meanwhile, produced an entertaining display in the men’s 55kg final against Australia’s Jye Dixon. The 22-year-old delighted the crowd with his lightning-quick footwork and crisp punching combinations, but Dixon’s accuracy and control ultimately proved decisive as Jadumani went down fighting 0-5.

Sakshi Chaudhary earned India’s its third gold with a 5-0 win over Ruby White of England in the women’s 51kg final.

White kept charging Sakshi in all the three rounds but the latter played within herself and scored points at will.

Priya Ghanghas’ hard-fought 4-1 victory over Canada’s Marie-Bathoul Al-Ahmadieh in the women’s 60kg summit clash sparked celebrations in the Indian corner.

Head coach Santiago Nivea hugged his support staff as the country claimed its fourth boxing gold of the Games, eclipsing the three it had secured at Birmingham in 2022.

Arundhati Choudhary put up a sparkling display to outwit Chantelle Reid of England 5-0 in the women’s 70kg gold medal bout. Although Reid appeared to be the aggressor early on, constantly moving forward and looking to land punches against her rivals, it was Arundhati who dictated the tempo with her sharp, direct combinations.

The Indian remained composed under pressure, countering Reid’s attacks with powerful straight punches and precise execution to take control of the contest and win the country its fifth gold.

Emma-Sue Greentree of Australia dashed India’s hopes of a sixth gold, defeating Lovlina Borgohain 4-1 in a split decision in the women’s 75kg final.

World.title: Counterfeit military combat uniform racket comes to light in Rajasthan
World.content:
A joint operation by the Army’s Intelligence units and the Rajasthan Police has uncovered a counterfeit military combat uniform racket in Rajasthan’s Sriganganagar district, leading to the seizure of nearly 1,000 metres of unauthorised Army-pattern combat cloth.

According to the Army, the operation was launched after a consignment of counterfeit combat cloth was seized in Bareilly in June this year. Investigators traced the material to a manufacturing source in Sriganganagar, prompting the Army’s Intelligence units to carry out a discreet probe.

The investigation identified a local firm as a key link in the supply chain, allegedly distributing counterfeit Army-pattern combat cloth to shops in Sriganganagar town as well as Lalgarh Jattan, Suratgarh, and other nearby markets.

Based on the Army’s interim investigation report shared with the Rajasthan Police in mid-July, a coordinated operation was carried out on July 30. Joint teams searched multiple shops across the district and seized around 1,000 metres of unauthorised new-pattern combat cloth.

Security risk
