Officials said the unauthorised possession, sale or use of military-pattern combat cloth is a punishable offence and poses a significant security risk by potentially facilitating the impersonation of armed forces personnel.

The investigation is continuing to identify the manufacturers, suppliers, and distribution network behind the counterfeit military-pattern fabric.

World.title: Worker injured in Kulgam attack dies; L-G pushes for SoPs to protect migrant labourers
World.content:
As the death toll in the Kulgam terror attack rose to two on Saturday (August 1, 2026), Jammu and Kashmir Lieutenant-Governor, Manoj Sinha, asked security agencies “to conduct a comprehensive review of the Standard Operating Procedures (SoPs) established to protect labourers from outside in J&K”.

Targeting the Centre over its “failure to contain terrorism”, J&K Deputy Chief Minister Surinder Choudhary demanded a high-level probe into the killings, while questioning the Centre’s peace narrative.

Also Read | Forces engaging two groups of terrorists in J&K’s forest areas

Suspected terrorists, in a targeted killing, fired upon two non-local labourers from Chhattisgarh on Friday (July 31) evening in Kulgam’s Kellam area. The attackers managed to flee after the attack under the cover of darkness.

One labourer, identified as Deepak Ratray, 24, was declared dead in a hospital late Friday evening. Bopinder Kumar, 28, also from Chhattisgarh, died during treatment. Both the deceased, who worked as labourers at a brick kiln, were cremated in Kulgam on Saturday afternoon under tight security arrangements.

J&K Chief Minister Omar Abdullah described the incident as “dastardly” and announced ex gratia relief of ₹10 lakh each for the next of kin of the deceased from the Chief Minister’s Relief Fund. This will be in addition to immediate assistance of ₹6 lakh each to be provided by the district administration.

Mr. Sinha said the J&K administration and the entire nation stand with the families.

Valley on alert

The attack, which is the second targeted attack in two weeks, has the security apparatus on tenterhooks in Kashmir. Frisking and search of vehicles were intensified across the Valley, especially on the Amarnath Yatra routes of Pahalgam and Baltal. Meanwhile, Mr. Sinha handed over an appointment letter to the son of Head Constable Ashiq Hussain Qureshi, who was killed in a similar attack on July 22, under the government’s compassionate appointment scheme.

The J&K L-G chaired a high-level security review meeting in Srinagar, which was attended by top security officials. A Lok Bhavan spokesperson said all the Deputy Commissioners and Senior Superintendents of Police (SSP) were directed by the L-G “to conduct a comprehensive review of the Standard Operating Procedures (SoPs) established to protect labourers from outside in J&K”.

The L-G directed the employers to provide insurance cover to non-local labourers and said their details should be registered with local police and district authorities. “We must intensify precise, high-impact anti-terror operations to neutralise the terrorists,” Mr. Sinha said.

‘Failed experiment’

Commenting on the sudden spurt in terror attacks, Mr. Choudhary said the region’s Statehood was ended, and Article 370 of the Constitution abrogated “on the promise that terrorism would be eradicated”. “Six years later, if innocent people are still being killed, the Centre must explain whether its experiment has failed,” Mr. Choudhary said.

J&K National Conference president, Dr. Farooq Abdullah, while condemning the attack, demanded a fair, transparent, and time-bound investigation to identify and punish the perpetrators of crime.

“It is difficult to ignore that whenever the demand for the restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s Statehood gains momentum, such disturbing incidents occur. Why does this repeatedly happen? The people deserve credible answers,” said Mr. Abdullah.

Kashmir chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq said that Islam upholds the sanctity of every innocent human life and unequivocally condemns the killing of innocent persons.

“Targeting poor labourers who have come to earn an honest livelihood is completely contrary to the teachings of Islam and the values of humanity. The spilling of innocent blood only brings more pain and suffering,” said the Mirwaiz.

He said violence as a means should be shunned; instead, the policy of accommodation, dialogue and engagement is the way forward to make South Asia a more peaceful and better place for all its people.

World.title: Vijay must visit Karnataka on August 3, says Premallatha Vijayakant
World.content:
Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay must visit Karnataka to hold talks, and the Tamil Nadu government must pass a resolution in the Assembly endorsing the Cauvery Water Management Authority’s directive to Karnataka to release 3,500 cusecs of water to Tamil Nadu, said the DMDK general secretary Premallatha Vijayakant in Hogenakkal on Saturday. She was leading the party’s protests against the proposed dam by Karnataka.

Speaking at the protests, she also urged the Tamil Nadu Chief Minister to meet the visiting Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and urge him to request his party’s government in Karnataka to release the water.

Underlining that Karnataka was not an enemy of Tamil Nadu and the Dravida Nadu included the four southern States, the DMDK leader differed with the opposition parties’ almost unanimous objection to the Chief Minister’s ‘proposed visit’ to Karnataka on August 3. If the Chief Minister could visit a temple in Karnataka for his personal gains, he definitely can visit Karnataka for the good of Tamil Nadu, she contended. And, so can the Karnataka Chief Minister. “Why can’t D.K. Shivakumar visit Tamil Nadu?” she asked.

Since, despite many court rulings, there has been no solution to the water sharing, it is imperative that the Chief Minister go to Karnataka for talks. “We want both Karnataka and Tamil Nadu to thrive and coexist. It is imperative for the Chief Minister to convene an all-party meeting and make a joint representation to the Prime Minister.”

Later addressing the media, she urged Mr. Vijay to step out of Chennai, visit Hogenakkal, Mettur, and the delta districts. “We ask the Chief Minister to come and see people’s problems,” Ms. Premallatha said.

Tamil Nadu, which used to be a power surplus State at one point, is now grappling with power shortage in even the Chief Minister’s own constituency, leading to the public are protesting on the streets. There is water shortage. The Chief Minister should work to turn the State into both a power and water surplus State, the DMDK leader said.

The protests also saw the participation of the DMK led by the party district secretary (West) P. Palaniappan. Before spearheading the protests in Hogenakkal, the DMDK leader inspected Biligundulu, the entry point of Cauvery into Tamil Nadu in Krishnagiri. She took out a bottle of water from Cauvery and poured it back into the river wishing water surplus and prosperity for Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

Ms. Premallatha also spoke in Kannada, directing her address to Mr. Shivakumar, and urged him to heed the CWMA’s directive, saying, “Air and water belong to all, and they cannot be confined to borders.”

World.title: World Breastfeeding Week celebrations begin with rallies and awareness sessions
World.content:
The World Breastfeeding Week celebrations took off in the city on Saturday, with government hospitals lining up rallies, human chains, interactive sessions to promote awareness on breastfeeding practices.

The Institute of Social Paediatrics, Government Stanley Medical College Hospital (SMCH), and the Department of Neonatology of the Institute of Child Health (ICH) and Hospital for Children have planned week-long events. As a part of this, the SMCH has also placed awareness posters in many Metrorail stations, including Airport, CMBT, Egmore, Central, Washermenpet and Wimco Nagar.

World Breastfeeding Week is celebrated from August 1 to 7 every year. This year’s theme is “Breastfeeding for a Sustainable Start in Life: Strengthen What Works”.

SMCH dean A. Aravind and Director of the Institute of Social Paediatrics J. Ganesh were present. The hospital is organising an interactive discussion on breastfeeding for mothers on August 2, followed by cultural programmes by undergraduate and postgraduate students on August 3. There will be an awareness and training session by a certified lactation consultant for postgraduate students on August 4, while cultural events by anganwadi workers to encourage breastfeeding and educate women about its benefits has been planned on August 5.

At ICH, the World Breastfeeding Week took off with a rally flagged off by the institute’s director Luke Ravi Chelliah. Doctors, nurses, and nursing students went around the hospital, holding placards and raising slogans to promote breastfeeding awareness among the general public.

Gopaul, retired Director and Superintendent of ICH, and Kuppulakshmi, director of the Institute of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, were present at the event.

Exclusively breastfed well babies were identified and presented gifts. ICH’s Department of Neonatology has planned week-long activities for creating awareness among various sectors of people.

Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research also launched the celebrations. The week-long programme comprises a series of academic sessions, community outreach initiatives, and public awareness activities, bringing together faculty members, students, and healthcare professionals.

Rela Hospital organised a 3-km walkathon from its hospital premises in Chrompet. Over 200 healthcare professionals, including doctors and nurses, took part in the event, along with members of the public.

World.title: UAS-B introduces low-cost technology to farmers to produce biochar, trains them to improve soil health
World.content:
Researchers at the University of Agricultural Sciences - Bangalore (UAS-B) are training 10 farmers each in 10 districts across Karnataka to produce their own biochar using crop residue left in their fields and the materials provided by the university.

Biochar is a lightweight, highly porous, charcoal-like substance made by heating organic biomass (like agricultural waste or wood) in a low-oxygen environment, a process called pyrolysis.

Krishna Murthy and his team from the Department of Science and Agriculture Chemistry, UAS-B, have used a simple and portable drum technology that doesn’t cost much to produce biochar.

Mr. Murthy explained, “We have come up with this idea keeping small and marginal farmers in mind. We have used a 200 litres portable drum with small holes drilled into it and a pipe fixed to it that works as a chimney. Farmers can dump the crop residue instead of burning it on their fields.”

This crop residue can be generated from coconut shells, sunflower head, mulberry prunings, among others.

He added, “We have identified 10 farmers each in Chitradurga, Tumakuru, Bengaluru Rural, Kolar, Chickballapur, Ramanagara, Mandya, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar and Hassan districts under Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) funded by the Union government. We are providing the drums to them free of cost and train them on how to produce biochar.”

The RKVY is a flagship central scheme launched in 2007 to boost holistic development in agriculture and allied sectors.

Method to produce biochar

Farmers can use any kind of crop residue and fill the drum with it. Fire is lit and the lid closed so that the entry of air is restricted. The air enters only through the holes. Due to limited oxygen, it burns and turns in to biochar in two to three hours, Mr. Murthy said.

“This biochar also looks like coal but it is not the same. In normal coal, the carbon content is lost, whereas in biochar, the organic carbon content is preserved through the process of pyrolysis,” he said. He further explained that where open burning releases almost all of a residue’s carbon as CO₂ within minutes, pyrolysis locks 50% to 80% of that carbon into a recalcitrant form that resists decomposition for years to decades once returned to the soil — directly rebuilding the Soil Organic Carbon stock that intensive cropping has depleted over the years. “We have experimented the same in our university and obtained positive results in increasing the fertility of soil. Hence, we decided to introduce it to the farmers,” he said.

Benefits for farmers

He also highlighted that field trials indicate biochar can improve crop productivity by 10% to 30% and water-holding capacity by 10% to 25%, with the largest gains in low-SOC soils — precisely Karnataka’s most affected areas.

According to the researchers in the Department of Science and Agriculture Chemistry, Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) is the most reliable indicator of long-term soil health, governing water retention, nutrient cycling and microbial activity. However, the organic carbon content in soil in Karnataka record has deteriorated sharply. The Bhoochetana initiative introduced by the State government in 2009 found 52% of sampled fields deficient in SOC, and a 2017-2024 State Agriculture Department analysis confirmed that more than half the State’s farmland now falls below the critical 0.5% threshold.

Kolar district is the most severely affected, with over 94% of its farmland in the low-SOC category. The black soil tracts of North Karnataka — Belagavi, Vijayapura, Kalaburagi, Bidar, Yadgir and Bagalkot — are similarly depleted under continuous cotton and oilseed cultivation. Coastal districts retain comparatively healthier SOC, aided by alluvial deposition and traditional mulching.

Dr. Murthy cited that the causes are interlinked especially disproportionate dependence on chemical fertilizers (Karnataka’s usage crossed 45 lakh tonnes in 2020-22), falling Farm Yard Manure use due to cost differentials (₹14,000/acre for manure vs. ₹3,000 for equivalent chemical Nitrogen Phosphorus and Potassium), shrinking livestock numbers (1.48 crore in 2007 to 1.14 crore in 2019), continuous monocropping, and the routine open burning of crop residue that destroys the very biomass-carbon soils need most.

World.title: Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar faces political tests on multiple fronts
World.content:
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar appears to have entered a politically challenging phase, with his leadership being tested simultaneously on multiple fronts — the Cauvery water-sharing issue, the long-pending expansion of the State Cabinet, the proposed Bidadi township project and the government’s drive to clear encroachments on footpaths.

The Chief Minister has increasingly found himself on the defensive. His appeal to his Tamil Nadu counterpart, C. Joseph Vijay, to postpone his proposed visit to Bengaluru in the wake of the Cauvery Water Management Authority’s (CWMA) direction on the release of water reflected the political sensitivity surrounding the inter-State river dispute.

Many visits to Delhi

The delay in the Cabinet expansion has emerged as perhaps the major political challenge before Mr. Shivakumar. Despite repeated visits to New Delhi, he has so far been unable to secure the Congress high command’s approval to fill the 20 vacant ministerial berths. His return from the national capital without a finalised list of new Ministers has fuelled speculation that the State leadership enjoys limited autonomy. Unlike his predecessor Siddaramaiah, who expanded his Cabinet to its full strength within days of assuming office, Mr. Shivakumar has had to wait for the party leadership’s clearance.

The Cauvery dispute presents a different set of political constraints. Any decision to release water to Tamil Nadu invites criticism from Kannada organisations, farmers and the Opposition, while disregarding the CWMA’s directions could expose the government to legal consequences. With little room for political manoeuvre, the government has struggled to strike a balance between protecting Karnataka’s interests and complying with statutory obligations. The BJP and the JD(S) have sought to portray the government as “weak” in defending the State’s interests. However, with copious rains on Saturday (August 1), the situation, at least for the time-being, seems to be easing.

Similarly, the proposed integrated township near Bidadi has exposed the tension between Bengaluru’s urban expansion and the concerns of farmers facing land acquisition. Although the government initially defended the project, sustained protests by farmers and Opposition parties compelled it to constitute a committee to examine its merits and demerits. While the move helped defuse immediate tensions, it also created the perception that the government had retreated from its original position under public pressure.

Footpath vs. livelihood

The government’s campaign to reclaim footpaths by removing encroachments, abandoned vehicles and other obstructions presents another political challenge. While the middle-class urban residents favour sanitised and more accessible public spaces, street vendors and small traders constitute an important political constituency. Any large-scale eviction without adequate rehabilitation risks generating political backlash, making the enforcement drive a delicate balancing act between urban governance and livelihood concerns.

None of these issues is likely to threaten Mr. Shivakumar’s leadership. However, they reinforce the perception that his government is spending considerable political capital on managing controversies and competing interests rather than advancing its governance agenda.

World.title: Centre to release its share of over ₹2,117 crore for disaster relief in advance to seven flood-hit States
World.content:
The Union government has approved the advance release of its share of the State Disaster Response Fund of ₹2,117.85 crore to support seven flood-affected States during the ongoing monsoon season, an official statement said on Saturday (August 1, 2026).

Of the affected States, Himachal Pradesh, Odisha, and Nagaland have already received the first instalment of the Central share for the financial year 2026-27.

“To ensure timely availability of funds for relief operations, Union Home Minister Amit Shah has approved the advance release of the second instalment of the Central share of SDRF to Himachal Pradesh and Odisha,” the statement said.

Himachal Pradesh has been sanctioned ₹193.95 crore and Odisha is to get ₹500 crore as their second instalments.

The advance release of first instalments has been approved for Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Gujarat, and Maharashtra by relaxing documentary requirements under applicable guidelines, considering the urgent need for resources for relief measures, the statement said.

The assistance approved for Arunachal Pradesh amounts to ₹44.55 crore, for Assam ₹379.35 crore, for Gujarat ₹500 crore, and for Maharashtra ₹500 crore.

“With this approval, a total of ₹2,117.85 crore has been made available to the flood-affected States to strengthen their ongoing relief and response measures,” the statement said.

Inter-Ministerial Central Teams (IMCT) have already been deputed to Arunachal Pradesh and Assam to assess damages. Two IMCT visits have been undertaken in Assam in view of the severity of the flood situation there, it said, adding, “On request of the Government of Nagaland, an IMCT is being constituted for the state.” The statement further said the Centre has been continuously monitoring the flood situation in close coordination with the State governments since the onset of the monsoon.

“Under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the government remains committed to extending all necessary assistance to states for effective relief, rescue and rehabilitation measures and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” it added.

World.title: Army major martyred in North Waziristan IBO: ISPR
World.content:
An army officer was martyred during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in the Razmak area of North Waziristan district, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said in a statement on Saturday.

During the operation, security forces also killed five terrorists affiliated with Fitna al Khawarij, according to the military’s media wing.

Fitna al Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).

The ISPR said that Major Hafiz Ihsan Elahi, 34, from Mianwali district, was “a brave officer who was leading his troops from the front, fought gallantly, paid the ultimate sacrifice” and embraced martyrdom.

Weapons and ammunition were also recovered from the killed terrorists, “who remained actively involved in numerous terrorist activities” against security forces and law enforcement agencies, as well as in the killing of civilians.

“Sanitisation operations are being conducted to eliminate any other India-sponsored terrorist found in the area. Relentless counter-terrorism campaign under the vision ‘Azm-i-Istehkam’ (as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country,” the ISPR statement read.

“Such sacrifices of our brave soldiers further reinforce our unwavering commitment of safeguarding our nation at all costs.”

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the government was implementing a comprehensive and effective strategy to “completely eliminate” the menace posed by the proscribed Fitna-al-Hindustan, Fitna-al-Khawarij and other terrorist outfits to the country.

Pakistan has seen a surge in terrorism since the banned TTP ended its ceasefire deal with the government in November 2022, vowing to increase attacks.

Last month, in the wake of multiple major attacks in Balochistan, Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir had reaffirmed that terrorism “emanating from across the borders will be crushed with full might of the state”.

On July 29, the military’s media wing said security forces killed 32 terrorists during operations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan.

7 terrorists killed in Nushki IBO

In a separate statement, ISPR said security forces killed “seven Indian-sponsored terrorists” during an IBO in Balochistan’s Nushki district on the night of July 30/31 July.

Among those was a would-be suicide bomber, the ISPR said, noting that the IBO was carried out on the “reported presence of terrorists belonging to Indian proxy, Fitna al Hindustan” — a term designated by the state for terrorist organisations in Balo­chistan.

During the operation, a terrorist hideout was “identified, monitored and busted through prompt surgical action by own forces, killing all seven Indian sponsored terrorists, including a suicide bomber”, the statement said.

It added that ammunition and improvised explosive devices found there were also destroyed on-site.

Sanitisation operations were underway to eliminate “any other Indian sponsored terrorist found in the area”.

The military’s media affairs wing reaffirmed that the counter-terrorism campaign under Vision Azm-i-Istehkam would continue “at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and -supported terrorism from the country”.

A day earlier, Balochistan Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti vowed that the state would not retreat “even an inch” in its fight against terrorism.

Last month, security forces killed at least 16 terrorists during “Operation Al-Azm” in Balochistan’s Mastung district, which was launched after a shooting on a Karachi-bound coach claimed three lives and injured five others.

Security concerns heightened in Balochistan after a spate of major terrorist attacks took place in early July, which prompted counterterrorism operations across the province.

World.title: Bilawal receives JAAC response on reconciliation commission, says AJK PM to consult stakeholders on way forward
World.content:
PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on Saturday said he had received a response from the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) to his letter proposing the establishment of a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, adding that the party would now consult key stakeholders to determine the way forward.

The PPP has repeatedly called for the establishment of a truth and reconciliation commission amid protests in AJK.

Over the past month, the regional administration and the JAAC have been at odds over various issues — most notably the committee’s demand to abolish the 12 seats in the region’s Legislative Assembly reserved for refugees from Indian-occupied Jammu and Kashmir who settled in mainland Pakistan after 1947, which has resulted in protests across the region.

In a post on X, Bilawal welcomed the group’s “willingness to engage with the proposed commission” as a possible institutional mechanism to address the crisis, noting that the proposal had also been endorsed by the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly.

The PPP chairman maintained that his “foremost priority” is to help bring an end to the “ongoing crisis” and provide relief to the region’s people and restore normal life in AJK as “soon as possible”.

“The loss of every precious life is a national tragedy.”

Bilawal said he would now consult AJK Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore, who would seek initial input from the federal government and other relevant stakeholders to determine whether there was sufficient common ground to move forward with a mutually agreed proposal.

Earlier, Bilawal said he had been campaigning for the formation of the commission for the past month.

Addressing a public gathering of party workers in Muzaffarabad earlier this week, the PPP chairman said: “It is necessary that during these historic elections, we restore peace and maintain fairness and transparency. To honour the future of Kashmir and Pakistan’s stance on Kashmir, this is not about anyone’s victory or defeat. The state and the protesters will have to accept this recommendation from the PPP.”

The region’s legislative assembly had also endorsed a resolution asking for the establishment of an independent reconciliation commission to investigate the violence and pave the way for a negotiated settlement.

JAAC ban

The regional government on June 5 declared the JAAC a proscribed organisation and placed it under the First Schedule of the region’s anti-terrorism act.

The notification by AJK’s Home Department said the group was “engaged in terrorism” and acted in a manner “prejudicial to peace and security” of the state.

It further stated that JAAC was involved in “creating anarchy in the state by intimidating public, promoting hatred and creating a sense of insecurity in society and public at large etc”.

Following the ban, local authorities launched a crackdown against the organisation, arresting scores of its leaders and activists from different areas.

In a televised press conference on July 28, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar alleged the involvement of militant elements within JAAC, adding that they were pursuing a foreign agenda and backed by Indian funding.

The information minister reiterated claims made earlier in the day by the region’s information secretary and a senior police official that a significant number of protesters participating in the proscribed JAAC demonstration in AJK were affiliated with Fitna Al Khawarij.

World.title: Renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja, others perish in Broad Peak avalanche, climbing company confirms
World.content:
Renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja died along with other team members in a powerful avalanche on Broad Peak, his climbing company confirmed on Saturday.

The avalanche struck on Thursday, cutting off contact with the international expedition led by 43-year-old British-Nepali climber Purja.

“It is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak,” Purja’s company Elite Expeditions said on social media.

“We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive,” it added.

The remains recovered so far — flown by helicopter to hospital for formal identification — included an American woman, an Omani woman and a Nepali man, the Gilgit-Baltistan government said in a statement released on Friday night.

Purja, who served with Britain’s Brigade of Gurkhas before joining the Special Boat Squadron of the Royal Marines, broke multiple climbing records since becoming a full-time mountaineer and tour guide.

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah offered his condolences over the “tragic” deaths of Purja and the other climbers, which he said “has shocked us”.

“The physical journey of all the deceased climbers… has been interrupted, but the history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring,” Shah said in a statement on social media.

Police in GB said in a statement that high-altitude porters and rescue teams were carrying out a second day of the operation on Saturday after the search was paused due to difficult weather conditions a day earlier.

Rescuers and army helicopters had been scouring the area and teams stayed at the base camp overnight, according to the GB government.

“The rescue operation is being conducted under extremely challenging terrain and high-altitude weather conditions by the Pakistani army in coordination with local high-altitude climbers and rescuers,” it said.

Powerful avalanche

The avalanche struck while the mountaineers were on a mission to summit Broad Peak (8,047 metres, or 26,400 feet) on Thursday and while the team was ascending at an altitude of around 6,600 metres, according to regional authorities.

The expedition comprised 10 people — including Purja, five Nepalis, a Pakistani, an Omani, an American, and a climber from China.

The team was last in contact on Thursday morning, the official statement said, with reports emerging that evening of the powerful avalanche.

“Data from their tracking devices indicates that they were thrown hundreds of metres down the mountainside,” Naila Kiani, from Pakistan’s Alpine Club, told Le Monde newspaper.

Fida Ali, a climber in the area who worked closely with Purja since 2023, told AFP their focus for the climbing season was summiting Broad Peak, but they had first tackled another mountain, G2, in harsh weather.

Ali also joined the expedition to Broad Peak in its initial stages but returned early to accompany a Russian climber who was feeling the effects of exhaustion — narrowly avoiding the fatal avalanche.

“I wanted to go with him (Purja) but couldn’t and came back with her. I was part of the team but survived,” he told AFP.

Super peaks

Purja had written on X this week that he was close to becoming the first person to climb all 14 “super peaks” twice without oxygen.

“Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down,” he wrote.

He had climbed all 14 “eight-thousanders” (peaks above 8,000 metres) in six months and six days between April and October 2019 — then a record.

Broad Peak is the world’s 12th highest mountain, located in the Karakoram range in northern Pakistan, and is regarded as one of the toughest and most technical climbs of all the 8,000-metre-plus ascents.

It was first summited in 1957 by an Austrian team.

World.title: US to make visa bond programme permanent for people from dozens of countries
World.content:
The US State Department will make permanent a visa bond programme that could require applicants from 50 countries, mostly from Africa, to post bonds of up to $20,000 when seeking US visas, according to a federal notice posted online on Friday.

The Federal Register notice applies to B1 and B2 visas, which are issued for business and tourism travel.

“Consular officers may require covered nonimmigrant visa applicants to post a bond of up to $20,000 as a condition of visa issuance, as determined by the consular officers,” the notice said.

“The 2025 visa bond pilot, which provided a framework for the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of the Treasury to assess the feasibility of administering a visa bond programme, has provided sufficient data to suggest that a visa bond programme is an effective tool for enforcing compliance among bonded visa holders.”

In the pilot programme, consular officers could require bonds of $5,000, $10,000 or up to $15,000. The final rule eliminates the $5,000 option and raises the maximum bond to $20,000.

The final rule goes into effect on August 3 when it is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register. In the list of 50 countries for whose citizens this programme applies, 30 are from Africa.

US officials say the policy is intended to reduce visa overstays. Immigration advocates argue it will deter legitimate travel to the United States.

Rights advocates say President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown violates free speech and due process, while creating an unsafe environment for ethnic minorities and encouraging racial profiling. Trump has defended the measures as necessary to bolster national security.

While Trump says he wants to curb illegal immigration, his administration has made legal immigration more difficult, for example, by imposing new and expensive fees for applicants of certain visas and by enforcing social media vetting for applicants and immigrants already in the country.

World.title: PML-N, PPP leaders resume talks to ease tensions over AJK polls
World.content:
MUZAFFARABAD: Senior leaders of the PML-N and PPP on Saturday resumed talks aimed at defusing tensions between the two parties following the latter’s allegations of rigging in four of the 13 constituencies in Mirpur division during the first phase of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) elections.

The PPP and the PML-N — coalition partners in the Centre — have been engaged in a war of words since the PML-N emerged in the lead during the first phase of polls. The PPP has accused the PML-N of rigging in Mirpur and demanded re-polling.

The latest round of talks followed two earlier meetings — the first at a local hotel on Thursday night and the second before noon on Friday.

The PML-N delegation comprised Prime Minister’s Adviser Rana Sanaullah, Federal Minister for Kashmir Affairs Amir Muqam, and PML-N AJK chapter secretary general and MLA-elect Chaudhry Tariq Farooq.

Representing the PPP were former Senate chairman Nayyar Bokhari, former federal minister Qamar Zaman Kaira and AJK Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore, who also serves as secretary general of the party’s AJK chapter.

PPP leader Nadeem Afzal Chan attended the Friday meeting but was absent from today’s session.

The meetings reviewed security arrangements ahead of the second phase of polling on Sunday. Both sides agreed that the Election Commission, as well as the divisional and district administrations, should leave no room for lapses in ensuring extraordinary security measures so that voters could exercise their franchise freely.

According to sources, the discussions also focused on the PPP’s allegations of rigging and its subsequent demand for repolling in certain constituencies.

The PPP was told that neither the government nor any institution had facilitated or backed rigging and that, if irregularities had occurred at any polling station, they were localised incidents rather than the result of any organised plan.

“It was not planned or pre-planned rigging but isolated acts at places where supporters of one candidate enjoyed numerical dominance over their opponents. Such incidents have unfortunately been part of the territory’s polling atmosphere and have also been witnessed in previous elections,” a source quoted the PML-N leaders as telling their counterparts.

The PML-N leadership maintained that, unlike the PPP, it had begun election preparations well in advance and had enforced greater organisational discipline through constituency-level planning.

The PPP, they claimed, had remained under the impression that the elections would be delayed by a year and that the 12 refugee constituencies would be abolished, which prevented it from focusing on electoral preparations in time.

The meeting also discussed ways to address the complaints through both political dialogue and legal channels, the source said.

According to the sources, the PPP had initially raised objections to the results in four constituencies: Charhoi, Sehnsa and Nakyal in Kotli district, and Barnala in Bhimber district. However, it later withdrew its allegations regarding Sehnsa and Barnala.

Saturday’s discussions centred on Charhoi, where PPP AJK president Chaudhry Yasin lost to the PML-N’s Raja Riasat, and Nakyal, where PPP candidate Javed Iqbal Budhanvi was defeated by the PML-N’s Raja Ayaz Ahmed.

The sources said the PML-N had presented a detailed analysis of the results, showing that while its candidates had secured more than 80 per cent of the votes at some polling stations, the PPP had also won more than 80pc of the votes at others.

“If any irregularities occurred, they occurred on both sides, and a mechanism has been discussed to address them, legally and politically,” said a PML-N leader.

The meeting tasked both regional secretary generals — Rathore and Farooq — with contacting the Election Commission to explore a legal resolution to the dispute.

Another meeting had been scheduled for Saturday afternoon, but it could not be held because Sanaullah and Muqam had to leave for Islamabad owing to urgent engagements.

Both parties traded barbs earlier this week after the conclusion of the first phase of elections in AJK, with the PPP chairman alleging rigging in the polls and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz urging the PPP to accept defeat.

The PML-N grabbed nine out of the 13 constituencies of AJK’s Mirpur division in the elections.

In a televised statement, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz hailed the “outstanding victory” of the PML-N in the first phase of the AJK elections, urging the PPP to accept defeat.

“The PPP should have accepted its defeat by affirming the spirit of democracy, but I felt aggrieved by the kind of words used by PPP leaders.”

“The state does not decide election results; only the people make this decision,” she said in response to PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s allegations.

On Thursday, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari warned that a stolen election in AJK would start a “countdown” for the federal government.

“If you steal [the election] … write it down, take my guarantee, that a countdown will start for your federal government,” he warned. “If you steal my mandate, I will come for your throne.”

World.title: PPP, PML-N continue war of words on eve of Muzaffarabad elections
World.content:
The PPP and the PML-N continued lambasting each other on Saturday, extending their rhetoric from the ongoing elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) to the other party’s previous tenures in power.

The PPP and the PML-N — coalition partners in the Centre — have been engaged in a war of words since the PML-N emerged as the winner in the elections in AJK’s Mirpur division. The PPP has accused the PML-N of rigging in Mirpur and demanded re-polling.

The political temperatures remain heated as the second phase of AJK elections is set to be held tomorrow in nine constituencies of Muzaffarabad division. The third phase is scheduled for August 10 in all 12 refugee constituencies, and 11 constituencies of Poonch division.

In the latest exchange, PML-N senior leader Rana Sanaullah remarked on President Asif Ali Zardari’s role as he responded to PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s allegations of rigging in the 2024 general elections.

“If you call the votes secured by the prime minister votes of Forms-47, then on what forms has the president gotten votes on?” Sanaullah said.

On Wednesday, Bilawal had taken a direct jibe at Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, saying: “If someone is sitting on the PM’s seat, or someone is sitting on the CM’s position today, even a child knows that it is not because of the people’s votes or your performance but because of Form-47.”

Sanaullah, also the prime minister’s aide on political affairs and a federal minister, was addressing a gathering in Jhelum Valley alongside Kashmir Affairs Minister Amir Muqam.

Sanaullah further said: “If you say to Mian Nawaz Sharif that he became the prime minister for the first time or every time through rigging, […] then remember, it is also discussed here that someone also became the prime minister for the first time after breaking apart the country.”

He was referring to PPP founder Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who became the president of Pakistan in December 1971 after the secession of Bangladesh (then-East Pakistan) following the 1970 elections.

In August 1973, Bhutto took the oath as the prime minister in 1973 under the new Constitution.

Sanaullah also took a jibe at Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, whose recent remarks have sparked a fresh debate in political circles on the matter of creating new provinces.

Calling Naqvi a “blessed one” of President Zardari, the PML-N leader said the interior minister had “made the [political] journey of 30 years in three-and-a-half years”.

“You began from where and have now reached where, and now you realise that this system is completely dysfunctional.”

In his speech, Muqam criticised the PPP’s governance in Sindh, saying that no performance of the party could be seen.

He also said the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) — a scheme that the PPP often takes credit for launching — was not “anyone’s personal programme but the government’s”.

Earlier on Saturday, PPP leader Saeed Ghani alleged that the PML-N had never won a general election without rigging.

This followed a press briefing by Punjab’s education and sports ministers, where they said that the chief ministers of Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had nothing to show for their performance.

PML-N never won an election without rigging: Ghani

Addressing a press conference in Karachi, Ghani said, “The PPP did not secure power through rigging in any of the elections held till today.

“On the other hand, however many times the PML-N has secured power, it has not been without rigging.”

PPP leader Saeed Ghani addresses a press conference in Karachi on Aug 1, 2026. — DawnNewsTV

Ghani, also the Sindh labour minister, made the allegation as he responded to a PML-N member calling on the PPP to not “give lectures on democracy”.

“If you do not want to give the PPP the right to speak on democracy, then will you give it to Gen Musharraf or Gen Zia, or the leaders created by them?” he quipped, referring to the two former military dictators.

The PPP leader said he “did count the 1985 election”, alleging that PML-N supremo and ex-premier Nawaz Sharif “conspired” against ex-prime minister Mohammad Khan Junejo.

He further claimed that his party “became a target of rigging” in the 1988 and 1990 elections, which resulted in the PML-N winning. He went on to allege that the PPP was again “controlled and prevented from forming a government in Punjab” in 1993.

Ghani alleged that the PPP was restricted to “16-17 seats” in the 1997 general elections, when Nawaz’s PML-N again formed the government.

He contended that although the PPP secured power in 2008, the “PML-N was made to win seats, especially in Punjab, through rigging during Musharraf’s tenure”.

Ghani claimed that the PML-N was “made to win” the 2013 elections as well.

“Then the elections in 2024 [took place]. No matter how many times they say, everyone, even children, know that the PML-N was badly defeated in the elections,” he asserted.

The PPP leader alleged that Nawaz, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz “lost their own seats and then blame us”.

Ghani made the remarks after explaining the rationale for his party’s stances on new provinces in Sindh and Punjab, stressing that it was based on the wishes of the people.

He emphasised that the Constitution required any such move to be made through the elected representatives in the provincial assembly concerned.

He noted that the “people of Sindh, its representatives and its assembly say there is no need for further provinces in Sindh”.

On the other hand, Ghani pointed out, the Punjab Assembly and the Senate had passed resolutions over a decade ago calling for two new provinces in Punjab.

“If the people and the elected representatives of Sindh say that there is no need for any new province in Sindh, then no one in Punjab has the right to say whether there should be a new province in Sindh or not,” Ghani asserted.

He went on to stress that the PPP advocated for more provinces in Punjab as the “people of Punjab and their elected representatives” desired that.

The PPP leader emphasised that his party “represented” the citizens of each of the provinces when taking a stance for Sindh and Punjab.

At the outset of his press conference, Ghani also took exception to comments made by “two ministers”, saying it seemed that they “did not know anything about Sindh”.

“They are restricted within a circle called Maryam Nawaz. They only see and say what she tells them, shows them and explains to them,” he said in an apparent reference to the Punjab ministers.

World.title: ‘Enough is enough’: MQM-P leaders, Shahid Khaqan back creation of new administrative units
World.content:
Former premier Shahid Khaqan Abbasi and MQM-P leaders Dr Farooq Sattar and Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui on Saturday backed the creation of additional administrative units in the country.

On Thursday, Naqvi urged all political parties to “settle” various national-level issues, including the question of creating new provinces .

Addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 being held in Islamabad, Naqvi said there was “only one solution” to improving the country’s overall condition: “You will have to take [the matter of] administrative units, provinces or whatever you may call it, to the public.”

Addressing a press conference in Karachi today, MQM leader Dr Farooq Sattar said that, due to immense population growth, additional administrative units were essential to ensure proper governance.

“No country in the world has seen population growth as fast as ours,” he said. “We need to manage and administer that, but how will we do that without additional administrative units?”

Education Minister Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui and MQM Deputy Convener Dr Farooq Sattar address a press conference in Karachi on August 1, 2026. — Screengrab via YouTube/Dawn News

Sattar noted that, with such a large population, questions arose about how administrations would be able to address fundamental issues and ensure effective service delivery.

“Two things have become clear: we need administrative units. Enough is enough,” he declared.

“The ad-hocism we have seen for around 80 years must end. [Interior Minister] Mohsin Naqvi presented a clear administrative framework for Pakistan’s future in his speech, which is welcomed by citizens from all walks of life.”

“Pakistan’s economy is tied to its political and administrative structure.”

“We need curative treatment, not symptomatic treatment,” he stated.

Sattar added that the door needs to be left open for Gen-Z to play a representative role in Pakistan’s political, economic and social landscape.

“Political parties should move in this direction, as they are of the opinion that the system is infertile; it cannot ensure people’s prosperity or progress, build national consensus or strength, or guarantee the country’s security,” he stated.

“If we want to avail ourselves of these benefits, Pakistan must walk among the world with its head held high; the youth have to stand on their feet; we have to look the world and the IMF (International Monetary Fund) in the eye and talk to them. New administrative units are essential for this; without them, we will not move forward.”

Speaking before Sattar, Education Minister Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui noted that the conference addressed by Naqvi was an economic one, not a political one.

“We understand that there are no higher administrative units other than districts and divisions within a province. With One Unit, provinces were dissolved, but they returned after the end of the One Unit scheme in a different form,” he said, addressing the press conference.

“This issue of the limits of administrative units never existed, nor was it part of Pakistan’s politics. Are these [units] so sacred that we cannot talk about them? When nobody spoke about them, we did,” Siddiqui added.

He also stated that no matter which province people live in, they are still living within Pakistan, noting that the state itself is indivisible.

“The Constitution demands the division of provinces. But because of the pressure from a growing population, the procedures outlined in 1973 can no longer be enforced. This is why the MQM submitted an amendment bill in the National Assembly; it was not opposed and has been supported by the standing committee,” Siddiqui said.

“This MQM demand, which is in accordance with Pakistan’s population growth, is an administrative necessity and addresses the country’s economic issues,” he added.

“Our voice is being echoed by others. Today, we thank you all for highlighting this need during the month of Pakistan’s independence.”

Siddiqui said the party further believed that the current system of democracy, “where benefits never reach the people”, was not needed.

Ex-PM Abbasi says system needs to be changed

Former prime minister and Awaam Pakistan convener Shahid Khaqan Abbasi also addressed a press conference at the National Press Club in Islamabad, stating that the current state of affairs could not continue for much longer, but noted that the government was beginning to realise it.

“I am grateful to my interior minister for acknowledging after four or five years that the country is not running,” he stated. “It should have been discussed in parliament or the cabinet. The country knows it is not running, but it has finally dawned on the rulers.”

Abbasi added that the military’s spokesperson had acknowledged this during his press conference on Friday and that reform was the only way to keep the country functioning, but “there are always people who do not want meaningful change”.

“This is a matter of interests; if we talk about reforms in this country, then those whose interests do not align with reforms will oppose them,” he added. “The country is not being run well; we do not have money, and we are not ready to undertake reforms.

“Reforms are needed in this country; otherwise, the situation will get worse. Your debts, costs and taxes will continue to increase.”

Abbasi noted that simply creating new provinces would not solve the issue, but that the entire system needed to be changed.

“After 78 years, we don’t know how to buy flour. Our farmers have been ruined, and today we are even importing wheat by spending precious dollars,” he said, alleging that those in power were more interested in purchasing official vehicles and aircraft than addressing the hardships faced by ordinary citizens.

He stressed that constitutional supremacy and the rule of law were necessary for political stability and economic growth.

“Without the rule of law, investment will not come, and without investment there can be no sustainable economic progress,” Abbasi said.

Various political parties have demanded the creation of more provinces or administrative units to ensure better governance.

The MQM-P — an ally of the PML-N-led ruling coalition — has been demanding that Karachi be designated a province separate from Sindh.

However, the PPP, which rules Sindh and is also an ally of the PML-N government at the Centre along with MQM-P, has strongly opposed the suggested move.

On the other hand, the PPP and the PTI have long advocated for a South Punjab province .

A day prior, Inter-Services Public Relations chief Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry commented on Naqvi’s remarks about the need for new administrative units in Pakistan: “We have been saying this earlier also as a primary stakeholder in security that good governance is essential for the security and stability of Pakistan.”

“Now our population is 240-250 million people, and we still have four provinces. We have to see whether this is serving the purpose of good governance. That debate has to be sensibly held by politicians, by those in power, even those who have previously been in power, and those who are responsible to the people of Pakistan,” the DG ISPR said, adding that it had to be done according to the will of the people of Pakistan.

Later on Friday, PPP Secretary-General Nayyar Bokhari said that the party’s Central Executive Committee (CEC) will deliberate on creating new administrative units, which should be created through the mechanism provided in the Constitution rather than by executive order.

“The Constitution of Pakistan has clearly laid down the complete procedure. Without a two-thirds majority in the relevant provincial assembly, the National Assembly and the Senate, neither the creation of new provinces nor any alteration in provincial boundaries is possible,” he told Dawn.

“New provinces cannot be created through an executive order. They can only be created through a constitutional decision of parliament,” he added.

Additional reporting by Ikram Junaidi

World.title: July deadliest month of 2026 as 205 lives lost, 401 terrorists killed: PICSS
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Violence linked to terrorist attacks and counter-terrorism operations intensified sharply in July, making it the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security personnel among 205 people killed, while 401 terrorists were eliminated.

The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based think tank, said in its monthly security assessment that fatalities among security personnel and terrorists rose substantially during the month as terrorist violence increased and security forces intensified counter-terrorism operations.

According to the report, at least 112 security personnel lost their lives during July, the highest monthly toll since January 2023 and the second-highest recorded in more than a decade.

In January 2023, 114 security personnel were martyred, including around 102 in the suicide bombing at Peshawar Police Lines, the report recalled.

It said 401 terrorists were killed during July, the highest number recorded in a single month in more than a decade.

On the other hand, 74 civilians and 19 members of peace committees lost their lives in July. The death toll among peace committee members was also the highest recorded in a single month during the past decade.

According to PICSS, the 232 injuries during July included 101 security personnel, 103 civilians, 14 peace committee members and 14 terrorists.

The data showed that, compared with June, security personnel deaths increased by 195pc, rising from 38 to 112. Terrorist deaths increased by 109pc, from 192 to 401, while civilian deaths rose by 21pc, from 61 to 74.

The institute recorded at least eight suicide attacks during July, including five vehicle-borne suicide attacks. The think tank noted that this was the highest number of suicide attacks recorded in a single month during the past decade.

Kidnapping incidents also doubled during the month, rising by 100pc from 33 in June to 66 in July.

Province-wise breakdown

It stated that the security situation deteriorated most significantly in Balochistan, where the overall death toll increased by 241pc, from 109 in June to 372 in July.

Security personnel deaths in Balochistan increased from six in June to 62 in July, representing a rise of 933pc. Terrorist deaths rose from 75 to 238, while civilian deaths increased by 93pc, from 28 to 54. Eighteen members of peace committees were also killed in the province.

According to the report, mainland Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, excluding the merged districts, recorded 154 deaths in July, compared with 75 in June, representing an increase of 105pc. The number of people injured rose from 60 to 98.

Security personnel deaths in mainland KP increased from 12 to 38, while terrorist deaths rose by 192pc, from 37 to 108. Civilian deaths, however, declined by 73pc, falling from 26 in June to seven in July. One member of a peace committee was also killed in the province.

Data showed a slight decline in overall deaths in the merged districts of KP, formerly known as Fata. The region recorded 79 deaths in July, compared with 85 in June.

The number of people injured in the merged districts declined by 37pc, from 60 to 38. Security personnel deaths increased from six to 11, while terrorist deaths declined by 24pc, from 72 to 55. Civilian deaths rose by 86pc, increasing from seven to 13.

In Sindh, it recorded two terrorist attacks in which one security personnel member was killed. The province had recorded 12 deaths in June. Security forces also arrested six suspected terrorists during counter-terrorism operations in Sindh.

Punjab, Islamabad, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and Gilgit-Baltistan witnessed no terrorist violence during July. However, security forces arrested three suspected terrorists during operations conducted in Punjab.

Overall, the data showed that the first seven months of 2026 witnessed 2,786 deaths linked to terrorist violence and counter-terrorism operations.

Those killed included 1,857 terrorists, 463 civilians, 434 security forces personnel and 32 members of peace committees. The average martyrdoms per month among security forces increased from 56 in 2025 to 62 in 2026, while average deaths of civilians increased from 48 to 66, and average deaths among the terrorists increased from 178 to 265 per month.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing.
