World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018834/The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.title: The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018834/The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.content:
From “don’t come,” to “the more customers, the better.” These were the refrains made by the owner of a chicken hotpot restaurant in southern China famous for shirking fame and which has recently drawn criticism for perceived hypocrisy due to its rapid expansion.

In April, “Mo’s Chicken Hotpot,” in the southern Guangdong province’s Foshan City, went viral after the recommendation of a popular food vlogger. The eatery drew crowds for its signature medicinal hotpot made from freshly slaughtered chickens — and whose healing properties included causing diarrhea, according to notices in the restaurant.

During the initial vlogger’s visit, the restaurant’s owner, surnamed Mo, insisted that customers should “not come” as he would not be able to handle the popularity. Nevertheless, the restaurant began drawing thousands of customers a day, including celebrities and influencers.

But the restaurant’s expansion to five branches in Guangdong and Shanghai — with another expected to open in the southern city of Shenzhen next year — and frequent online s in the months since have drawn ridicule, domestic media reported this week. Social media users argue the restaurant’s current activities contradict Mo’s previous rejection of fame.

Earlier interviews quoted Mo as saying he had no plans to raise prices or open new outlets, leading some online to question whether his indifferent persona had been a marketing strategy from the beginning.

As of this month, Mo said the restaurant has hired a 20-person livestreaming team and broadcasts twice a day. “We can’t afford not to livestream,” he told domestic media. “The pressure is just too great.”

The eatery’s official account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, now has around 500,000 followers. It posts two to three times a week, mainly skits promoting its signature chicken hotpot alongside health tips. Several videos have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

The restaurant also sells meal kits, Chinese medicine, herbal teas, and local specialties such as salt-baked chicken via its online store.

The rating for Mo’s Chicken Hotpot on review platform Dianping has fallen from a peak of 4.8 out of 5 in April to 3.7, according to domestic media. Negative reviews mention inconsistent food quality, flies and poor hygiene standards in the restaurant, and high prices.

Visitor numbers have also fluctuated. In June, domestic media reported that sales at the original restaurant had fallen from 200 to 400 orders a day to fewer than 20 a day by the end of the month. However, Mo told domestic media in mid-July that the restaurant handles no fewer than 150 orders a day.

In a video interview with domestic media, Mo responded to the criticism, saying, “At first, when we suddenly became so popular, I really didn’t want the attention. We were so busy, it made me want to throw up.”

“Now I actually want the business to be even better,” he added. “When fortune gives you an opportunity like this … and there’s money to be made, why wouldn’t I try to make money? I’d be a fool not to.”

Mo also admitted that despite the restaurant’s expansion and livestreaming business, profits remain limited.

“Traffic comes quickly, and it disappears just as quickly. After a month or two, how do you sustain it? It’s really hard,” adding that if another wave of popularity were to come, he would “honestly close shop and stop.”

Mo also joined the second season of popular domestic cooking competition show “The Divine Dish,” which premiered Wednesday. He was eliminated in the first round.

“The ingredients (he used) were good, but his technique was poor,” one of the show’s judges said of his signature chicken hotpot.

On his Douyin account, Mo responded to his elimination, saying, “I will continue to use the finest ingredients and simplest methods to cook you the familiar chicken hotpot that warms your heart.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Weibo, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018835/Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.title: Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018835/Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.content:
Editor’s note: The theme of the third Shanghai Public Relations Academic Symposium on Irish Literature, held on July 26, was playwright George Bernard Shaw’s eight-hour visit to Shanghai in the 1930s, when China’s cultural and anti-imperialist movements were gaining momentum. The following is an account of the writer’s time in the city and its impact on Chinese intellectuals.

When George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright and novelist, paid a brief visit to Shanghai as part of his global voyage in 1933, the city’s intellectuals were thrilled.

Before his arrival, articles about Shaw had been published in various newspapers and magazines. Some discussed his Communist advocacy in Hong Kong, while others talked about how his satirical writing style had influenced European society.

According to a biography of Soong Ching Ling, the Chinese politician and wife of Sun Yat-sen, sometimes called the “father of modern China,” Shaw arrived at Wusongkou port — today the Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal in northeastern Shanghai — at 6 a.m. on Feb. 17 aboard the Empress of Britain, accompanied by his wife, the political activist Charlotte Payne-Townshend. At 5 a.m., Soong went to Wusongkou with Yang Xingfo, a social activist and patriotic democrat, to welcome the couple. At Shaw’s invitation, she joined him on board for breakfast.

More than 200 reporters rushed to Wusongkou early that morning, but Shaw initially refused to go ashore, telling Soong that apart from her, there was no one in Shanghai he wanted to meet, nor anything he wanted to see. But in the end, Soong persuaded him to pay a visit to the city. They took a steamship to Lanlu Wharf in today’s Yangpu District, where he finally went ashore. The reporters waiting at Wusongkou left empty-handed — not a single photograph of Shaw was taken.

At 10:30 a.m., Soong and Shaw disembarked and set out for the city’s downtown. Shaw met and talked with several left-wing Chinese intellectuals, including Yang, former Peking University president Cai Yuanpei, literary icon Lu Xun, writer and linguist Lin Yutang, and the American journalists Harold Isaacs and Agnes Smedley.

Later, at the invitation of the Chinese branch of PEN International, a global association of writers founded in London in 1921, Shaw and other Chinese intellectuals visited the World College on Route Ferguson (now Wukang Road) to attend a gathering with local PEN members. When Shaw met Mei Lanfang, the renowned Peking opera artist and founder of Shanghai’s Left Theatre Club, he expressed his puzzlement over the differences between Eastern and Western theater.

“Will you please tell me how a Chinese actor can do anything in the midst of such infernal uproars as one hears on your stage?” he asked. “In our theater, they put a man out if he sneezes. But you have gongs and cymbals and the competition of half the audience and innumerable vendors. Don’t you object?”

Mei explained that Peking opera was a folk art first performed in the open air, and drums and gongs were then used to attract people to the show. This tradition had simply endured.

Around 3 p.m., Shaw finally spoke with some Chinese and foreign reporters in the garden of Soong’s residence, discussing socialism, national oppression, Eastern culture, and revolutions, among other topics. Afterward, Soong accompanied Shaw back to the Empress of Britain, which then carried the playwright northward to Beijing.

Although Shaw spent just over eight hours in Shanghai, his visit sparked considerable discussion and reverberations among the city’s left-wing intellectual circles. The writer and poet Yu Dafu wrote in Free Talk, a supplement of the Shun Pao newspaper, that he hoped Shaw could tell the world, in his own sarcastic tone, about Japanese imperialism and its invasion of China.

At the time, intellectuals including Lu Xun and the poet and translator Qu Qiubai were working to build a central stronghold for China’s left-wing cultural movement. After Shaw’s departure, they, along with partners Xu Guangping and Yang Zhihua, began compiling reports from various newspapers and periodicals about the Irish novelist’s short visit. The collection was published in March 1933 by Yecao Shudian, or Wildgrass Bookshop, under the title “George Bernard Shaw in Shanghai.”

In the preface, Lu wrote: “Those who truly welcomed him were the Chinese people, as well as the literary and artistic circles that stood by the people. The Chinese people did not regard him as a ‘revolutionary leader’ or a ‘thoroughgoing socialist writer,’ much less as an idol. They regarded Shaw as a loyal friend of the oppressed people of the world, and of China.”

Editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from the Shanghai Lu Xun Museum, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018830/How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.title: How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018830/How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.content:
This is the first article in a two-part series exploring how Chinese culinary terms came to be included in the Oxford English Dictionary (OED).

For more than two decades, I have studied how Chinese words enter the English language, particularly through food. So when the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) released its second batch of updates this past June, one updated entry felt especially meaningful to me: “Cantonese.” For the first time, the dictionary formally recognized the word as a culinary term, defining it as food prepared in the style of Guangzhou and the surrounding region in southern China, as well as the restaurants that serve such cuisine.

The entry is accompanied not just by a simple definition, but by a timeline of citations tracing the term’s culinary history. The earliest example dates back to April 6, 1892, when New Jersey’s Trenton Times referred to “Fashionable Cantonese dishes.” This phrase shows that the term was already being used in relation to food more than a century ago, long before the era of modern globalization.

Western interest in Cantonese cuisine also stretches back to the late 19th century. The OED cites an 1894 report from The Washington Post describing a dim sum dumpling as “shaped exactly like a fishing creel.” By 1908, The New York Herald was explaining the dish to its readers by comparing it to a “second cousin to steamed sponge cake.” These early descriptions reveal how unfamiliar foods were introduced to Western audiences through comparisons with things they already understood.

Over the following decades, Cantonese cuisine continued to leave its mark. A 1950 publication by the Hong Kong Young Women’s Christian Association highlighted “Cantonese specialties” such as turnip pudding, while a 1997 culinary memoir recalled dining at a large “Cantonese restaurant” where dim sum was served from rolling trolleys. More recently, a 2015 article in The Guardian recommended Wong Chi Kee in Hong Kong for its “traditional Cantonese congee.”

These citations connect to a broader ecosystem of existing terms. The Cantonese practice of yum cha, literally “drinking tea,” the social meal of dim sum and tea traditionally enjoyed in the morning, was added to the dictionary in 2016, while dim sum has appeared in the dictionary since 1989.

Today, my research shows that the dictionary contains a vocabulary of 25 Cantonese culinary terms. Beyond the widely recognized dim sum and yum cha, the list includes char siu, wonton, chop suey, hoisin sauce, egg foo yung, and moo goo gai pan. These are no longer treated as foreign concepts requiring lengthy explanations; they have become established English words.

Yet this lexicographical milestone is not simply a retrospective look at history; it also reflects a living culture. Just months earlier, in March 2026, three new additions expanded the OED’s Cantonese culinary vocabulary: dan tat (egg tart), pineapple bun, and yin yeung (a Hong Kong drink combining milk tea and coffee). Their inclusion highlights that Cantonese cuisine is not a static relic of the past. It continues to evolve, innovate, and influence the English language. This ongoing linguistic exchange shows that the relationship between East and West remains an active and continuing process.

The contrast with other regional Chinese cuisines highlights that global influence is not simply a product of modern international presence. Shanghai, for instance, is one of China’s most globally connected cities, yet its local Benbang cuisine has left far fewer traces in the English language. Cantonese cuisine’s deep roots in English developed instead through generations of migration, trade, and everyday use.

Etymologically, “Cantonese” derives from “Canton,” the former English name for Guangzhou, which was first recorded by Portuguese traders in the 16th century. Over time, the term evolved from a geographic reference into a marker of a distinct cultural and culinary identity. This reflects a broader historical reality: Cantonese cuisine established an overseas presence earlier than many other regional Chinese cuisines, spreading through centuries of maritime trade and migration.

Historically, because the vast majority of early Chinese immigrants to many Western countries came from Guangdong, Cantonese restaurants dominated many Chinatowns. Iconic establishments such as New York’s Port Arthur Restaurant, which opened in 1897 and introduced upscale Cantonese dishes to Western diners, and San Francisco’s Shanghai Low, a Cantonese restaurant that adopted a Shanghai-inspired name to appeal to Western customers, did more than serve food. They became gathering places for immigrant communities and helped establish Cantonese cuisine’s prominence in Western societies.

As a linguist, I often argue that translation is not merely a tool for communication between languages; it is also a means of cultural understanding. The inclusion of these terms shows that English speakers are capable of adopting culinary vocabulary from other languages on its own terms.

For readers interested in exploring this vocabulary, here are eight popular Cantonese culinary terms currently included in the OED, with condensed definitions for clarity.

Many of the early Cantonese restaurants that introduced these dishes to Western audiences have since disappeared. Yet the vocabulary they helped popularize has endured, and a new generation of Cantonese restaurants continues to thrive in Chinatowns and communities around the world. The OED’s recognition of Cantonese cuisine reflects this longer history of cultural exchange: carried across borders by generations of immigrants, Cantonese food has become a lasting part of the global culinary vocabulary.

(Header and in-text images: Visuals from VCG, edited by Ding Yining/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.title: China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.content:
Chinese state-owned bookstore chain Xinhua Bookstore is partnering with food delivery giant Meituan to roll out a nationwide same-day book delivery service, promising to deliver books in under an hour.

The agreement, signed on Friday at the 34th National Book Expo in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, will connect the more than 10,000 Xinhua stores across China to Meituan’s instant retail network, Instashopping. Customers ordering through the network will be able to receive books in as quickly as 30 minutes.

The initiative marks the expansion of multiple pilot initiatives in the last two years comprising several regional Xinhua branches, including in Zhejiang, Shanghai, and the southern city of Shenzhen.

Founded in 1937, Xinhua is China’s largest and oldest bookstore chain.

Instant retail combines online ordering with inventories from nearby physical stores and a network of couriers to deliver products rapidly, typically in under one hour. China’s instant retail market is expected to surpass 1 trillion yuan ($150 billion) in 2026 and double to 2 trillion yuan by 2030, according to a report by the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.

The push into instant retail comes amid intensifying competition between China’s e-commerce platforms and weakening demand for printed books. The country’s book retail market totaled roughly 110 billion yuan in 2025, down 2% from 2024, according to a report by Chinese analytics firm OpenBook.

Jiang Chuanyang, chairman of Xinhua’s Zhejiang branch, said at the event that China’s book market is evolving to comprise e-commerce, local instant retail, and physical bookstores. More than 100 stores in the province were active on Instashopping throughout 2025, generating combined sales of several million yuan, according to domestic media.

But the picture is more mixed for independent bookstores.

Su Shanna, brand manager of Yinxu, a chain of five bookstores in the eastern coastal city of Xiamen, told Sixth Tone that instant delivery orders account for roughly 15% of the company’s monthly revenue. The store joined Instashopping in May 2025, and also accepts on-demand orders through its WeChat mini program, fulfilling local deliveries through courier services such as SF Express and JD Logistics.

“It’s more of a bonus than a lifeline,” Su said, noting that demand for instant book delivery remains limited to a handful of scenarios. These include parents ordering extracurricular reading materials or textbooks for their children, tourists ordering books to their hotels, and patients looking for something to read during hospitalization.

Instant retail fills the gap where consumers need a book immediately and traditional e-commerce can’t meet the demand, according to Jiang Han, a senior researcher at Beijing-based think tank Pangoal.

But books are a low-profit business. Because instant retail platforms take a cut of bookstore sales, instant delivery is unlikely to become a major profit driver, he said.

The service’s real value isn’t in generating significant new revenue, but in generating new revenue sources, Jiang added. “Its significance should be on how it helps bookstores reconstruct their connection to readers.”

Jiang said that bookstores are increasingly trying to become “cultural service hubs” by diversifying their revenue sources, selling tourism-related products, and integrating with the local community. Instant retail is part of this trend.

In the case of Yinxu, members pay an annual fee of 188 yuan, which gives them discounts on books, book delivery services, and tickets to local performances, as well as access to various community activities.

“The key to success depends on whether bookstores can offer irreplaceable cultural experiences and emotional value,” Jiang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from iNueng/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018827/China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.title: China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018827/China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.content:
One graduate trained to restore ancient artifacts now generates AI video clips for short dramas. Another, schooled in landscape design, builds virtual scenery instead of physical sets.

Both are part of a hiring surge across China’s film industry, as AI creates demand for hybrid creative roles and cuts production timelines from months to days. Recruitment for AI video editors jumped 179% year over year in June, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

At one cultural communications company in Zhengzhou, capital of China’s central Henan province, monthly production of AI-generated short dramas has risen from a handful to nearly 100, according to CCTV. The expansion has created demand for AI video editors and “card pullers,” who write prompts, generate footage, and select clips that fit a production’s characters and plot.

The shift is drawing workers from fields including design, animation, digital media, and information technology, according to recruitment platform Zhaopin. AI film roles typically pay between 8,000 and 20,000 yuan ($1,100 to $2,800) a month, depending on experience.

“This indicates that AI is not simply a substitution, but a technological enabler that is driving the transformation of traditional professions and roles,” Li Qiang, a vice president at Zhaopin, told CCTV.

AI is also changing how short dramas are made. Some productions that once required crews of dozens can now be completed by a few people, or even one creator handling scripts, storyboards, visuals, and effects. CCTV reported that AI has compressed some production cycles from months to days, with certain episodes completed in hours and effects and previsualization work becoming three to 10 times faster.

Director He Ziqiang, an early adopter of AI filmmaking tools, has added AI storyboard artists, image generators, card pullers, and editors to his team, many without formal film training.

“Anyone can make their own film, as long as they have ideas,” He told CCTV. “This will greatly enrich artistic creation and vitality, enabling more talented ordinary people to express themselves through AI.”

The hiring surge comes as China’s short-drama industry’s annual output value approached 90 billion yuan in 2025, nearly double the previous year, while some AI-generated productions have reported net profit margins above 50%.

Li Yuan, who is not related to Li Qiang, founder of a Henan-based AI film company, told domestic media his firm had cut the cost of producing a drama from 300,000 yuan to 50,000 yuan while increasing output.

“We thought large models would take longer to nail video fluency, but they got it done in the first quarter of this year,” Li told state media.

But he also cautioned that AI short dramas remain at an early stage, with both the technology and audience tastes still evolving. “Only when the market stabilizes can creators and platforms offer better products,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Staff at a short-drama production company use AI tools during post-production in Jiaxing, Zhejiang province, July 21, 2026. VCG)

World.title: LPA inside PAR develops into Tropical Depression Luis
World.content:
Tropical Depression Luis is the Philippines' 12th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for August

MANILA, Philippines – The low pressure area (LPA) inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) developed into a tropical depression at 8 pm on Saturday, August 1, and was given the local name Luis.

Luis is the country’s 12th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for August.

As of 10 pm on Saturday, Luis was located 360 kilometers east of Daet, Camarines Norte, moving west at 15 kilometers per hour (km/h).

The tropical depression has maximum sustained winds of 45 km/h and gustiness of up to 55 km/h.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Luis is projected to stay over the Philippine Sea. But if its forecast track shifts westward, it could make landfall in Northern Luzon or Central Luzon, or go near these areas.

Luis might also strengthen into a tropical storm by Monday, August 3, while moving over the sea east of Central Luzon. However, it may be downgraded back to a tropical depression by Tuesday, August 4, and into an LPA or remnant low by Wednesday, August 5.

PAGASA immediately raised Signal No. 1 for portions of Southern Luzon in its initial bulletin released at 11 pm on Saturday. The following areas are covered, which means they will have strong winds from Luis:

Polillo Islands

northern part of Camarines Norte (Daet, Talisay, Paracale, Jose Panganiban, Capalonga, Vinzons)

northern part of Catanduanes (Pandan, Caramoran, Bagamanoc, Panganiban)

The weather bureau added that the southwest monsoon or habagat and the periphery or outer bands of the tropical depression will bring strong to gale-force gusts to these areas:

Sunday, August 2

Marinduque, Romblon, Caluya Islands, Siquijor, Southern Leyte, Camiguin, Dinagat Islands

Monday, August 3

most of Luzon, most of Visayas, Lanao del Norte, Camiguin, Surigao del Norte, Dinagat Islands

Within a 24-hour period beginning Sunday evening, August 2, Luis is also expected to trigger moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters) in Isabela, Quirino, and Aurora. Floods and landslides are possible in these provinces.

PAGASA earlier said two to four tropical cyclones could develop within or enter PAR in August. – Rappler.com

World.title: Revilla’s P1-M bail: What ‘weak evidence’ bought him
World.content:
Revilla is out of jail for now, but this does not mean he's completely off the hook. His graft and malversation cases are still active and his trial is still ongoing.

Former senator Bong Revilla is temporarily out of jail after the Sandiganbayan 3rd Division granted his bail petition on his malversation case.

Revilla is facing graft and malversation cases over a P92.8-million flood control ghost project in Bulacan. He was arrested in January and spent over six months in detention at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas.

While graft is bailable, malversation is not, so the former senator had to file a petition for bail and attended weeks-long hearings at the Sandiganbayan. Ultimately, the 3rd division justices decided to grant Revilla temporary liberty in a resolution made public on July 31.

The court, however, did not grant the petition for bail of Revilla’s co-accused, which includes former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) engineers Brice Hernandez, Jaypee Mendoza, and Arjay Domasig, among others.

The three justices — Chairperson Associate Justice Karl Miranda, Associate Justice Ronald Moreno, and Associate Justice Fritz Bryn Anthony delos Santos — were unanimous in denying the motions of almost all of Revilla’s co-accused. Moreno wanted to grant Christina Mae Pineda’s bail, but was outvoted.

However, Miranda was the lone dissenter in granting Revilla’s bail. Both Moreno and Delos Santos believed that the former senator must be given temporary liberty.

Play Video

Revilla not yet acquitted

For grave offenses like malversation of public funds, bail is not automatic. An accused like Revilla has to file a petition for bail.

The court then holds summary hearings where the prosecution presents its evidence and witnesses, solely for the purpose of determining whether the evidence of guilt is strong. This threshold is important because if the court, after the bail hearings, finds that the evidence is weak, it grants the bail petition of the accused.

This is what happened to Revilla. The evidence against him, in so far as the bail hearings are concerned, was found to be weak, that is why his petition was granted.

For his fellow accused, however, the court found the evidence to be strong. Their request was denied.

Remember, these summary hearings and evidence were intended only for the bail petition, and excluded the actual malversation case.

Revilla is out of jail for now, but this does not mean he’s completely off the hook. His temporary liberty means he won’t have to remain under the custody of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Payatas, but he will still have to attend his graft and malversation hearings.

His innocence will only be determined at the end of court’s trial. The prosecution may also present additional evidence during the trial proper.

“A finding of strong evidence of guilt after the conclusion of a bail hearing is not equivalent to a finding of guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It is primarily based on evidence being initially established by the prosecution prior to resting on the presentation of its evidence-in-chief,” the 176-page resolution penned by Delos Santos said.

“It is by no means an exhaustive inquiry of guilt — especially as to the elements of the crime and the degree of participation. It is limited only to the assessment of a subset or sample of the entirety of the prosecution’s evidence,” it added.

The prosecution automatically adopts its evidence presented during the bail hearings for its mother case. It may also present additional evidence during the trial proper.

“As a matter of practice, the evidence presented in support of a bail application are adopted as part of the evidence-in-chief. Although the prosecution may present additional evidence,” National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers president Ephraim Cortez told Rappler.

Evidence vs Revilla is weak

Moreno and Delos Santos found that the prosecution failed to show strong evidence of guilt on the part of Revilla.

Revilla was dubbed by the Office of the Ombudsman a proponent, or a politician whose job is to ensure that a specific DPWH project will be funded by the national budget. In exchange, a public official gets a commission or alleged kickback from the scheme.

This was how the supposed “kalakaran” or corruption scheme inside the DPWH worked.

To prove their allegations, the prosecution presented state witnesses former DPWH undersecretary Roberto Bernardo, former DPWH engineer Henry Alcantara, and DPWH Metro Manila regional director Gerard Opulencia, as well as some DPWH staff. They also presented documentary printouts that bear the initials “SBR,” supposedly standing for “Senator Bong Revilla.”

This evidence was supposed to prove that Revilla allegedly:

Obtained a list of projects from DPWH officials and employees to fund them

Facilitated and caused the inclusion of these projects in the national budget

Received kickbacks from doing all of these

Meanwhile, Philippine courts have identified the elements of malversation. They are as follows:

The offender is a public officer

He or she had custody or control of funds or property by reason of the duties of his or her office

Those funds or property were public funds or property for which he or she was accountable

He or she appropriated, took, misappropriated or consented or, through abandonment or negligence, permitted another person to take them

However, the court said there was no evidence narrating how Revilla allegedly facilitated the project’s inclusion in the national budget. It explained that being the chairperson of the Senate committee on public works did not mean that he had the power to author a budget “that is binding not only on said Committee but even on the Senate itself as a plenary body as well as the Bicameral Committee of Congress.”

The court said that the testimony about Revilla allegedly obtaining a list of projects from the DPWH did not prove the malversation’s last element that “he appropriated, took, misappropriated or consented or, through abandonment or negligence, permitted another person to take them.”

According to the court, the prosecution also failed to present an iota of proof that Revilla expressly or impliedly agreed that, at the time of allegedly receiving the kickbacks, his co-accused would commit malversation in the future.

“At best, accused Revilla’s alleged receipt of the kickbacks (as testified to by the witnesses in the bail hearings) could only support a mere assumption that he may have had predicted that the same funds would later on be recovered by private contractors (and some of his co-accused who may have had private contractors as dummies) from the sum appropriated for the project in this case),” the ruling explained.

“More importantly, at the time accused Revilla allegedly received his ‘commitments,’ the cash supposedly involved in the deliveries came from private persons as testified. At that time, the funds involved insofar as accused Revilla is concerned were not public in character,” it added.

The court also explained that a government project has four stages: planning or proposal; funding; implementation; and post-auditing. It said that the crime of malversation, at least based on the evidence so far, happened during the implementation stage.

The Sandiganbayan said Revilla’s alleged receipt of advance commissions happened before the implementation stage.

“This necessarily implies that the funds he received coming from the private contractors did not come from public coffers to be considered as ‘public funds’ under the definition of the crime of malversation,” said the court.

Play Video

Miranda dissents

Miranda, who dissented in the decision to grant Revilla bail, said he disagreed with the conclusions that there was no evidence that the former senator facilitated the inclusion of the funding and that he had no alleged participation in the malversation.

On top of this, Miranda also disagreed with the conclusion that there was nothing connects the act of obtaining the list of projects and facilitating the funding of the subject project “to the eventual understanding that the recovery of the advance kickbacks allegedly paid to Revilla will be recovered by his co-accused by way of malversation.”

The chairperson believes that the prosecution was able to present strong evidence against Revilla, explaining that the former senator’s alleged acts may only be appreciated when contextualized within the “kalakaran” scheme inside the DPWH.

The chairperson believes that it was wrong to treat the advance payment as an independent and isolated offense, since the contractor will have to rely on future offenses to recover the commitment through public funds.

“Ultimately, it is the government that is charged for the bribe that the contractor has paid the project proponent,” said Miranda.

The magistrate also said that the testimonies of Bernardo, Alcantara, Opulencia, and Bernardo’s aides prove that commitments were collected for 2025 projects, where Revilla acted as proponent. He also added that there was “strong evidence” that these kickbacks were delivered to Revilla in his white house compound in Cavite in the first quarter of 2025.

For Miranda, there was no need to prove that Revilla personally intervened in the congressional deliberations to ensure that the project would be funded. Miranda explained that the DPWH project would not have been included in the national budget law had it not been for the following reasons:

Revilla’s allocation provided by former DPWH secretary Manuel Bonoan

Revilla’s request from Bernardo for the list of projects for “allocation”

Alcantara’s “transmittal of the list of projects to Undersecretary Bernardo, which list included the subject project, as part of projects for funding from Revilla’s allocation”

Bernardo’s transmittal of the list of projects for funding from Revilla’s allocation to Bonoan and the late DPWH undersecretary Cathy Cabral

Revilla’s follow-up with Bernardo, Bonoan, and Cabral for the inclusion of projects

“Miranda thus concludes that it is difficult to justify that the accused who personally benefited from the scheme is granted provisional liberty, while his co-accused are kept incarcerated despite lack of proof that they gained anything from the commission of the crime charged,” said the magistrate in his dissenting opinion. – Rappler.com

World.title: More in the tank: EJ Obiena finding groove again
World.content:
After a string of setbacks knocked him out of the world’s top 10, Filipino pole vault star EJ Obiena steadily regains his form, with recent results pointing to a career resurgence

Don’t count EJ Obiena out just yet.

After a series of setbacks dropped him out of the top 10 of the world pole vault rankings, Obiena is steadily finding his groove again, with his recent results suggesting a promising career resurgence.

“I’m very happy, I’m very proud. I think I’m slowly, slowly getting back to the confidence that I used to have. I’m excited to keep competing and see what the season has in store for me,” Obiena told Rappler.

Change of scenery

His return to form has been shaped by the foundation he built in Formia, Italy, under the tutelage of renowned Ukrainian coach Vitaly Petrov, and the new chapter he is forging in Athens, Greece, where he now trains with the group of his good friend and Olympic medalist Emmanouil Karalis.

Now 30 years old, Obiena made the tough decision to part ways with Petrov and move out of Formia after his former training partners, China’s Huang Bokai and Saudi Arabia’s Hussain Al-Hizam, took on new responsibilities outside of the sport.

According to Obiena, Huang became a father, while Al-Hizam got married, with both athletes seeing limited action over the past year.

“Those two guys that I usually train with day in, day out were not with me for the past year and a half, I would say. So therefore, it’s tougher. It’s harder for me to train alone,” said Obiena.

“I just knew I needed someone to train with. And there’s nobody coming to Formia. It’s a decision that unfortunately needed to be made. And with that, I believe we both understood that and we both believed that it’s the best path for me to go. That’s why Vitaly agreed and it was a mutual decision from that day.”

Linking up with Karalis proved to be a no-brainer for Obiena.

Obiena knows Karalis is someone who can bring the best out in him, the Greek star ranking second only to reigning two-time Olympic champion and world record holder Armand Duplantis of Sweden in the world rankings.

After Duplantis, Karalis owns the second-highest mark in the history of the sport with a 6.17-meter clearance.

Working with Karalis has also allowed Obiena to benefit from the expertise of a well-rounded coaching staff led by Polish mentor Marcin Szczepanski, which is also a big reason why he relocated to Athens.

“Training with Emmanouil is highly beneficial for me because he’s someone that’s jumping higher right now and has jumped consistently. I want to have that day-in, day-out competition every time I step on the track,” said Obiena.

“At the same time, I know there’s not going to be a lot of drama because I’ve trained with him. I’ve seen how this guy is. I love the guy, I respect him, and I believe he respects me. I think with that, it’s almost like a no-nonsense decision to decide I want to train with this guy.”

But even as he embarked on a new chapter in his career, Obiena does not want to lose sight of his roots as he makes it a point to stay in touch with Petrov, who was instrumental in his rise as a top pole vaulter throughout their 12-year partnership.

Under Petrov, Obiena reached a career-high No. 2 ranking, won historic silver and bronze medals in the World Athletics Championships, and became the only Asian member of the exclusive six-meter club.

“Vitaly has been more than just a coach to me. Vitaly has been like my father here. He’s been a really, really good coach, and at the same time, a really, really good life mentor. So that decision was not easy” said Obiena.

“Even though it was mutually, I would say, achieved upon doesn’t make it less difficult. It’s like, quote unquote, getting a divorce. Let’s put it that way. It’s a relationship that I still really cherish. I’m very thankful to what Vitaly has done and still doing.”

“I call him from time to time. I don’t want to lose my connection with Vitaly. He has opened doors — so much doors — for me… and it says a lot about the way he is.”

Back on track

The change of scenery seems to be working wonders for Obiena.

After falling short of the 5.80-meter bar for nearly a year, Obiena cleared the height in three straight meets in July, posting 5.81 meters for fourth place in the Fly Athens in Greece, 5.80 meters for sixth place in the Gyulai Istvan Memorial in Hungary, and a season-best 5.85 meters for second place in the Meeting Madrid in Spain.

His clearance in the Meeting Madrid is actually his highest in two years, or since he made 5.90 meters in the Paris Olympics, where he lost the bronze to Karalis on countback.

“It’s not just because I moved here, suddenly I jump high. It’s cumulative work that I’ve done for the last year and a half. And with that, I hope that I continue to show what I could do and I believe that there’s more in the tank,” said Obiena.

For Obiena, seeing his efforts pay off has been a breath of fresh air after two challenging years following the Olympics.

He battled injuries during and after the Olympics that sidelined him for months then slipped out of the world top 10 after a string of disappointing finishes, including a failed bid to reach the final of the 2025 World Athletics Championships.

Obiena now ranks 14th in the world.

It got to the point where Obiena questioned whether he still had what it takes to perform at the elite level.

“You always question if you can still do it. I think it’s a question that you ask yourself every time there’s a rough day. Am I still the same guy? Am I still capable? Am I still able to compete at the highest level? Am I still happy with what I’m doing? Am I still able to make the sacrifices? That’s a constant question, it’s not just on a bad day, on a good day,” he said.

“I gave myself a bit of an ultimatum. If this year I don’t jump over 5.80 and I keep jumping 70, 70, 70, then maybe, maybe it’s time to consider being done with the sport. But thankfully, God-willing, I feel like I have more than 5.80 in me and I’m slowly, knock on wood, slowly and trying to stay healthy. We’ll see how the season goes.”

On Friday, July 31, Obiena captured his sixth gold of the year by ruling the 1st International Pole Vault Meeting in Halberstadt, Germany, where he tallied 5.76 meters.

That result bodes well for Obiena as he aims to once again crack the world top 10.

“A really realistic goal for me is to be back in the top 10 in the world. It’s not going to be simple, it’s not easy, but I believe it’s doable. I hope that I would have that possibility in the near future,” he said.

Obiena also looks forward to his title defense in the Asian Games to be held from September 19 to October 4 in Nagoya, Japan, where he is touted as one of the Philippines’ top gold bets.

“I’m just excited to compete and be having fun again in competition and seeing what I could do,” he said.

“Having a positive mindset is always helpful, not like clueless positivity but like real positivity that comes within. I think that’s very helpful for me right now. I hope it continues,” Obiena added.

“I guess I’m a little bit more mature, I have a deeper respect for the sport that I do, understanding what it takes to be at the top of the game, not take anything for granted. A bit of knowledge here and there, a little bit smarter hopefully day in, day out.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Who is Katrina Llegado, Miss Supranational 2026?
World.content:
WINNER. Taguig's Katrina Llegado gives the Philippines its second Miss Supranational crown on Saturday, August 1 (Manila time).

The 'perfectly imperfect' Taguig stunner gives the Philippines its first Miss Supranational crown in 13 years

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines won its second Miss Supranational crown on Saturday, August 1 (Manila time) in Poland courtesy of Katrina Llegado.

Llegado, who hails from Taguig City, beat 66 other contestants to take home the country’s first crown in 13 years after Mutya Datul pulled off the same feat in the pageant’s 2013 edition in Belarus.

Play Video

Many hats

Llegado wears many hats. Born on November 9, 1997, she is a cum laude graduate from De La Salle University, earning her degree in finance in 2018. Before becoming a beauty queen, Llegado had worked in a bank.

Despite going down a different path, Llegado did not let go of her business roots, as she co-founded the cosmetics brand Clocheflame in 2021.

In 2023, meanwhile, she became a Philippine Air Force reservist.

A seasoned queen

This is not Llegado’s first rodeo.

She is a familiar face among pageant fans, having competed in her first national pageant in 2019 at Miss World, where she was eventually given the responsibility to represent the Philippines at Reina Hispanoamericana in Bolivia. She finished as 5th runner-up.

Come 2022, then-24-year-old Llegado set her sights on another major national pageant: Miss Universe Philippines. Llegado managed to top the swimsuit challenge, and wrap up the overall competition as 2nd runner-up.

Still, Llegado knew her Miss Universe Philippines journey wasn’t over yet. She returned three years later in 2025 with an even fiercer bid for the crown. It was in Miss Universe Philippines 2025 that she was named Miss Supranational Philippines 2026.

Llegado’s road to the top, however, was not easy. Like any beauty queen carrying the weight of public expectations, the Taguig stunner struggled with self-doubt, and acknowledging that she needed to seek help was what allowed her to come back stronger the second time around.

“[Asking for help] really helped me focus on the things that I can control [and] to focus on myself and really uplift and enrich who you are. I think that really helped me all throughout this journey,” she told Rappler after her Miss Universe Philippines 2025 stint.

Play Video

Road to Miss Supranational 2026

Come Miss Supranational 2026 at the Strzelecki Park Amphitheater in Nowy Sącz, Poland, Llegado had put on a show-stopping performance that allowed her to achieve her historic feat of bringing home the Philippines’ second-ever crown in the pageant.

But it was her winning Q&A response that helped seal her victory. Llegado was asked to talk about the moment she stopped compressing herself to fit other people’s expectations, to instead embrace her true self.

“I always believed that we should never fit into a mold. We are perfectly imperfect. I am someone who struggles [with] perfection, but I am here today doing my best and becoming my best version. And here in Miss Supranational, I know I belong. I know a place for me, and this is becoming Supra, above and beyond,” the 28-year-old Filipina answered.

Llegado was crowned by Miss Supranational 2025 Eduarda Braum of Brazil.

Trailing behind the Filipina winner is France’s Ève Gilles (1st runner-up), Brazil’s Lara Marina (2nd runner-up), Nigeria’s Gift Ndah (3rd runner-up), and Czech Republic’s Karolína Gorylová (4th runner-up). – Rappler.com

World.title: Meta’s AI splurge lays bare its compute conundrum
World.content:
ZUCKERBERG. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026

Meta says renting out AI computing power is an option, but insists bigger profits lie in selling AI services

Meta can simultaneously fuel its own AI ambitions and rent out its scarce computing capacity to bolster returns, CEO Mark Zuckerberg signaled on Wednesday. The problem is: investors aren’t buying it.

The Instagram owner is splurging billions to build compute — chips, servers, energy and data centers that power AI — leaving it with free cash flow of just $784 million in the second quarter to run and grow its business. That collapse, of 91% from a year ago, drove its stock down more than 9% on Thursday.

Pressed by analysts for details on Meta’s plans, Zuckerberg framed compute as a scarce strategic asset that the company should keep and build around, rather than simply sell for short-term profit.

But he acknowledged that the company had received a number of offers for its computing capacity from businesses that wanted to deploy their own AI plans “at a meaningful premium” over what it invested to build that capacity.

That tension sits at the heart of Meta’s challenge in diversifying its revenue stream. Renting out compute could ease Meta’s cash-flow squeeze, but would also divert scarce resources from its own push to build AI models and services.

Having built its fortune selling ads on Facebook and Instagram, the company is now trying to take on larger rivals including Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon that have deep ties to enterprises, an early and lucrative market for AI.

Microsoft on Wednesday showed how its AI bets were paying off even as its free cash flow fell 23%. The Windows maker breezed past expectations for growth in its Azure cloud unit and Copilot assistant thanks to a huge base of corporate customers and its early AI build-out, sending its stock up over 13%.

Spending like a cloud giant

“We believe that there will continue to be a significantly higher margin on selling intelligence rather than selling compute directly, but we think that there’s a big opportunity obviously to sell compute as well,” he said, as he painted a picture of what Meta hopes to build with its AI spending spree.

Zuckerberg argued that AI-powered personal assistants could become a mass-market product used by billions of consumers, while business agents could eventually help companies handle customer service, sales and marketing.

But beyond broad references to subscriptions and enterprise services, he offered few specifics on how those businesses would justify Meta’s massive AI spending.

Responding to a question from J.P.Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth, who noted that Meta was also purchasing capacity from third parties while selling compute, Zuckerberg said Meta was intentionally investing ahead of demand.

“There is a lead time where we’re investing in building out these data centers now. They come online at some point in the future. You obviously are not getting value out of them until they’re online,” he said.

“Meta is spending like a hyperscaler without a hyperscaler’s business model,” said Josh Gilbert, online investing platform eToro’s lead APAC analyst, referring to large cloud companies.

“Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon can point their data center dollars at cloud businesses that sell compute straight back out the door, but Meta doesn’t have the same outlet, so every dollar of build-out leans on the ads business.”

Metaverse scare

Meta’s massive AI spending push has unnerved some investors, who are drawing parallels to the company’s costly pivot to the metaverse — a bet that racked up tens of billions of dollars in losses without becoming a large revenue generator.

Its free cash flow slump in the April-June quarter was the steepest since late 2022, when the metaverse bet attracted similar investor scrutiny.

Still, Meta raised the low end of its capital spending forecast by $5 billion, lifting the range to between $130 billion and $145 billion.

That echoes Alphabet, which raised its own forecast by $15 billion last week, reported its first cash burn on record and was punished with a 7% share drop.

Meta CFO Susan Li said on a post-earnings call that the spending was justified because the industry had “underbuilt historically” for AI demand, making existing capacity “extremely valuable.”

She said capacity would remain tight “for the foreseeable future,” creating opportunities for Meta to generate returns through products, enterprise services and compute sales.

But responding to a question from Wells Fargo analyst Ken Gawrelski on whether Meta planned to internally use all its compute capacity through 2027, Li ended the call much as Zuckerberg had started it: arguing Meta could find profitable uses for additional compute both inside and outside the company, without indicating where those returns would ultimately be the greatest.

“The earnings call felt a lot like a good old-fashioned brainstorming session,” said Bernstein analyst Mark Shmulik. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Waste of taxpayers’ money’: Caloocan residents slam ‘useless’ drainage project
World.content:
Residents of Libis Espina Street in Caloocan City lament the continued flooding in their area despite millions spent on a road rehabilitation and drainage project

MANILA, Philippines – Since the southwest monsoon or habagat began last May, residents of Caloocan City have again borne the brunt of what they describe as “substandard” infrastructure projects in their communities.

In June, as heavy rains inundated parts of Metro Manila, the Batang SoCal Facebook page posted a photo of ankle-deep flooding in Libis Espina Street where the road and drainage system had just been “rehabilitated.”

In the comments section of the post, Caloocan residents took turns lambasting the P9.6-million road rehabilitation and drainage system (Phase 3) project in Libis Espina carried out by Dreamworx Builder and Trading Incorporated. The project is situated between Barangay 14 and Barangay 16.

Vegetable and fruit vendor Karen Libiran shared their sentiment. “Nagsasayang lang [sila] ng pera. Hindi rin nawawala ‘yung baha sa pag-aayos nila,” she told Rappler when asked about the recent project in the community.

(They’re just wasting money. The flooding remains even after they finished the project.)

“‘Yun ‘yung purpose ng pag-aayos nila di ba? Para mawala ‘yung baha. E ganoon din e, wala rin namang nangyayari,” Libiran added.

(That’s the purpose of the rehabilitation, right? To prevent flooding. But it’s still the same.)

Libiran’s sister-in-law, fellow vendor Jessica Santiago, said there was some improvement in the appearance of the street gutters but the flooding problem was not addressed.

“Umayos nga ‘yung kanal pero hindi nawala ‘yung baha,” Santiago told Rappler. (The street gutter improved but the flooding is still there.)

Impact on livelihood

For fish vendor Liza Cadiz nothing has improved in the area of Libis Espina Street, Barangay 14, Caloocan, where she sells her wares. Waist-level flooding is a regular occurrence whenever there’s prolonged heavy rains, hampering their livelihood.

“Malaking epekto talaga kasi bukod sa bumabaha, hindi kami makatinda, wala rin kaming mapakyaw. Walang pakyaw, e [kapag] may bagyo. Matumal talaga,” she told Rappler in an interview.

(It hugely affects us because aside from flooding, we can’t sell, we can’t buy in bulk. There’s no wholesale because of a typhoon. Business is really slow.)

Whenever she learns that there will be bad weather, Cadiz would opt to stay at home. There was a time, she said, when her table piled with fish floated and got swept away by floodwater.

She said the project was supposed to fix the flooding problem but nothing was solved, raising questions about the construction and funds for that project.

Pedicab driver Lolito Layson said nothing changed in the area where he waits for passengers, despite seeing Libis Espina Street being rehabilitated almost every year.

Flooding affects his livelihood, as passengers would choose tricycles that can better navigate flooded streets. Those who pick him would have to squat on their seats to keep themselves dry.

Asked about the rehabilitation project, Layson said it looked okay on the surface but when put to the test, the drainage system could not handle the volume of water. The flooding situation, he said, remained the same.

The rehabilitation project was 96.72% accomplished according to the transparency website of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

The DPWH transparency website shows proof of accomplishment of the project as well, but it only in the Libis Extension alley, which is in Barangay 16. This road floods even when it’s not raining. Authorities only budged after public complaints and social media posts.

According to a DPWH project billboard, the project was supposed to have started in March 2025 and completed months after, in August 2025.

But residents, including tricycle drivers, pedicab drivers, and vendors in the community whom Rappler talked to echoed Batang SoCal’s Facebook post that the project only began construction in February this year and was completed in July.

Rappler reached out to the Metro Manila 3rd District Engineering Office and Dreamworx for their comments. The DPWH Stakeholder Relations Service and Dreamworx have acknowledged our request. We will update this story once they respond to our queries.

Root of the problem

Libis Espina, Barangay 14, and Barangay 16 are part the Dagat-Dagatan area, which spans portions of Caloocan, Malabon, and Navotas. The whole area was such named as it used to look like a virtual sea with private fishponds that were connected to Manila Bay. The first Marcos government expropriated the fishponds and reclaimed the area for a pet project of Imelda Marcos, who was human settlements minister at the time, according to a paper published by the Ateneo de Manila University.

The purpose of this reclaimed area was to make way for a “massive low-cost housing project” that was pursued despite warnings of massive flooding in surrounding areas without proper mitigation systems in place. As predicted, the project led to flooding in Malabon and other areas because the natural waterways were plugged in — a problem that persists to this day.

Eventually, Caloocan became one of the most flood-prone cities in Metro Manila. Twenty barangays in the city, including Barangay 14, have been identified as areas that are at “very high risk” of flooding by 2020 and 2030, according to a study published in the Journal of Urban and Regional Planning.

Rappler earlier reported that decades of costly flood-mitigation infrastructure have failed to provide relief to Caloocan residents. – Rappler.com

Eunicito Barreno is a 2026 Aries Rufo Fellow. He is a senior journalism student at the University of the Philippines Diliman, where he is also news staffer at the Philippine Collegian, the university’s official student publication.

World.title: Trump says ICC campaign aimed at defending Netanyahu, not himself
World.content:
TRUMP. US President Donald Trump disembarks Air Force One at Morristown Municipal Airport in Morristown, New Jersey, US, July 31, 2026

Trump defends campaign against ICC, claims it's to protect allies like Netanyahu, not himself, as five countries announce plans to withdraw from the court.

MARYLAND, US – US President Donald Trump said on Friday that a US campaign to dismantle the International Criminal Court was intended to defend Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and others from prosecution, not himself.

Trump made the comment after Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a cabinet meeting at Camp David that five countries had announced plans to quit the court since the United States launched a campaign earlier this month against what it says is a threat to US sovereignty.

“There’s no information that they’re after me,” Trump said.

“It could happen, but just so you know … he (Rubio) is not trying to defend me. He’s trying to defend Bibi and various other people,” Trump said, using Netanyahu’s nickname. “But there are many people that shouldn’t be looked at that way. But there is no indication that I’m one of them at this moment.”

Rubio responded that the people in biggest danger were US service members, who he said could face prosecution years later over their actions in war.

The ICC was established in 2002 by the international community to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. It asserts jurisdiction only if a member state is unable or unwilling to prosecute atrocities itself.

The United States ​has never been a member of the court.

However, the ICC statute also gives the court the power to prosecute atrocity crimes committed on the territory of member states by ​nationals of non-member states.

Trump’s opposition toward the court goes back to his first term. It surfaced again with a plan to penalize ICC officials, an idea developed in November 2024 when Trump was reelected ‌and the ⁠ICC issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza conflict.

Rubio earlier this month denounced the court based in The Hague, citing calls from activists for the ICC to investigate US personnel over actions like the deportation of migrants or US strikes on boats that officials say are carrying narcotics.

The Trump administration has said it would lobby other countries to leave the court and use travel bans and further sanctions against the ICC and affiliated organizations to try to undermine the court, which is being opposed in the courts by ICC judges and US advocacy groups which accuse the administration of violating their free speech rights. – Rappler.com
