A burst of six straight Australia goals either side of half-time propelled the home team to a 13.13 (91) to 6.5 (41) victory in an entertaining AFLW international played before a capacity crowd of 9,017 at North Sydney Oval on Saturday.

Australia led at every break, by margins of 12, 30 and 41.

Ireland thrilled the crowd, which included a large contingent of their fans, with several fast, flowing passages of play In the first half, but couldn't stay the course against a polished and more consistent Australia.

The home team won the physical battle, tallying 35 more contested possessions.

Australian captain and North Melbourne star Jasmine Garner was named player of the match.

Ebony Marinoff topped Australia's possession count with 25, from Ash Riddell and Nina Morrison 21 each.

For Ireland, Erika O'Shea led their possession tally with 21, followed by skipper Orla O'Dwyer with 19.

North Melbourne players were leading goalkickers for both teams, with Tahlia Randall bagging four for Australia and Blaithin Bogue three for Ireland.

Australia piled on three goals in the first six minutes with Sydney's Zippy Fish kicking the first, but Ireland responded with three goals of their own either side of quarter time.

The home team kicked two goals early in the second and Ireland replied in kind, before another Australian surge proved decisive.

Ireland's goal-kicking accuracy kept them in the game for most of the first half, as they kicked 5.0 to Australia's 5.6, before the home team took over and maximised their opportunities.

The home team kicked the only two goals of the third quarter and two to one in the last.

Australian rucks Mim Strom and Matilda Scholz dominated the hitouts, giving Australia a whopping advantage in that area.

The home team dominated in the air, taking 38 more marks and limiting Ireland to just eight in the first half.

Ireland's Aine McDonagh left the field clutching her right arm late in the second quarter.

It wasn't all bad for the Irish, however.

Niamh McLaughlin (centre) kicked an amazing goal for Ireland against Australia but her team went down at North Sydney Oval. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

North Melbourne and County Fermanagh player Bogue proved almost impossible to stop early on, kicking three goals for the game.

She also set up the goal of the game in the final quarter, producing a World Cup-like cross from the right forward pocket for Niamh McLaughlin to get her foot to the ball and flick it casually over the Australian defence and through.

The Irish didn't give up, despite the lop-sided scoreboard, and another Kangaroos player Vikki Wall (County Meath) delivered a bump that drew gasps from the crowd in the final quarter as she dispossessed Australia's Ella Roberts in midfield before setting up an attack.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Russian missile attacks on Kyiv kill at least ten and injure dozens
World.content:
Russian attacks on Ukraine's capital have killed at least 10 people and injured more than two dozen others, local officials say, with strikes damaging homes and causing fires across the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service said the latest Russian attack overnight into Saturday struck five regions of Kyiv, killing nine people and wounding 28 others, including four children.

Russia's defence ministry said on Saturday it had launched a "massive strike" against "Ukrainian military-industrial complex facilities and logistics centres in Kyiv".

In Kyiv's Darnytsky district, the attacks damaged multiple buildings and vehicles, with authorities reporting seven people killed and 14 wounded in the area.

Two people were killed and eight others were wounded in Solomiansky district, where strikes damaged a five-storey residential building.

One more person was killed in the Kyiv region where the attacks damaged several warehouses, regional officials said.

The deadly attacks damaged multiple buildings and vehicles. (AP Photo: Efrem Lukatsky)

Ukraine and Russia have ramped up attacks on each other in recent months.

"It's getting worse by the day," 64-year-old Liudmyla Nakonechna told the Associated Press from a basement shelter where she was taking cover as an air alarm sounded for another wave.

" Whereas before there was an attack once every two weeks, or maybe once a week, now it happens practically every day. It is incredibly hard to bear this psychologically. "

As Moscow has increased its long-range strikes on Ukrainian towns and cities, Kiev has pressed its allies for air defence support.

Ukraine downed only one of 27 Russian ballistic missiles during the attack as the country lacks interceptors for the US Patriot systems, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The world's largest lake, where two wars collided in a show of strength A large inland sea connecting military supply lines through Russia and Iran could now be a pivotal theatre for two major wars that are usually thought of as separate.

Mr Zelenskyy said that Russia launched a total of 35 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles and 185 attack drones.

The capital Kyiv was the primary target of the attack, he said.

Earlier this week, Mr Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump for talks, and said following the meeting that Mr Trump had agreed to license the production of Patriot missiles to Ukraine.

But Mr Trump said on Friday that Washington would have to be "very careful" about giving Ukraine a licence to produce the missiles.

Russia's ministry of defence on Saturday said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed 274 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Reuters/AFP/AP

World.title: 'We are not a monoculture and never have been,' Penny Wong tells Garma Festival
World.content:
Historic relationships formed over hundreds of years between First Nations peoples and their Pacific neighbours offer Australia a "strategic national advantage", Foreign Minister Penny Wong has told Garma Festival.

"Centuries before Europeans arrived, First Nations people connected Australia with the world," Ms Wong told those gathered in north-east Arnhem Land for the second day of the nation's largest Indigenous gathering.

"As Australia's foreign minister, I am proud that this history — once under-utilised — is now part of Australia's foreign policy."

Ms Wong used her keynote address to emphasise her "shared vision for the Pacific region", acknowledging Prime Minister of Timor-Leste Xanana Gusmão and leaders from the Marshall Islands, Kiribati, the Solomon Islands, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Palau, and Tonga in the audience.

Penny Wong used her keynote address to emphasise her "shared vision for the Pacific region". (ABC News: BIlly Cooper)

'We are not a monoculture and never have been'

Appearing on behalf of the prime minister, who was absent from the festival, Ms Wong rejected the idea of Australia as a 'monoculture' and emphasised Australia's "common ground" with other countries.

"We are not a monoculture and never have been," she said.

"That is why the Albanese Labor government has been determined to include more of Australia's history and voices in our foreign policy."

Prime Minister of Timor-Leste Xanana Gusmão also gave a keynote address. (ABC News: BIlly Cooper)

As a Yanyuwa woman, Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy described her own family's cultural and trade connections to the people of Macassar.

"We taught them about the trees to use for the ropes to make," she said in her keynote address.

"They taught us about the sails. We showed them where the trepang was.

"They would live with us for many, many seasons before they went back. And we would do the same."

Malarndirri McCarthy says the looming closure of a Rio Tinto mine will bring big changes to north-east Arnhem Land. (ABC News: Billy Cooper )

A focus on land rights

On the 50th anniversary of land rights, Ms McCarthy described the "alien moment" of her family having to prove their connections to the land.

"It was 50 years ago that the Yanyuwa people, my families, were the first to be tested under the Aboriginal Land Rights Act Northern Territory," she said.

Albanese's absence looms large over Garma The theme of this year's Garma Festival is "bukmak", a Yolŋu word meaning "everyone", but the prime minister's decision not to attend may indicate how high on the government's priority list Indigenous affairs sit.

"I was only a little girl, but I remember my grandfathers, my Mimi (grandmother) and my Kurdis (grandfathers), my kujakas (mothers) all thinking and talking about how they were going to prove they were Yanyuwa and that they belonged to this land around the Borroloola region.

"How did they explain that their relationship has been there for thousands of years?"

Ms McCarthy acknowledged the previous announcement made by Gumatj Corporation leader Djawa Yunupiŋu.

As the ABC's Matt Garrick reported earlier on Saturday, Mr Yunupiŋu used his Garma Festival speech to announce the creation of a breakaway remote Northern Territory land council to help drive direct economic development for his people.

"We are going to the top of the mountain," Mr Yunupiŋu said.

The creation of the Dilak Land Council would put the ability to make economic development decisions into the hands of his people, and away from the powerful Northern Land Council (NLC) which oversees communities across much of the Top End.

Cape York Institute leader Noel Pearson has called for major reform to remote community oversight. (ABC News: Billy Cooper )

'The most beautiful unrequited letter of love in Australian political history'

Cape York Institute leader Noel Pearson used his keynote address to call for an overhaul of how remote Aboriginal communities are managed.

Mr Pearson last spoke at Garma festival in 2023, the year of the Voice referendum.

"The Uluru Statement from the Heart was our prayer to the Australian people," he said on Saturday afternoon.

"There was hope in its words.

"The statement was written with love. It stands as probably the most beautiful unrequited letter of love in Australian political history.

"For those of us who urged faith, hope and love, there is an account to be given for the hopes raised, the faith urged and the love lost in the referendum."

Mr Pearson said he stood at Garma "with great reluctance" three years after the failed Voice referendum.

"What right has anyone to raise hopes when those hopes were so badly misplaced? What right has anyone to offer a vision that turns out to be a mirage?" he asked.

"That is the source of my hesitation to speak of these things. But I cannot allow the failure of the referendum to excuse me from my responsibility."

On the second afternoon of Garma Festival, attendees gathered for the buŋgul, a Yolŋu cultural ceremony. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

A call for an overhaul

He referred to a map from the Australian Electoral Commission in the wake of the referendum that showed where the majority of voters of yes marked in blue and no marked in orange.

"The blue dots that voted Yes correspond with remote and discrete indigenous communities in Far Northern Queensland and the Torres Strait, the Northern Territory and the central and western deserts, and the northern and desert regions of Western Australia," Pearson said.

He called for a "fundamental structural reform to the governmental jurisdiction" of these blue-dot communities in remote Australia to become "the sole jurisdiction of the Commonwealth".

"These communities and their lands would still come under the shared jurisdiction of the relevant states and territories for most functions governed by the state's constitutional responsibilities, but the administrative relationship for Aboriginal affairs would lie with the Commonwealth," he said.

Buŋgul is a cultural ceremony Yolŋu clans have been performing for thousands of years. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Also in attendance on Saturday was Labor MP Luke Gosling, the day after he faced Darwin Local Court charged with two counts of assaulting NT Administrator David Connolly.

When asked whether she backed Mr Gosling to keep the role of special envoy for defence, veterans' affairs and Northern Australia, Penny Wong told the ABC that he was "entitled to the same legal processes that you would be entitled to in this situation".

On the other side of the Garma site the youth forum was underway, as were sessions exploring Milkarri, the sacred and ancestral voice of Yolŋu women and Yirrkala printmaking as well as the daily buŋgul, a cultural ceremony Yolŋu clans have been performing for thousands of years.

World.title: Diamonds disaster: Australia stunned by Jamaica in historic loss
World.content:
SportNetballCommonwealth Games Diamonds disaster: Australia stunned by Jamaica in historic loss Hannah Kennelly Updated August 2, 2026 — 3:50am ,first published 11:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: As the siren sounded on the Diamonds’ semi-final clash with Jamaica, only Commonwealth Games debutant Sophie Dwyer stood between Australia and unwanted history. The Diamonds – who had never lost a Games semi-final before – were down by one goal to Jamaica and Dwyer had an opportunity to tie the game and force extra time. The dejected Diamonds after losing their semi-final against Jamaica. Getty Images She lined up and took the shot from long range, but the ball bounced off the rim. Cue pandemonium for Jamaica, who stormed the court in ecstasy over their 46-45 victory, celebrating as if they’d already won the gold medal. In some ways, they had.



The Diamonds entered the competition as the clear favourites, cruising through their opening rounds and easily defeating England, Tonga, South Africa, Northern Ireland and Malawi. But they were ill prepared for a fiery Jamaican side in the semi-final. Kate Moloney admitted after the loss that it “hadn’t quite sunk in yet” and said Dwyer should not bear the burden of the loss. When Dwyer missed her shot after the buzzer, Moloney went to comfort and embrace her teammate. “We will wrap our arms around her. It’s a full team loss, it’s not on one person. We should not have been in the position where we needed to shoot a goal after the siren,” Moloney said. “Really disappointing but credit to Jamaica, they really came out and really gave it to us,” she said. “We probably just didn’t execute the way we needed to.”



It was a packed house at the Hydro, where the Prince and Princess of Wales and their three children were among the spectators. The crowd was clearly pro-Jamaica, but Moloney dismissed suggestions that had any effect on the playing group, saying “we don’t really notice too much of that.” “We know that at our best we beat anyone, and today we probably just weren’t at our best,” she said. “We’ll have a look at it and take lots of learnings and come out stronger tomorrow.” The Diamonds will now have to settle for a chance at bronze against England on Sunday instead of trying for back-to-back gold medals, the first time they will sit out the decider since netball became a full part of the Commonwealth Games program in 1998. This time, it will be the Jamaicans taking on New Zealand in the gold medal match.



The Diamonds had no answer for Jamaica’s aerial superiority in the first half, as the Sunshine Girls overpowered them with sheer force and speed – aided by a truly stupendous performance from Shamera Sterling Humphrey, who used all 190 centimetres of her height to intercept and create crucial turnovers. Sterling-Humphrey recently won the 2026 Super Netball grand final with the Adelaide Thunderbirds back in Australia. Her presence in the Jamaican squad was deadly for the Australians, who struggled to stop her. In the final five minutes of the last quarter, the umpire’s whistle could barely be heard as the crowd turned up the volume in favour of the Jamaican side. Jubilation: Jamaica celebrate winning through to the gold medal match. Getty Images Their bench was no less involved, cheering, encouraging, advising and waving the flag throughout the entire match. It reached fever pitch as Dwyer’s shot missed and they stormed the court, jumping on top of each other.



Australia’s bench looked stunned, with coach Stacey Marinkovich staring stony-faced while other players leaned forward with their hands covering their mouths. Sterling-Humphrey said if anyone was going to beat the Diamonds, it was going to be the Jamaicans. “We have the inside information on them [the Diamonds] and thanks to the Suncorp Super Netball season for giving us the upper hand, playing them week in, week out,” she laughed. It’s been an extraordinary year for Sterling-Humphrey, who has been candid and vulnerable about her postpartum journey. “My bubs is somewhere in the stands cheering his mommy on,” she said.“I’m so proud of the year I’ve had, battling postpartum depression.”

World.title: Commonwealth Games LIVE: Diamonds miss gold medal match for first time; Denny celebrates gold with baby son
World.content:
Aussie Sienna Newton has poked fun at herself a day after she finished fourth in the women’s T38 long jump, suffering a wardrobe malfunction before her final attempt.

Newton had previously jumped a career best 4.70 metres and was competing for a potential bronze medal on her sixth and final jump.

However as the clock ticked down, Newton struggled to remove her pants. The athlete has an acquired brain injury, and lives with a weakness in her left hand and spasticity in her knee and foot.

“Between the countdown clock and trying to wrestle off a pair of pants with a left hand that I can’t feel, it wasn’t exactly an easy task,” Newton posted alongside a video of her wardrobe struggles.

World.title: The Blues are seizing their moment. It’s time Josh Fraser seized his, too
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The Blues are seizing their moment. It’s time Josh Fraser seized his, too Andrew Wu August 2, 2026 — 1:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Under Josh Fraser, Carlton have learnt to seize the moment. It’s time their interim coach did the same. Fraser will decide this week if he puts his hat in the ring for the top job. He’d be mad not to. “I haven’t put my hand up for the job yet,” Fraser said with a chuckle after the Blues marked the 250th games of Patrick Cripps and Nick Haynes with a stunning 76-point obliteration of the Brisbane Lions, 24.10 (154) to 11.12 (78). Josh Fraser’s record as Blues interim coach is impossible to ignore. AFL Photos “I spoke about this in the press conference during the week that I’ll take a little bit of time [to decide].



“I’m mindful that I’ve said that previously and that decision’s getting closer, but, post that press conference, my sole focus has been on tonight.” Related Article AFL 2026 Harry Dean kicked his first AFL goal on a dream night for the Blues. His dad, a Carlton great, missed it Unless you’re David Parkin (or Alex Jesaulenko and a couple of others from before the Great Depression), you only get one chance to coach Carlton – and Fraser may never get a better opportunity to realise his aspiration of landing a senior role. Perhaps Fraser would like more time to be the finished article, but not many coaches go into a selection process having been at the helm of four clubs at state league level, and put together a 9-2 run as an interim senior AFL coach. He has put the Blues in the driver’s seat to claim what three months ago seemed the unlikeliest of wildcard slots.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects “I’m almost convinced that you’re never a finished produced in terms of being ready [for a senior role], but I’m open-minded to how I keep getting better,” Fraser said. The Blues job would have to be one of the most sought after posts in recent times. New coaches tend to take over a club at or near disrepair, in need of a rebuild. Carlton bosses may not believe their list is ready to regularly beat the best, but nor is it in need of an overhaul like Essendon, the other club searching for a coach. The Blues’ side against the Lions had six players aged 21 or under, all of whom played important roles. Smith will likely win the Rising Star award, and cult figure defender Harry Dean, who had the crowd in raptures with his first goal, will finish on the podium.



View post on X Cody Walker will join them after the draft, and with North Melbourne’s and Gold Coast’s second-round picks to come, plus another two first-round selections next year, they have the means to acquire further top-end talent. The Carlton community were all aboard the ill-fated Teague train seven years ago. It’s standing room only on the Fraser freight train. The near 41,000 fans in a partisan Blues crowd roared as one on Saturday night when Fraser emerged on the big screen congratulating his players.



The warmth with which his men embraced him brought back memories of the player power behind Paul Roos’s promotion in 2002. Blues players, of course, will not have a say in who will coach them next year, but Fraser is building a compelling case. View post on X It has been a long time since Carlton played as complete a home-and-away game as this turbocharged performance. The Blues’ calling card is contest and clearance but seldom has it been accompanied by the electrifying ball movement, ferocious pressure and clean skills shown against the Lions. No wonder Marvel Stadium was rocking.



“It felt like we had 19 out there tonight,” Mitch McGovern said. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘I wouldn’t be going to Essendon’: Matthews slams Bombers; Lyon again eyeballs reporters in presser Headed by an equal career-best of five goals from Brodie Kemp, Carlton had a joint league record 16 goalkickers for their tally of 24, a sign of how Fraser has taught his men to spread the load after the departure of Charlie Curnow. It was fitting that in Cripps’ milestone game, the Blues strapped the captain on their backs rather than have their leader carry them to victory. Despite Cripps being shaded by old foe Josh Dunkley, who held him to 18 possessions, the Blues dominated the midfield. The Lions could not stop Jagga Smith, who finished with 29 possessions and two goals. His capacity to win the ball inside and get it moving was a key factor in the game.



The first-season star, whose 2025 was wiped out by a knee injury, claimed the Robert Walls Medal, though either of his running mates Sam Walsh or George Hewett would have been worthy winners of the award struck in honour of the Carlton great and former Brisbane Bears coach. “I think we’re at a stage where we don’t need him to be our best player each week,” Fraser said of Cripps. Nick Haynes and Patrick Cripps were both chaired off after their 250th games. AFL Photos “Not to say that he’s not going to have games where he’s influential, and he’s had those games for us, but part of where we’re going in terms of leaving his club in a better place is making sure that other players assume responsibility, and ‘Crippa’ doesn’t feel like he has to do everything.” Under former coach Michael Voss, particularly as they slid to a 1-8 record, the Blues could not identify key points in games to manage momentum swings. This has changed under Fraser, who is bedding down a style at 10-10 which values control of the game through the retention of possession.



The Lions’ three late goals before half-time after a powerful 20 minutes may have unravelled Carlton earlier this year, but not now. “It’s just understanding the moments and the time of the game,” Fraser said. As D-Day for Fraser looms, those words could just as easily apply to him. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Carroll declares integrity a non-negotiable – and defends his own
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Carroll declares integrity a non-negotiable – and defends his own Chip Le Grand August 2, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state’s peak anti-corruption agency will be given a broader remit as soon as possible to stamp out public sector malfeasance, conflicts of interest and improper influence that falls short of criminal conduct, as new Premier Ben Carroll seeks to restore public trust in government. Carroll said he would immediately seek advice on whether proposed changes to IBAC’s jurisdiction due to come into force at the end of next year could be brought forward. “If we can bring it forward, I will,” he said. Ben Carroll on Sunday: “I want to be a premier that is listening, that hears the message and gets on with it.” Wayne Taylor He promised that a special prosecutor working in tandem with a royal commission into the building industry to secure criminal convictions would be given whatever time and resources they need to clean up the corruption-plagued major projects sector. “I’m going to lead with integrity,” Carroll said. “Integrity is non-negotiable. It’s fundamental.



“I’m hoping the public will at least see that I’m trying to do the right thing by them.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson released on Saturday her proposed terms of reference for a royal commission and a suggested list of witnesses including Daniel Andrews, Jacinta Allan and Carroll. Related Article Exclusive

Construction royal commission Bombshell briefing reveals top officials’ CFMEU warning to Allan Carroll said the terms of reference would be finalised this week and he had a shortlist of candidates for the roles of commissioner and special prosecutor. In seeking to explain the events that led up to last week’s dramatic change of Labor leader and premier, Carroll also addressed questions about his personal integrity.



He insists that he remained a loyal deputy to Allan until last Monday, when a delegation of cross-factional leaders told the former premier she had lost the support of her own government and urged Carroll to challenge for the leadership. It is less clear whether, as deputy premier, he made the case inside government for a royal commission or more urgent Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission reforms – steps he now says are crucial to restoring public faith in a 12-year-old Labor government. Related Article Visual Story

Construction royal commission Slow, then fast: The downfall of a premier under siege Two cabinet ministers have told The Age – and Carroll did not deny – that last Tuesday’s fateful caucus meeting was the first time he advocated for a royal commission into Big Build corruption in any government forum. When pressed on whether he counselled Allan privately to establish a royal commission, Carroll did not answer directly but said it was clear the former premier was not for turning.



“I didn’t raise things where it looked like the deputy and premier were on different sides of the fence,” he told The Age in an exclusive interview. “I raised with the premier a number of times that she needed to do something. Privately, I have also been talking to colleagues about a royal commission. “We spoke most Sunday nights before every cabinet meeting. She was very clear with her views and always sought my support. The role of the deputy is to give the premier support. Even when I disagreed with her privately, I’ve always backed her publicly and in the cabinet room. “The premier has known I have been wanting transparency and accountability for a long time.”



The comments are unlikely to heal the internal party wounds created by last week’s bruising leadership change. In a wide-ranging interview, Carroll revealed other instances where he disagreed with government decisions but was unable to publicly ventilate his concerns while upholding cabinet solidarity. Carroll admitted for the first time that a secret decision taken by the Allan government to delay by three years its commitment to fully fund public schools was a $2.4 billion funding cut and the wrong thing to do. The decision, which was exposed by The Age, is at the heart of the bitter wage dispute between the government and teachers. It was taken by the government’s budget and finance committee, of which the premier and deputy premier are members. Carroll, who is also education minister, opposed the move but failed to stop it. “I argued ferociously in the cabinet subcommittee process,” Carroll said. “I did speak up about it.” He said cabinet confidentially prevented him from publicly discussing the funding cut, even after it was revealed by this newspaper.



“When cabinet arrives at a position you need to support that position.” Carroll said the current pay offer before teachers, while generous, was not enough to fully fund government schools under the Gonski formula. He raised with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week the need to lift school funding in Victoria and deliver the long-awaited Gonski reforms. Related Article Opinion

School funding In the so-called education state, Gonski puts our schools stone-cold last Chip Le Grand State political editor “I am committed to try and get full and fair funding for our public schools,” he said. He agreed the tax burden on business in Victoria, particularly since increases to payroll tax and land tax announced by former treasurer Tim Pallas in 2023, needed to be lightened. The tax rises were announced as temporary but are due to remain in force until 2033.



“We want to be competitive with NSW. We’ve got to do everything we can to make it easy to start a business in Victoria and grow a business,” Carroll said. “We’ve also just got to support everyday Victorians who are working hard every day. We are in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis which is hurting and biting and it has no end in sight.” One of the 2023 tax increases removed the payroll tax exemption for non-government schools. While the impost was adjusted in this year’s budget to impact fewer schools, Carroll left open the possibility of scrapping it altogether. “I think this was a necessary measure for the time, but I’m always open to continue working with the sector,” he said. Carroll said the planned Suburban Rail Loop, the most expensive infrastructure project in the state’s history, was a good concept undermined by the way it was developed, in secret, under then-premier Daniel Andrews in the lead-up to the 2018 election.



While the government’s contractual commitments to the SRL and the project’s financial assumptions will be reviewed by cabinet, Carroll said the rail line already under construction needed to be built. Related Article Victorian Parliament Down to business: Carroll leaves door open to work-from-home changes “I have always believed the project is a great concept. The problem with the SRL is its gestation period – it never had one. Airport rail had been talked about for 100 years. SRL was never part of the public discussion. It came as a surprise to a lot of people, including cabinet members. “However, the project does have merit and the project does need to continue. I’m not going to stop contracts or rip up contracts. That era is over.” He acknowledged concerns expressed by Victoria’s integrity agencies about the budget squeeze on their operations and capacity to expose corruption, misconduct and financial mismanagement.



“We need strong, independent agencies – IBAC, the Auditor-General, the Ombudsman. We are stewards of our public finances and institutions. That’s a role I take very seriously.” When asked about reports that he wants to change legislation, currently before parliament, to give people a legal right to work from home two days a week, Carroll said the government would consider sensible amendments but not move any itself. Loading Since taking the leadership, he has been repeatedly questioned and attacked by the opposition over comments he made six weeks ago, referencing his daughter, in which he vowed to support Jacinta Allan through to the state election. He said it was not the first time he had made the comment and that he previously wrote to Allan expressing the same sentiment.



Related Article Analysis

Victorian election The hatred of Jacinta Allan was unfair. But it had become visceral Carroll and Allan had a private meeting in the premier’s office the day before Tuesday’s leadership spill. Neither has disclosed what was discussed. Carroll said that by then, the political reality had changed, with an unrelenting corruption scandal cruelling whatever chance Allan and Labor had to remain in power after the November 28 state election. “We’d all been out door-knocking and it was very clear we weren’t getting the message through,” he said. Instead, voters were outraged at the estimated $15 billion cost of the Building Bad scandal documented by this masthead. “I want to be a premier that is listening, that hears the message and gets on with it. That’s why my first act was to call the royal commission. It’s why I will give the police commissioner every power and resource he needs. It’s why I will do what I can do to give IBAC the power and resources it needs. “And then, there are things I want to do that are part of Labor’s DNA.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: In a straight-laced city is one of the world’s least-boring art museums
World.content:
InspirationCulture holidays In a straight-laced city is one of the world’s least-boring art museums Brian Johnston August 2, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’m tired of art galleries. All those naked Greek nymphs. All those dreary saints porcupined with arrows, and double-chinned dukes trimmed in ermine. I soon feel headachy. I enjoy a park more than a battle scene. Cafes rather than Canalettos. Why look at paintings of dead people when, outside, living foreigners are doing strange things? Lausanne has views over Lake Geneva to the French Alps. The Art Brut Collection in Lausanne. Strange to me anyway. Daily routine to them, I presume. Isn’t that the point of travel? The world is refreshingly unusual, but shares human culture, and we learn that our differences aren’t so odd after all. Which brings me to Lausanne, a city so buttoned up that it barely glances at its stupendous views over Lake Geneva to the French Alps, but instead looks down on gorges and railway cuttings.



For most visitors, Lausanne’s attraction is the Olympic Museum. But you won’t learn anything about scandal and corruption at the IOC’s official museum – though you will see Cathy Freeman’s running shoes. 



The creators whose work is displayed here spent time in mental institutions or prisons, or both. Nothing unusual there; Caravaggio and van Gogh did, too. But none had art training. They disregarded art movements and public opinion and never painted for a patron or audience. Related Article Europe It’s not the French Riviera, but this land-locked version is just as entrancing Regular art museums have little to say about artists, but the extensive biographies here are worth reading, and fascinating. Who decides who is an artist? Many revered artists had troubled lives and odd visions. For that matter, the poet T. S. Eliot was recovering from a breakdown at a sanatorium in Lausanne when he wrote The Waste Land. That’s one question the collection makes you ponder. Another is what art is. One person’s masterpiece might be another’s obsessive doodle. Does it matter what art is made from? You’ll see stone figures hewn from stolen milestones, and lonely-looking people carved from cork. Collages made by a pastry cook use crushed eggshells and glued-together breadcrumbs.



Clement Fraisse used a broken spoon to carve into the wooden panels of his cell. The shadowy human figures, geometric shapes and Buddhist-like wheels of life are strangely haunting. Abduction of a Bride of Gaul created by the Swiss outsider artist Aloise Corbaz around 1917. Franz Opitz created Swiss scenes depicting sheep in green fields and chalet window-boxes cascading with petunias. All seems bucolic. Then you notice the grass is fluorescent, the mountains like shards of stained glass. The sheep have frightening metallic faces, and flowers are cruelly imprisoned in small squares. Fraisse’s carvings seem like an escape into a calmer world, Opitz’s paintings a reflection of his tormented life. But my favourites are the works of Willem van Genk, perhaps because, confined to an orphanage as a child, he dreamed of faraway places. His complicated painted papercuts and collages, inspired by his adult travels, feature New York trains, serene Buddha statues, Thai beaches and Saharan dunes sprouting cherry trees. They aren’t tourist brochures however: rushing traffic, derelict buildings and shunting yards are depicted, too.



Does it take a troubled mind to be honest? Are beautiful places surrendering to urban blight? Is travel an escape from society, or only an illusion of one? And who is normal and who is mad? Good questions. Give me a van Genk over the silly pastoral paintings of Watteau and Fragonard any day, and you have me hooked. A textile sculpture by Danielle Jacqui, a major figure in Art Singulier (Marginal Art), displayed at the Collection de l’Art Brut museum. THE DETAILS Fly



Swiss operates codeshare flights to Geneva via Singapore and Munich. Direct trains from Geneva airport to Lausanne take 45 minutes. See swiss.com Stay Ibis Lausanne Centre is conveniently located and is a short walk from Collection de l’Art Brut and the city centre. Rooms from CHF118 ($213). See accor.com Visit Collection de l’Art Brut is open daily except public holidays and (other than July-August) Mondays. Admission is CHF12 ($22); it is free on the first Saturday of each month. See artbrut.ch



More lausanne-tourisme.ch The writer travelled at his own expense.

World.title: No Dylans, no worries: Ponga pandemonium buries Broncos as a new star emerges
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 No Dylans, no worries: Ponga pandemonium buries Broncos as a new star emerges Nick Wright August 1, 2026 — 10:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Deprived of their superstar Dylans and with their season teetering, Kalyn Ponga issued a reminder to the NRL that the Knights were far from a spent force as long as he remained in the action. The Newcastle skipper proved a Suncorp Stadium menace, often leaving the Brisbane Broncos defence clutching at him in desperation as he orchestrated a 30-6 triumph to keep them embedded in the top eight. Reece Walsh of the Broncos takes on the defence of Kalyn Ponga of the Knights at Suncorp Stadium on Saturday Getty Images Ponga’s first-half exploits were enough to signal his intent – producing a pair of linebreak assists while also shrugging off a tackle and firing a pass for Dom Young to score as the Knights took a 14-0 half-time lead. It was an opening stanza which left the Broncos pondering which footy gods they angered as Adam Reynolds (concussion) and Xavier Willison (leg gnash) missed most of the match, and Deine Mariner and Reece Walsh were both sent to the sin bin.



Both Broncos’ sin binnings were contentious – Mariner deemed to have pulled Jermaine McEwen off an attacking chance, while Walsh was pinned for a hair pull on Young after joining a fight McEwen (also sent for 10 minutes) added fuel to as an unnecessary instigator. When Ponga wasn’t terrorising the Brisbane defence, his remaining attacking linchpin Fletcher Sharpe was doing all he could to offset the season-ending injury losses of Dylan Brown and Dylan Lucas. Related Article NRL 2026 Watch: The costly moments that sealed Broncos fate, and how they can avenge freefall It took less than three minutes for Sharpe to shrug off three defenders and open the scoring with the scything run, before going on to finish with 168 running metres and two linebreaks, before he pounced on a loose ball and scoring his second to close out the contest. The Broncos were left to rue a slew of wasted opportunities – a dropped pass by Josiah Karapani with the line in sight the most obvious in the first half, while Ben Hunt’s forward pass early in the second term for Kotoni Staggs to barge across also deemed forward.



Only a few minutes later, a Walsh cutout pass for Grant Anderson gave them another opportunity, only for the latter to be pushed into touch by Greg Marzhew before being able to ground the ball. From the very next set, a break from Young down the right-hand touchline ended up in Ponga’s hands, with the Queensland Maroons No.1 finding an offload for Phoenix Crossland to score. Payne Haas of the Broncos in action in the round 22 clash. Getty Images Brisbane stayed in the fight through some Walsh magic – the marquee man jumping into dummy-half and helping unleash Mariner, before the star fullback gathered the kick ahead to score. But a dropped ball from Mariner coming out of trouble sealed their fate – a brilliant put down in the corner from Marzhew after a Bradman Best flick pass ending any hopes of a Broncos’ comeback.



The win keeps the Knights just one win shy of the top four, with a bye still to come in round 27. A new star emerges Remember the name: Francis Manuleleua. Newcastle appears to have unearthed one of rugby league’s most promising young forwards, with the 22-year-old backrower producing a miracle pass and showcase of physicality to put his name in lights. One week on from what was a breakout performance from the rising star – in which he scored, set up a try and made two linebreaks in a one-point loss to the Roosters – Manuleleau ensured he would remain on pundits’ lips on the Knights’ run to the finals.



His 100 running metres and 31 tackles said enough. But it was an instinctive and ridiculous 20-metre cutout pass during broken play for Marzhew to cross in the corner that will be replayed in highlight reels for the rest of the season. His tackle in the shadows of half-time on Pat Carrigan, forcing a knock on with his pressure from the inside as the Broncos went on the attack one last time, was another sign of the potential eight-game Kiwi prospect possessed. While the loss of Lucas to a serious ankle injury has been a dagger-blow to the Knights’ top four hopes, Manuleleua, has presented enough hope to the Newcastle faithful that they had an X-factor in their pack to challenge the best of the competition. What’s left for Broncos to salvage? Has the time come for Broncos coach Michael Maguire to begin planning for season 2027?



Brisbane will welcome a quartet of recruits next year – Jonah Pezet, Mitch Barnett, Shawn Blore and Knights rival Dane Gagai all joining the Red Hill rebuild. But after Willison was forced from the action within six minutes, the lack of depth through the middle was made glaringly clear. Payne Haas, who will join South Sydney from next season, was easily the most dangerous forward for Brisbane with 111 running metres, although the unheralded Jaiyden Hunt (143 metres) punched above his weight. The medical retirement of Corey Jensen – who suffered a pulmonary embolism – has left the club without the same front-row partnership that delivered premiership glory in 2025. Rookie enforcer VJ Semu played the most minutes of his fledgling NRL career – running for 50 metres and making 33 tackles from 39 minutes. He needs to keep being exposed to this level to put him in the best position possible to make use of his 110kg frame regularly next year. Reynolds’ category one concussion ruling will keep him out of next week’s Battle of Brisbane against the Dolphins. That will likely thrust Tom Duffy into the fray, and there is an argument he should be given the rest of the campaign to prove he is the long-term successor to the retiring champion. Brisbane’s ruck manipulation has also been lacking in 2026, but looked far more potent when Billy Walters – in his second NRL game back from a ruptured ACL – was thrown into the action. He was denied a try assist by a Ben Talty knock on, and has been tipped to ink a contract extension. Whatever decision Maguire makes, it has gotten to a stage where forward-planning must be a priority.

World.title: Diamonds disaster: Australia stunned by Jamaica in historic loss
World.content:
SportNetballCommonwealth Games Diamonds disaster: Australia stunned by Jamaica in historic loss Hannah Kennelly Updated August 2, 2026 — 3:50am ,first published 11:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: As the siren sounded on the Diamonds’ semi-final clash with Jamaica, only Commonwealth Games debutant Sophie Dwyer stood between Australia and unwanted history. The Diamonds – who had never lost a Games semi-final before – were down by one goal to Jamaica and Dwyer had an opportunity to tie the game and force extra time. The dejected Diamonds after losing their semi-final against Jamaica. Getty Images She lined up and took the shot from long range, but the ball bounced off the rim. Cue pandemonium for Jamaica, who stormed the court in ecstasy over their 46-45 victory, celebrating as if they’d already won the gold medal. In some ways, they had.



The Diamonds entered the competition as the clear favourites, cruising through their opening rounds and easily defeating England, Tonga, South Africa, Northern Ireland and Malawi. But they were ill prepared for a fiery Jamaican side in the semi-final. Kate Moloney admitted after the loss that it “hadn’t quite sunk in yet” and said Dwyer should not bear the burden of the loss. When Dwyer missed her shot after the buzzer, Moloney went to comfort and embrace her teammate. “We will wrap our arms around her. It’s a full team loss, it’s not on one person. We should not have been in the position where we needed to shoot a goal after the siren,” Moloney said. “Really disappointing but credit to Jamaica, they really came out and really gave it to us,” she said. “We probably just didn’t execute the way we needed to.”



It was a packed house at the Hydro, where the Prince and Princess of Wales and their three children were among the spectators. The crowd was clearly pro-Jamaica, but Moloney dismissed suggestions that had any effect on the playing group, saying “we don’t really notice too much of that.” “We know that at our best we beat anyone, and today we probably just weren’t at our best,” she said. “We’ll have a look at it and take lots of learnings and come out stronger tomorrow.” The Diamonds will now have to settle for a chance at bronze against England on Sunday instead of trying for back-to-back gold medals, the first time they will sit out the decider since netball became a full part of the Commonwealth Games program in 1998. This time, it will be the Jamaicans taking on New Zealand in the gold medal match.



The Diamonds had no answer for Jamaica’s aerial superiority in the first half, as the Sunshine Girls overpowered them with sheer force and speed – aided by a truly stupendous performance from Shamera Sterling Humphrey, who used all 190 centimetres of her height to intercept and create crucial turnovers. Sterling-Humphrey recently won the 2026 Super Netball grand final with the Adelaide Thunderbirds back in Australia. Her presence in the Jamaican squad was deadly for the Australians, who struggled to stop her. In the final five minutes of the last quarter, the umpire’s whistle could barely be heard as the crowd turned up the volume in favour of the Jamaican side. Jubilation: Jamaica celebrate winning through to the gold medal match. Getty Images Their bench was no less involved, cheering, encouraging, advising and waving the flag throughout the entire match. It reached fever pitch as Dwyer’s shot missed and they stormed the court, jumping on top of each other.



Australia’s bench looked stunned, with coach Stacey Marinkovich staring stony-faced while other players leaned forward with their hands covering their mouths. Sterling-Humphrey said if anyone was going to beat the Diamonds, it was going to be the Jamaicans. “We have the inside information on them [the Diamonds] and thanks to the Suncorp Super Netball season for giving us the upper hand, playing them week in, week out,” she laughed. It’s been an extraordinary year for Sterling-Humphrey, who has been candid and vulnerable about her postpartum journey. “My bubs is somewhere in the stands cheering his mommy on,” she said.“I’m so proud of the year I’ve had, battling postpartum depression.”

Aussie Sienna Newton has poked fun at herself a day after she finished fourth in the women’s T38 long jump, suffering a wardrobe malfunction before her final attempt.

Newton had previously jumped a career best 4.70 metres and was competing for a potential bronze medal on her sixth and final jump.

However as the clock ticked down, Newton struggled to remove her pants. The athlete has an acquired brain injury, and lives with a weakness in her left hand and spasticity in her knee and foot.

“Between the countdown clock and trying to wrestle off a pair of pants with a left hand that I can’t feel, it wasn’t exactly an easy task,” Newton posted alongside a video of her wardrobe struggles.

World.title: The Blues are seizing their moment. It’s time Josh Fraser seized his, too
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The Blues are seizing their moment. It’s time Josh Fraser seized his, too Andrew Wu August 2, 2026 — 1:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Under Josh Fraser, Carlton have learnt to seize the moment. It’s time their interim coach did the same. Fraser will decide this week if he puts his hat in the ring for the top job. He’d be mad not to. “I haven’t put my hand up for the job yet,” Fraser said with a chuckle after the Blues marked the 250th games of Patrick Cripps and Nick Haynes with a stunning 76-point obliteration of the Brisbane Lions, 24.10 (154) to 11.12 (78). Josh Fraser’s record as Blues interim coach is impossible to ignore. AFL Photos “I spoke about this in the press conference during the week that I’ll take a little bit of time [to decide].



“I’m mindful that I’ve said that previously and that decision’s getting closer, but, post that press conference, my sole focus has been on tonight.” Related Article AFL 2026 Harry Dean kicked his first AFL goal on a dream night for the Blues. His dad, a Carlton great, missed it Unless you’re David Parkin (or Alex Jesaulenko and a couple of others from before the Great Depression), you only get one chance to coach Carlton – and Fraser may never get a better opportunity to realise his aspiration of landing a senior role. Perhaps Fraser would like more time to be the finished article, but not many coaches go into a selection process having been at the helm of four clubs at state league level, and put together a 9-2 run as an interim senior AFL coach. He has put the Blues in the driver’s seat to claim what three months ago seemed the unlikeliest of wildcard slots.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects “I’m almost convinced that you’re never a finished produced in terms of being ready [for a senior role], but I’m open-minded to how I keep getting better,” Fraser said. The Blues job would have to be one of the most sought after posts in recent times. New coaches tend to take over a club at or near disrepair, in need of a rebuild. Carlton bosses may not believe their list is ready to regularly beat the best, but nor is it in need of an overhaul like Essendon, the other club searching for a coach. The Blues’ side against the Lions had six players aged 21 or under, all of whom played important roles. Smith will likely win the Rising Star award, and cult figure defender Harry Dean, who had the crowd in raptures with his first goal, will finish on the podium.



View post on X Cody Walker will join them after the draft, and with North Melbourne’s and Gold Coast’s second-round picks to come, plus another two first-round selections next year, they have the means to acquire further top-end talent. The Carlton community were all aboard the ill-fated Teague train seven years ago. It’s standing room only on the Fraser freight train. The near 41,000 fans in a partisan Blues crowd roared as one on Saturday night when Fraser emerged on the big screen congratulating his players.



The warmth with which his men embraced him brought back memories of the player power behind Paul Roos’s promotion in 2002. Blues players, of course, will not have a say in who will coach them next year, but Fraser is building a compelling case. View post on X It has been a long time since Carlton played as complete a home-and-away game as this turbocharged performance. The Blues’ calling card is contest and clearance but seldom has it been accompanied by the electrifying ball movement, ferocious pressure and clean skills shown against the Lions. No wonder Marvel Stadium was rocking.



“It felt like we had 19 out there tonight,” Mitch McGovern said. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘I wouldn’t be going to Essendon’: Matthews slams Bombers; Lyon again eyeballs reporters in presser Headed by an equal career-best of five goals from Brodie Kemp, Carlton had a joint league record 16 goalkickers for their tally of 24, a sign of how Fraser has taught his men to spread the load after the departure of Charlie Curnow. It was fitting that in Cripps’ milestone game, the Blues strapped the captain on their backs rather than have their leader carry them to victory. Despite Cripps being shaded by old foe Josh Dunkley, who held him to 18 possessions, the Blues dominated the midfield. The Lions could not stop Jagga Smith, who finished with 29 possessions and two goals. His capacity to win the ball inside and get it moving was a key factor in the game.



The first-season star, whose 2025 was wiped out by a knee injury, claimed the Robert Walls Medal, though either of his running mates Sam Walsh or George Hewett would have been worthy winners of the award struck in honour of the Carlton great and former Brisbane Bears coach. “I think we’re at a stage where we don’t need him to be our best player each week,” Fraser said of Cripps. Nick Haynes and Patrick Cripps were both chaired off after their 250th games. AFL Photos “Not to say that he’s not going to have games where he’s influential, and he’s had those games for us, but part of where we’re going in terms of leaving his club in a better place is making sure that other players assume responsibility, and ‘Crippa’ doesn’t feel like he has to do everything.” Under former coach Michael Voss, particularly as they slid to a 1-8 record, the Blues could not identify key points in games to manage momentum swings. This has changed under Fraser, who is bedding down a style at 10-10 which values control of the game through the retention of possession.



The Lions’ three late goals before half-time after a powerful 20 minutes may have unravelled Carlton earlier this year, but not now. “It’s just understanding the moments and the time of the game,” Fraser said. As D-Day for Fraser looms, those words could just as easily apply to him. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Carroll declares integrity a non-negotiable – and defends his own
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Carroll declares integrity a non-negotiable – and defends his own Chip Le Grand August 2, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state’s peak anti-corruption agency will be given a broader remit as soon as possible to stamp out public sector malfeasance, conflicts of interest and improper influence that falls short of criminal conduct, as new Premier Ben Carroll seeks to restore public trust in government. Carroll said he would immediately seek advice on whether proposed changes to IBAC’s jurisdiction due to come into force at the end of next year could be brought forward. “If we can bring it forward, I will,” he said. Ben Carroll on Sunday: “I want to be a premier that is listening, that hears the message and gets on with it.” Wayne Taylor He promised that a special prosecutor working in tandem with a royal commission into the building industry to secure criminal convictions would be given whatever time and resources they need to clean up the corruption-plagued major projects sector. “I’m going to lead with integrity,” Carroll said. “Integrity is non-negotiable. It’s fundamental.



“I’m hoping the public will at least see that I’m trying to do the right thing by them.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson released on Saturday her proposed terms of reference for a royal commission and a suggested list of witnesses including Daniel Andrews, Jacinta Allan and Carroll. Related Article Exclusive

Construction royal commission Bombshell briefing reveals top officials’ CFMEU warning to Allan Carroll said the terms of reference would be finalised this week and he had a shortlist of candidates for the roles of commissioner and special prosecutor. In seeking to explain the events that led up to last week’s dramatic change of Labor leader and premier, Carroll also addressed questions about his personal integrity.



He insists that he remained a loyal deputy to Allan until last Monday, when a delegation of cross-factional leaders told the former premier she had lost the support of her own government and urged Carroll to challenge for the leadership. It is less clear whether, as deputy premier, he made the case inside government for a royal commission or more urgent Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission reforms – steps he now says are crucial to restoring public faith in a 12-year-old Labor government. Related Article Visual Story

Construction royal commission Slow, then fast: The downfall of a premier under siege Two cabinet ministers have told The Age – and Carroll did not deny – that last Tuesday’s fateful caucus meeting was the first time he advocated for a royal commission into Big Build corruption in any government forum. When pressed on whether he counselled Allan privately to establish a royal commission, Carroll did not answer directly but said it was clear the former premier was not for turning.



“I didn’t raise things where it looked like the deputy and premier were on different sides of the fence,” he told The Age in an exclusive interview. “I raised with the premier a number of times that she needed to do something. Privately, I have also been talking to colleagues about a royal commission. “We spoke most Sunday nights before every cabinet meeting. She was very clear with her views and always sought my support. The role of the deputy is to give the premier support. Even when I disagreed with her privately, I’ve always backed her publicly and in the cabinet room. “The premier has known I have been wanting transparency and accountability for a long time.”



The comments are unlikely to heal the internal party wounds created by last week’s bruising leadership change. In a wide-ranging interview, Carroll revealed other instances where he disagreed with government decisions but was unable to publicly ventilate his concerns while upholding cabinet solidarity. Carroll admitted for the first time that a secret decision taken by the Allan government to delay by three years its commitment to fully fund public schools was a $2.4 billion funding cut and the wrong thing to do. The decision, which was exposed by The Age, is at the heart of the bitter wage dispute between the government and teachers. It was taken by the government’s budget and finance committee, of which the premier and deputy premier are members. Carroll, who is also education minister, opposed the move but failed to stop it. “I argued ferociously in the cabinet subcommittee process,” Carroll said. “I did speak up about it.” He said cabinet confidentially prevented him from publicly discussing the funding cut, even after it was revealed by this newspaper.



“When cabinet arrives at a position you need to support that position.” Carroll said the current pay offer before teachers, while generous, was not enough to fully fund government schools under the Gonski formula. He raised with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week the need to lift school funding in Victoria and deliver the long-awaited Gonski reforms. Related Article Opinion

School funding In the so-called education state, Gonski puts our schools stone-cold last Chip Le Grand State political editor “I am committed to try and get full and fair funding for our public schools,” he said. He agreed the tax burden on business in Victoria, particularly since increases to payroll tax and land tax announced by former treasurer Tim Pallas in 2023, needed to be lightened. The tax rises were announced as temporary but are due to remain in force until 2033.



“We want to be competitive with NSW. We’ve got to do everything we can to make it easy to start a business in Victoria and grow a business,” Carroll said. “We’ve also just got to support everyday Victorians who are working hard every day. We are in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis which is hurting and biting and it has no end in sight.” One of the 2023 tax increases removed the payroll tax exemption for non-government schools. While the impost was adjusted in this year’s budget to impact fewer schools, Carroll left open the possibility of scrapping it altogether. “I think this was a necessary measure for the time, but I’m always open to continue working with the sector,” he said. Carroll said the planned Suburban Rail Loop, the most expensive infrastructure project in the state’s history, was a good concept undermined by the way it was developed, in secret, under then-premier Daniel Andrews in the lead-up to the 2018 election.



While the government’s contractual commitments to the SRL and the project’s financial assumptions will be reviewed by cabinet, Carroll said the rail line already under construction needed to be built. Related Article Victorian Parliament Down to business: Carroll leaves door open to work-from-home changes “I have always believed the project is a great concept. The problem with the SRL is its gestation period – it never had one. Airport rail had been talked about for 100 years. SRL was never part of the public discussion. It came as a surprise to a lot of people, including cabinet members. “However, the project does have merit and the project does need to continue. I’m not going to stop contracts or rip up contracts. That era is over.” He acknowledged concerns expressed by Victoria’s integrity agencies about the budget squeeze on their operations and capacity to expose corruption, misconduct and financial mismanagement.



“We need strong, independent agencies – IBAC, the Auditor-General, the Ombudsman. We are stewards of our public finances and institutions. That’s a role I take very seriously.” When asked about reports that he wants to change legislation, currently before parliament, to give people a legal right to work from home two days a week, Carroll said the government would consider sensible amendments but not move any itself. Loading Since taking the leadership, he has been repeatedly questioned and attacked by the opposition over comments he made six weeks ago, referencing his daughter, in which he vowed to support Jacinta Allan through to the state election. He said it was not the first time he had made the comment and that he previously wrote to Allan expressing the same sentiment.



Related Article Analysis

Victorian election The hatred of Jacinta Allan was unfair. But it had become visceral Carroll and Allan had a private meeting in the premier’s office the day before Tuesday’s leadership spill. Neither has disclosed what was discussed. Carroll said that by then, the political reality had changed, with an unrelenting corruption scandal cruelling whatever chance Allan and Labor had to remain in power after the November 28 state election. “We’d all been out door-knocking and it was very clear we weren’t getting the message through,” he said. Instead, voters were outraged at the estimated $15 billion cost of the Building Bad scandal documented by this masthead. “I want to be a premier that is listening, that hears the message and gets on with it. That’s why my first act was to call the royal commission. It’s why I will give the police commissioner every power and resource he needs. It’s why I will do what I can do to give IBAC the power and resources it needs. “And then, there are things I want to do that are part of Labor’s DNA.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: In a straight-laced city is one of the world’s least-boring art museums
World.content:
InspirationCulture holidays In a straight-laced city is one of the world’s least-boring art museums Brian Johnston August 2, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’m tired of art galleries. All those naked Greek nymphs. All those dreary saints porcupined with arrows, and double-chinned dukes trimmed in ermine. I soon feel headachy. I enjoy a park more than a battle scene. Cafes rather than Canalettos. Why look at paintings of dead people when, outside, living foreigners are doing strange things? Lausanne has views over Lake Geneva to the French Alps. The Art Brut Collection in Lausanne. Strange to me anyway. Daily routine to them, I presume. Isn’t that the point of travel? The world is refreshingly unusual, but shares human culture, and we learn that our differences aren’t so odd after all. Which brings me to Lausanne, a city so buttoned up that it barely glances at its stupendous views over Lake Geneva to the French Alps, but instead looks down on gorges and railway cuttings.



For most visitors, Lausanne’s attraction is the Olympic Museum. But you won’t learn anything about scandal and corruption at the IOC’s official museum – though you will see Cathy Freeman’s running shoes. 



The creators whose work is displayed here spent time in mental institutions or prisons, or both. Nothing unusual there; Caravaggio and van Gogh did, too. But none had art training. They disregarded art movements and public opinion and never painted for a patron or audience. Related Article Europe It’s not the French Riviera, but this land-locked version is just as entrancing Regular art museums have little to say about artists, but the extensive biographies here are worth reading, and fascinating. Who decides who is an artist? Many revered artists had troubled lives and odd visions. For that matter, the poet T. S. Eliot was recovering from a breakdown at a sanatorium in Lausanne when he wrote The Waste Land. That’s one question the collection makes you ponder. Another is what art is. One person’s masterpiece might be another’s obsessive doodle. Does it matter what art is made from? You’ll see stone figures hewn from stolen milestones, and lonely-looking people carved from cork. Collages made by a pastry cook use crushed eggshells and glued-together breadcrumbs.



Clement Fraisse used a broken spoon to carve into the wooden panels of his cell. The shadowy human figures, geometric shapes and Buddhist-like wheels of life are strangely haunting. Abduction of a Bride of Gaul created by the Swiss outsider artist Aloise Corbaz around 1917. Franz Opitz created Swiss scenes depicting sheep in green fields and chalet window-boxes cascading with petunias. All seems bucolic. Then you notice the grass is fluorescent, the mountains like shards of stained glass. The sheep have frightening metallic faces, and flowers are cruelly imprisoned in small squares. Fraisse’s carvings seem like an escape into a calmer world, Opitz’s paintings a reflection of his tormented life. But my favourites are the works of Willem van Genk, perhaps because, confined to an orphanage as a child, he dreamed of faraway places. His complicated painted papercuts and collages, inspired by his adult travels, feature New York trains, serene Buddha statues, Thai beaches and Saharan dunes sprouting cherry trees. They aren’t tourist brochures however: rushing traffic, derelict buildings and shunting yards are depicted, too.



Does it take a troubled mind to be honest? Are beautiful places surrendering to urban blight? Is travel an escape from society, or only an illusion of one? And who is normal and who is mad? Good questions. Give me a van Genk over the silly pastoral paintings of Watteau and Fragonard any day, and you have me hooked. A textile sculpture by Danielle Jacqui, a major figure in Art Singulier (Marginal Art), displayed at the Collection de l’Art Brut museum. THE DETAILS Fly



Swiss operates codeshare flights to Geneva via Singapore and Munich. Direct trains from Geneva airport to Lausanne take 45 minutes. See swiss.com Stay Ibis Lausanne Centre is conveniently located and is a short walk from Collection de l’Art Brut and the city centre. Rooms from CHF118 ($213). See accor.com Visit Collection de l’Art Brut is open daily except public holidays and (other than July-August) Mondays. Admission is CHF12 ($22); it is free on the first Saturday of each month. See artbrut.ch



More lausanne-tourisme.ch The writer travelled at his own expense.
