World.title: No Dylans, no worries: Ponga pandemonium buries Broncos as a new star emerges
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 No Dylans, no worries: Ponga pandemonium buries Broncos as a new star emerges Nick Wright August 1, 2026 — 10:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Deprived of their superstar Dylans and with their season teetering, Kalyn Ponga issued a reminder to the NRL that the Knights were far from a spent force as long as he remained in the action. The Newcastle skipper proved a Suncorp Stadium menace, often leaving the Brisbane Broncos defence clutching at him in desperation as he orchestrated a 30-6 triumph to keep them embedded in the top eight. Reece Walsh of the Broncos takes on the defence of Kalyn Ponga of the Knights at Suncorp Stadium on Saturday Getty Images Ponga’s first-half exploits were enough to signal his intent – producing a pair of linebreak assists while also shrugging off a tackle and firing a pass for Dom Young to score as the Knights took a 14-0 half-time lead. It was an opening stanza which left the Broncos pondering which footy gods they angered as Adam Reynolds (concussion) and Xavier Willison (leg gnash) missed most of the match, and Deine Mariner and Reece Walsh were both sent to the sin bin.



Both Broncos’ sin binnings were contentious – Mariner deemed to have pulled Jermaine McEwen off an attacking chance, while Walsh was pinned for a hair pull on Young after joining a fight McEwen (also sent for 10 minutes) added fuel to as an unnecessary instigator. When Ponga wasn’t terrorising the Brisbane defence, his remaining attacking linchpin Fletcher Sharpe was doing all he could to offset the season-ending injury losses of Dylan Brown and Dylan Lucas. Related Article NRL 2026 Watch: The costly moments that sealed Broncos fate, and how they can avenge freefall It took less than three minutes for Sharpe to shrug off three defenders and open the scoring with the scything run, before going on to finish with 168 running metres and two linebreaks, before he pounced on a loose ball and scoring his second to close out the contest. The Broncos were left to rue a slew of wasted opportunities – a dropped pass by Josiah Karapani with the line in sight the most obvious in the first half, while Ben Hunt’s forward pass early in the second term for Kotoni Staggs to barge across also deemed forward.



Only a few minutes later, a Walsh cutout pass for Grant Anderson gave them another opportunity, only for the latter to be pushed into touch by Greg Marzhew before being able to ground the ball. From the very next set, a break from Young down the right-hand touchline ended up in Ponga’s hands, with the Queensland Maroons No.1 finding an offload for Phoenix Crossland to score. Payne Haas of the Broncos in action in the round 22 clash. Getty Images Brisbane stayed in the fight through some Walsh magic – the marquee man jumping into dummy-half and helping unleash Mariner, before the star fullback gathered the kick ahead to score. But a dropped ball from Mariner coming out of trouble sealed their fate – a brilliant put down in the corner from Marzhew after a Bradman Best flick pass ending any hopes of a Broncos’ comeback.



The win keeps the Knights just one win shy of the top four, with a bye still to come in round 27. A new star emerges Remember the name: Francis Manuleleua. Newcastle appears to have unearthed one of rugby league’s most promising young forwards, with the 22-year-old backrower producing a miracle pass and showcase of physicality to put his name in lights. One week on from what was a breakout performance from the rising star – in which he scored, set up a try and made two linebreaks in a one-point loss to the Roosters – Manuleleau ensured he would remain on pundits’ lips on the Knights’ run to the finals.



His 100 running metres and 31 tackles said enough. But it was an instinctive and ridiculous 20-metre cutout pass during broken play for Marzhew to cross in the corner that will be replayed in highlight reels for the rest of the season. His tackle in the shadows of half-time on Pat Carrigan, forcing a knock on with his pressure from the inside as the Broncos went on the attack one last time, was another sign of the potential eight-game Kiwi prospect possessed. While the loss of Lucas to a serious ankle injury has been a dagger-blow to the Knights’ top four hopes, Manuleleua, has presented enough hope to the Newcastle faithful that they had an X-factor in their pack to challenge the best of the competition. What’s left for Broncos to salvage? Has the time come for Broncos coach Michael Maguire to begin planning for season 2027?



Brisbane will welcome a quartet of recruits next year – Jonah Pezet, Mitch Barnett, Shawn Blore and Knights rival Dane Gagai all joining the Red Hill rebuild. But after Willison was forced from the action within six minutes, the lack of depth through the middle was made glaringly clear. Payne Haas, who will join South Sydney from next season, was easily the most dangerous forward for Brisbane with 111 running metres, although the unheralded Jaiyden Hunt (143 metres) punched above his weight. The medical retirement of Corey Jensen – who suffered a pulmonary embolism – has left the club without the same front-row partnership that delivered premiership glory in 2025. Rookie enforcer VJ Semu played the most minutes of his fledgling NRL career – running for 50 metres and making 33 tackles from 39 minutes. He needs to keep being exposed to this level to put him in the best position possible to make use of his 110kg frame regularly next year. Reynolds’ category one concussion ruling will keep him out of next week’s Battle of Brisbane against the Dolphins. That will likely thrust Tom Duffy into the fray, and there is an argument he should be given the rest of the campaign to prove he is the long-term successor to the retiring champion. Brisbane’s ruck manipulation has also been lacking in 2026, but looked far more potent when Billy Walters – in his second NRL game back from a ruptured ACL – was thrown into the action. He was denied a try assist by a Ben Talty knock on, and has been tipped to ink a contract extension. Whatever decision Maguire makes, it has gotten to a stage where forward-planning must be a priority.

World.title: NPC: Mo'unga scores match-winning try for Canterbury against Auckland
World.content:
Richie Mo'unga has scored the winning try for Canterbury in his first NPC match since 2020, with the defending champions beating Auckland 38-31.

Mo'unga, who has spent the last three years playing in Japan, came on as a replacement in the second half on Saturday night, and while he had a few awkward moments, he turned on the class to split the Auckland defence in the 78th minute, when the scores were deadlocked.

The first half was helter-skelter, with Canterbury starting off where they left off last season, with early dominance at the breakdown seeing them score two tries in the first 11 minutes.

But Auckland stormed back when the red-and-blacks made a couple of errors, leaving a hole in their lineout for Sam Hainsworth-Fa'aofo to score and then gifting an intercept to Xavier Tito-Harris.

Canterbury then scored two more tries, but Auckland claimed one back to trail 26-21 at halftime.

There was a big cheer when Mo'unga took the field but he looked a bit rusty early, knocking forward a ball that bounced just in front of him and then missing a conversion he normally would have nailed.

Auckland had taken the lead for the first time in the 60th minute, but Canterbury hit back seven minutes later.

It was 31-all with 12 minutes to go and stayed that way, until Canterbury's forwards charged towards the Auckland line from a lineout after winning a penalty and Mo'unga got his hands on the ball playing halfback, fooling the defence with a dummy and scoring by the posts. He then converted it.

In earlier games today, Otago beat Southland 41-14, and Taranaki beat Counties Manukau 20 points to five.

On Friday night, Tasman pipped North Harbour 31-29 in Nelson, while Waikato opened the season with a 38-26 win over Bay of Plenty on Thursday.

World.title: Country Life: Hydroponics in Horowhenua
World.content:
There's no need for extra washing when it comes to these salad greens. The plants from Waikawa fresh are harvested straight from their trays where they're grown hydroponically.

"There's no bugs, there's no soil, there's no dirt. We don't clean these plants with any chemicals or chlorine, so we eat those lettuce straight out of the channels. They're just absolutely crispy clean ... and they haven't been touched by anyone the whole time it's been growing," Tony Dale-Low told Country Life.

He and wife Lisa Dale-Low made the move to growing salad greens and herbs almost a decade ago, trading in city life and corporate jobs for horticulture in Horowhenua.

Hydroponics in Horowhenua: Growing with water Country Life Download MP3 17m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

The couple had no growing experience before starting.

They'd spent a couple of years travelling around the country in a bus with their three children before coming up with a checklist of what they wanted for their next chapter.

"We wanted to be doing something productive, rather than something paper or computer-based. We wanted to be rural and we wanted to have a bit more flexibility with the kids. None of that was really sector specific or even location-specific," Lisa said.

The couple grow fancy lettuces and other herby greens hydroponically. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Hydroponic growing systems work by replacing soil with a water-based, nutrient-rich solution. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The water sourced from the 4500m2 of rooves of the many greenhouses, and the recent addition of solar power is also helping cut down on energy bills. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

After narrowing it down to the North Island they came across an existing hydroponic growing business near Levin - hydroponic systems work by replacing soil with a water-based, nutrient-rich solution.

That was in 2018 and after learning the ropes from the previous owners they've made it their own.

They grow the plants from seedlings themselves, also using hydroponics on a 'flood and drain table'.

"So this is set up on a timer. It runs three times a day and these tables will fill with nutrients or liquid with some fertilizer," Tony explained.

Seedlings, like these little basil sprouts, are also grown hydroponically. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The seedlings are easily plugged into the next growing space. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

It sits there for a few minutes before draining. Being fully automated means the team don't need to do any manual watering.

He said it helps the plants up well - making them more resistant to diseases and pests.

"[It] all definitely starts here in the propagating house. If we get it wrong here, then we have issues later. If we get it right, then we have so much more success."

Once the seedlings reach about three weeks, they're transferred to larger growing trays called 'gullies'.

"They look like downpipes, which in fact I think they are, actually straight off someone's house," Tony told Country Life.

"They've been drilled with a lot of little round holes and we plant the plant inside the holes. The nutrients get pumped around the greenhouse through these small whiskers."

Among some of the 'fancy' lettuces they grow, the oak leaf in red and green varieties. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The couple learned the art of hydroponics from the previous owners. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Over the cooler winter months, it gets too cold to grow basil so they replace this with growing watercress instead. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The system they use only requires liquid to be pumped to the top of the gully before gravity does the rest, drawing it down the channel, through the gutter back to the holding tank which is topped up with the water sourced from the 4500m2 of greenhouse rooves.

The water is reticulated meaning they only need to add more to account for evaporation or absorption by the plants.

In the central tank, a computer system checks to make sure the water has the right balance of nutrients and the right pH level - the acid or alkaline concentration - and runs a dosing system to adjust this when needed.

Tony and his green 'lettuce' Leaf - the old Nissan Leaf gets its power from solar panels on the farm and is used to run around the property for the many maintenance jobs. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Sustainability is a key part of Waikawa Fresh' operations.

The recent addition of solar power at the end of last year is also helping cut down on energy bills - it's even used to power an old Nissan 'lettuce' leaf they use on farm to run the maintenance gear around.

About two months after the plants have finished growing they'll be ready to be picked straight from the gullies with no extra washing required - "lovely and crunchy and and fresh".

From their hands where they're packed straight into bags, the harvested plants are taken straight to the chiller ready to be picked up by a truck that same day. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Getting the product to the market as fresh as possible is a key focus. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

World.title: Four in custody after staff assaulted, haul of perfume taken, police say
World.content:
Police responding to a report of a perfume heist say they quickly were able to quickly "sniff out" the leads and detain four young people.

Just before 2pm on Saturday, Hamilton police were called to a report that staff at a store at The Base shopping centre "had been assaulted and thousands of dollars' worth of perfume had been taken," a Police bulletin said.

"No weapons were used, nor were there any injuries."

Senior Sergeant Pete Simpson said officers who responded were given details about the possible identity of the suspects, and video captured by a person at the scene.

By 2:25pm on Saturday, officers had found "a bag full of the stolen items" at a nearby address, Simpson said.

Four young people were taken into custody, and are expected to appear in court on robbery charges next week.

World.title: Two new Auckland stations part of $2.4b rail spend
World.content:
Two new railway stations in South Auckland are among the final elements of a $2.4 billion government investment in Auckland's network, Minister for Auckland Simon Watts says.

He was speaking at the formal opening on Saturday of the Drury and Paerātā stops.

The stations will serve Drury, Paerātā, Franklin and South Auckland, with each station providing two platforms, 350 car parks and bus connections.

Services begin stopping at the new stations on Sunday. During the week, peak trains will run every 10 minutes.

Rail Minister Winston Peters at the opening of the new Drury station. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Other speakers at the opening were Rail Minister Winston Peters, KiwiRail chief metro officer Bevan Assink and Franklin ward councillor Andy Baker.

Watts said that while much of the recent investment in the rail network had been about preparing for the opening of the CRL, "the extension of the overhead electrification from Papakura to Pukekohe and these new train stations represent something more".

"Trains stopping at Drury and Paerātā stations from tomorrow and Ngākōroa station when it opens next year will help open up this part of Auckland.

"Around 130,000 more people are expected to be in the southern part of Auckland over the next three decades. More than 40,000 new homes are expected to be built, a new hospital in Drury, a number of new schools, new roads, including in time the Mill Road extension.

"For locals, it means ... being part of an Auckland that is properly connected to the rest of the city... It will give people greater confidence to move to this part of Auckland, knowing that they will not be reliant on their cars, and overall it's a great choice about where people live and how they get around," Watts said.

Auckland's new Paerātā railway station. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

KiwiRail's Bevan Assink gave the gathering some project numbers - 6500 cubic metres of concrete; 600 tonnes of locally sourced steel; 25,000 cubic metres of material moved to make way for the facilities.

"We've also planted around 40,000 trees and everything to beautify the area. Also there were 22 apprenticeships that were able to be enacted as part of this project and also 32 local companies were also involved in the project as well.

"So it just shows how broad and vast-reaching these projects can be in supporting the communities and everything around them," Assink said.

Franklin ward's Andy Baker told a story of two girls, aged 11 and 12, writing to him in 2011 to ask if Drury could get a railway station.

"They had done a petition here in Drury. They had hundreds and hundreds of signatures about wanting a park and ride and a station at Drury.

"One of those girls is here today - my daughter ... she may have had some egging on ... the other, the 11-year-old at the time ... is now an emergency doctor at Christchurch Hospital, so time has moved on.

"I did promise Emma it would be built before she left high school, which was 2015, but we haven't quite made that.

"But it shows that there's been a demand for this type of infrastructure in this area for a very, very long time. It is fantastic to see it today," Baker said.

RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Rail Minister Peters echoed Watts' figure of 130,000 more people expected in the area over coming decades "and infrastructure must come before growth - not years afterwards, as too often happens in this country".

"These stations are here because we funded them when last responsible for rail, as part of our wider commitments to unlock capacity, lift train frequencies, invest more than $500 million to get the network up to standard, and enable electric trains from Britomart right down to Pukekohe.

"While others say nice words about rail, we fund it, deliver it, and on this happy occasion are still here to open it.

"We will keep advocating for rail because taxpayers have built an asset with real potential to move people and goods efficiently - and we intend to make full use of it."

In an earlier statement, Transport Minister Chris Bishop said the stations were among the final elements of a $2.4 billion government investment in Auckland's rail network.

"The Auckland Rail Network Rebuild has been completed in time for the City Rail Link to open soon. We're also replacing level crossings across the network to support more frequent train services.

"The Third Main Line is now open, separating freight and passenger rail services, while the rail line to Pukekohe has been electrified. Looking ahead, new rail stations at Ngākōroa are also set to open in 2027.

The work was about investing in infrastructure "that would help our largest city to grow".

World.title: 5.2 magnitude quake strikes near Te Anau
World.content:
Te Anau has been hit by a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, just a week after being jolted by a 5.9.

The latest quake, at 3:23pm on Saturday, was centred 35 kilometres north-west of the town at a depth of 102 kilometres, GeoNet said.

Felt reports showed more than 1400 people felt the shaking, mostly in the lower South Island.

There were no immediate reports of damage.

On 25 July a magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck 40 kilometres north of Te Anau, sparking a brief tsunami warning and an evacuation notice for some areas of the West Coast, which was later cancelled.

On Friday night, a magnitude 4.6 quake jolted the lower North Island and upper South at 11:09pm. It was centred 30 kilometres offshore, north-west of Porirua at a depth of 38 kilometres, and more than 8900 people logged Felt Reports.

GeoNet scientist Jonathan Hanson said New Zealand has been living up to its Shaky Isles reputation. While it had been a busy few weeks in terms of earthquakes, overall it was not unusual.

There are typically 15 to 20 magnitude five events in the country every year, but having a couple approaching magnitude six in a month is less common.

"These deep earthquakes are typically widely felt," GeoNet wrote on Facebook on Saturday afternoon.

World.title: Rising shop violence demands stronger penalties: Retail NZ
World.content:
Retailers need stronger powers to protect staff and customers from violent repeat offenders, Retail NZ says, amid reports of rapidly escalating aggression.

The Justice Select Committee is recommending by majority that The Trespass Amendment Bill be passed into law.

The bill would give retailers the power to trespass people from multiple sites, double fines to $2000 and increase the maximum trespass period to three years.

Retail NZ chief executive Carolyn Young said violence in stores was on the rise, with people becoming more agitated and entering businesses with concealed weapons.

"They will come in with knives, with hammers, with screwdrivers, with machetes ... Some stores within their stores sell things that can be turned into a weapon ... People will come in to a hardware store and use things on their shelves to threaten staff to be able to steal goods or do harm to people," she said.

"We have also seen guns that have been presented in certain circumstances, and all of those things mean that it's not a safe environment for staff members or customers."

Young said clear guidance would be needed to ensure new powers were used appropriately.

'Not convinced' - Labour and Greens

Opposition parties have raised concerns about the proposed changes, while questioning if harsher penalties would work as an effective deterrent to retail crime.

Labour said that despite some improvements to the bill, it remained concerned about the proposed scope of multi-location trespass notices.

"We remain concerned that there will be situations when vulnerable individuals may be unable to access essential goods and services due to the scope of these notices.

"We are also not convinced that the increase in penalties will act as an effective deterrent and consider there are other policies that may more effectively address the drivers of crime," it said.

The Green Party said it did not support the bill and remained concerned that the increase in fines from $1000 to $2000 would be "unrealistic" for offenders, who often resorted to retail crime as a result of the cost-of-living crisis.

"It is important that we have the right balance between clarity for retail stores and safety of retail employees and owners. However, we do not believe this will result in the expected effect of deterrence for retail crime," it said.

World.title: Queenstown mayor wants ideas on relieving traffic snarls
World.content:
An influx of tourists is causing massive traffic problems across the Wakatipu Basin, the mayor of the Queenstown-Lakes District says.

The council was setting up a mayoral taskforce on reducing congestion, Mayor John Glover said.

"Our state highway networks are really struggling to cope at peak times ... we are seeing some significant gridlock.

"A drive that probably would have taken 10 minutes at times is taking 90 minutes," he said.

The gridlock was prompting complaints on social media. Those living in new housing developments were struggling to get on to the state highway as well.

"We actually need some traffic control to wave people through in the right places so that traffic can keep flowing," Glover said.

"Maybe a bit of human intervention to keep things going at some of these junctions might do the job."

World.title: Live: Aussies stun with boxing and cycling golds, athletics set for epic finale
World.content:
(Getty)

Australia's track program has pumped time and money into their relays over the past few years and it's culminated in some excellent results, including bronze and a national record in the men's 4x400m at the World Athletics Relays earlier this year.

At that meet in Gaborone, Botswana, the men's 4x100m quartet missed a medal by just 0.24 of a second and three quarters of that team ran the heats earlier today, with Josh Azzopardi, Chris Ius, Calab Law and Rohan Browning hitting the track.

They are expected to welcome back 100m silver medallist Lachie Kennedy, likely in Law's place, for the final (5:15am AEST) after what Josh Azzopardi described as "a training run" in the heat.

"I think it's almost a training run for us now just to get the baton around," Azzopardi said.

"It was really good, really clean, really comfortable. Coming into the final we'll throw a bit of caution to the wind and see how we go."

They were incredibly crisp with their changeovers as they finished third in their heat with a time of 38.69.

Browning, who fumbled the baton in the 2025 world championships final, said the biggest change he has seen is the depth on display, giving them the luxury of resting Kennedy in the qualifying run.

"There's so many guys we can call on," Browning said.

"We've got guys like Eddie [Nketia], at home guys like Gout [Gout], so I think the future of the team looks really strong, the stocks are really strong."

(ABC News: Che Chorley)

The women similarly finished third in their heat, running 43.52 without individual 100m bronze medallist and national record holder Torrie Lewis.

"We've done many, many camps over this season having to come off racing individually and then coming together as a team. But I honestly think that's made us push each other even more to run better times get more comfortable with each other, learn each other's strengths, and I think that's been a massive help for both the men's and women's teams."

Lewis is expected to come back in for tonight's final, replacing one of Ebony Lane, Chloe Mannix-Power, Georgia Harris or Monique Hanlon.

World.title: Dozens of greyhounds to land in Australia as NZ racing ban begins
World.content:
Chartered flights will ferry up to 150 greyhounds to Australia as trainers pivot from a racing ban coming into effect in New Zealand.

The ban, which was first announced in December 2024 and legislated in April this year, took effect on Saturday after years of animal welfare concerns.

Ten greyhounds were euthanised during New Zealand's final racing season, including one days before the ban began.

Heather Simpson, the Greyhound Transition Agency (GTA) head, said she was aware that Greyhound Racing New Zealand had organised charter flights for about 150 dogs to go to Australia to continue racing.

"There is nothing in the legislation that stops trainers choosing to export their dogs to Australia; some of these dogs actually will be partly owned by Australians," she told Radio New Zealand.

Greyhound ban legislation delayed until government gets support A bill to ban greyhound racing in Tasmania has been delayed until the government can secure enough support.

Greyhound racing remains legal in most Australian jurisdictions, banned only in the Australian Capital Territory.

Plans for an industry phase-out in Tasmania have stalled after the government pulled a bill from the upper house in April when it appeared not to have enough support to pass.

Word of the chartered flights first emerged through a leaked message from a private greyhound racing group, Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi told a Senate Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee hearing in April.

She said the move appeared "to be kind of a deliberate attempt to avoid" New Zealand's transition agency.

"If they survive, they will become the responsibility of Australians to rehome," she said.

"And you would know we're already in a rehoming crisis."

The greyhounds brought to Australia will be classed as "companion animals". (Reuters: Action Images/Scott Heavey)

Brant Smith, a senior biosecurity executive at the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries, told the senate hearing the government had been working with New Zealand's Ministry for Primary Industries on the dogs' import.

He said they would be classed as "companion animals", but may be used for racing once in the country.

"As to how they are then used, that's not something that we have control over thereafter because they're being imported as companion animals like other animals … and this is not unusual," he said.

Mr Smith said a similar contingent of greyhounds was imported to Australia in April 2025.

"In the previous consignment, I think approximately 80 came similarly, and they were just imported under our normal conditions," he said.

It is estimated a further 1,400 dogs will remain in New Zealand and require rehoming by the GTA.

Ms Simpson said the rehomed dogs would be regularly checked under a welfare program.

World.title: Broncos to 'look after each other' as title defence comes to early end
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos coach Michael Maguire has said the playing group will need to "look after each other" as their finals hopes were officially ended on Saturday night.

The Broncos will become the first reigning premier in 20 years to miss the finals after going down at home to the Newcastle Knights 30-6.

Brisbane has just six wins this season, in a premiership defence that has been hampered by injuries and poor performances.

With any faint hopes of making the finals ending with a 24-point loss to the Knights, Maguire told media the club would need to rally around each other in the face of a disappointing campaign.

"It is tough, because I've got a high regard on how these boys go about things," Maguire said.

"You can't fault how they try. Unfortunately at the moment, we're not getting things going our way.

"I feel for everyone that's going through it at the moment.

"But they're a group that support each other, and that's what it's about now.

"We've got to make sure that we look after each other through this period."

Brisbane becomes the first reigning premier to not make finals since Wests Tigers missed the top eight in 2006 after winning the grand final in 2005.

Earlier, Penrith winger Tom Jenkins has become the first player in 72 years to score multiple tries in 12 matches during a season, as the Panthers hammered the Canberra Raiders 42-18 in Mudgee.

The New Zealand Warriors consolidated their place in the NRL top four with a commanding win over the Gold Coast Titans.

Relive all of Saturday's NRL action in the blog below.

World.title: Fraser sheds light on coaching call as Blues record monster win over Lions
World.content:
Carlton's interim coach Josh Fraser says he will decide this week whether to join the club's process to find its next full-time coach.

Fraser's candidacy received another major boost as the Blues recorded a thumping 24.10 (154) to 11.12 (78) win over the Brisbane Lions at Docklands Stadium in club captain Patrick Cripps's 250th career game.

While Fraser began his coaching tenure by stating he wasn't interested in the full-time role, a stunning 9-2 record has caused him to reconsider his original position.

Carlton's win also enhanced its bid for a wildcard spot, with the Blues in 10th spot on the AFL ladder, four premiership points ahead of the ninth-placed St Kilda and the 10th-placed GWS Giants.

The Giants overcame a gritty Port Adelaide side to claim a 10.15 (75) to 9.9 (63) win at the Adelaide Oval to stay within touch of the final wildcard spot.

Earlier on Saturday, Sydney recorded a comeback 16.11 (107) to 13.10 (88) win against St Kilda at Docklands Stadium, but lost Will Edwards to a horror injury, with the result dealing a blow to the Saints' wildcard bid.

Meanwhile, Hawthorn survived a stiff test against North Melbourne before running out 14.15 (99) to 12.11 (83) winners in Tasmania.

In a curtain-raiser for the AFLW season, Australia recorded a 13.13 (91) to 6.5 (41) win against Ireland at North Sydney Oval as Jasmine Garner was named the Player of the Match.

Follow the live blog below for recap of all of Saturday's football action as it happened.

World.title: Boxer earns Tuvalu's first ever Comm Games medal without winning fight
World.content:
A boxer from Tuvalu earned her tiny South Pacific nation's first ever Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight overnight.

Tarona Taafaki lost her only bout in the women's 75-kilogram class to India's Lovlina Borgohain, losing every round on all three of the judges' cards.

Because there were only five entrants, Taafaki received a bye to the last four, meaning she was automatically guaranteed at least a bronze medal.

Tarona Taafaki arrives at the Commonwealth Games during the opening ceremony. (AP: Kin Cheung)

But her coach and father said the population of Tuvalu, an island south-east of Tonga, will celebrate the medal and use it to highlight a climate change emergency.

Badi Taafaki, whose son Pasoni competed earlier in the Games and lost his only bout at 70kg, told the British Press Association: "For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything.

"We're one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it's a stepping stone."

Tarona and Pasoni are the two eldest of eight children, all of whom are boxers. They are based in New Zealand in order to take advantage of better facilities.

"My children are very fortunate," Badi said.

"They have opportunities and facilities that I never had. Boxing is our whole life. Strength is in our bloodline."

Athletes on the island famously train on its airport runway, the most stable land mass on an island increasingly threatened by rising sea levels. Climate experts predict half of the nation's capital, Funafuti, could be submerged by 2050.

A group of locals play volleyball on the airport runway in Funafuti, Tuvalu. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

"Yes, we train on the airport runway," Badi said. "When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.

"If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change.

"It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades. Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can't sleep if there's a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes."

Tarona is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight. Australia's Taylah Robertson picked up a bronze in the women's flyweight category on the Gold Coast in 2018 despite losing her bout to England's Lisa Whiteside.

World.title: 72 years after the Miracle Mile, a young Aussie wants to rewrite history
World.content:
The mile world record had been stuck at four minutes, 1.4 seconds for nine years when England's Roger Bannister stepped onto the track at Oxford in May, 1954.

Near the same university where he earned his medical degree, Bannister operated with surgical precision to reach his ultimate goal of becoming the first man to dip under four minutes for the mile.

But, as is so often the case, once a barrier is broken, it reminds others they too can do what just yesterday seemed impossible.

And, sure enough, 45 days later Australian John Landy went around the Turku track in Finland four times in 3:58 flat.

It set the stage for the so-called Miracle Mile at the 1954 British Empire and Commonwealth Games.

Roger Bannister (329) in action against John Landy. (Getty Images: Mark Kauffman/Sports Illustrated)

It was a moment when the sporting world's eyes were firmly locked on Vancouver, regardless of any connection to the Commonwealth, to watch the best middle distance runners to that point in history face off.

Eight runners made it to the final, but all eyes were on just two as Bannister, who set his sub-four-minute mark of 3:59.8 on a home track with friends pacing for him, would face Landy in the purest competition settings.

The Australian took the lead after one lap and led for the next kilometre and change, going out hard in an attempt to use his superior stamina, as Bannister called it, to negate the Englishman's famous final burst.

Roger Bannister breaks the tape in the one-mile final in Vancouver. (Getty Images)

Having felt Bannister on his heels and seen his shadow sticking firm under him for the entire race, Landy took one look over his left shoulder about 100 metres out on the final bend, and in that moment Bannister burst past unsighted on the right and flew home to victory.

Both runners finished under four minutes, marking another piece of history.

An exhausted Bannister after the race. (Getty Images: Fox Photos)

A 60-year sabbatical

Despite that glorious event, and a race of almost exactly 1,600 metres seeming to make sense on the world-standard 400m track, the mile was only run at three more Commonwealth Games before swapping it out for the 1,500m after 1966.

New Australian record holder Cameron Myers said it can become prestigious once again.

"I think it's a way we can attract more people into the sport," he said.

"Americans still love it, so I think it's just something that regular people can resonate a little bit more with."

Cameron Myers is supremely confident in his mile. (AP: Alastair Grant)

At the time of its last Commonwealth outing in Kingston, the Caribbean nations were yet to become the sprint powerhouses we now know them to be, so the mile had been considered the blue-riband event at the Games.

And it returns 60 years later, with Glasgow hoping to host another historic night tonight.

"It's obviously a very prestigious part of the Commonwealth Games and its history, so it's really exciting that it's come back in this year and allowed us to attack it," said Abbey Caldwell, one of three Australian competitors in the women's final.

Abbey Caldwell is part of Australia's stacked middle-distance stocks. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Caldwell will run alongside Jessica Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth from 6:45am (AEST), and she believes they have a genuine chance of a podium sweep.

"There's always the pressure of you want to go and achieve those medals, and you want to be the first Australians to do that," she said.

"But we're also in a very fortunate position to have three very strong Australians going into this, so it's a really nice opportunity for us to go take those history books and cement them as Australians."

Jess Hull (second from right) leads an elite pack of Australian middle distance runners. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Whether they win them or not, the men (from 5:55am) will get the honour of running for the first Commonwealth Games mile medals in six decades.

And in that race lies a chance for Australia to reverse the misery of Bannister's late pass in 1954.

Young Aussie wants to spoil the party

Including Bannister's first trip under the milestone mark, the mile record was broken 19 times in 44 years, when the great Moroccan Hicham El Guerrouj ran 3:43.13 in 1999.

His record stood for 27 years, which the astute among you may recognise as bringing us up to the here and now.

Well, two weeks ago, to be exact.

Josh Kerr played up to the crowd as he qualified for the final. (Supplied)

Just before the start of the Glasgow Games, Scottish 1,500m world champion Josh Kerr ran 3:42.66.

Just two weeks earlier at prestigious Prefontaine Classic, 20-year-old Myers broke Ollie Hoare's Australian record, running 3:46.06, setting up a tantalising shootout on the mile's return.

"Kerr's going to want to make a move at some point, and he's shown he's the fittest in the field," Myers said.

"I think he'll want to make a move and I'm not going to let him go."

Landy described the Miracle Mile as "like a title fight", and just like a battle for a belt, styles make fights.

We saw a preview in their separate heats, where both won but Myers was five seconds faster than Kerr.

Myers jumped to the front of his pack and led the whole way home with clinical efficiency, while Kerr sat in the pack until the last lap before ambling to the front and revving up the crowd with 150 metres to go.

Josh Kerr fired up the Glasgow crowd as he coasted into the final. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The Scotstoun Stadium crowd will be baying for Kerr and 2022 world champion in the 1,500m Jake Wightman, but young buck Myers is out to prove himself in an elite field.

"I'm a competitor, I don't want to lose," he said.

"I'm not going there to come second, so I'll have a crack at him the best I can and if I blow up trying, so be it.

"Everyone's cheering for the Scots, and I'm sure they want to go 1-2, so I'm trying to spoil that."

The mile start line sits 9.34 metres behind the start/finish line. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Myers will also be running alongside teammates, with reigning 1,500m Commonwealth champion Ollie Hoare and 24-year-old Adam Spencer making it through.

The final night of the athletics program on the penultimate day of the Games feels like the perfect time for a clash between the hosts and the runaway medal tally toppers.

If the Aussies can ruin the party, they would have done what Landy couldn't 72 years ago.

And Myers is well aware of the opportunity in front of him.

"Hopefully I can reverse the roles."

World.title: Nina Kennedy is often superhuman, but in Glasgow she was a super human
World.content:
That's not how this was meant to go.

When Nina Kennedy steps into an athletics arena, the expectation is gold, and she carries herself accordingly.

The definition of a smiling assassin, Kennedy's friendly demeanour disguises a competitor's heart that beats with propulsive force.

It launches her down the runway and, usually, to great heights.

In Glasgow, Kennedy fell short of her own lofty goals and the standards we've come to expect from her, but still came away with silver in the women's pole vault final, albeit in a final that won't go down as one of the greats.

Kennedy snags silver, teen grabs surprise gold Flag bearer Nina Kennedy settles for silver in the pole vault and Australia's sprint stars return to the track after a host of medals at the velodrome.

Tailwinds at Scotstoun Stadium have been helping the sprinters, hindering the throwers, terrifying the hurdlers, and on Friday night, local time, making life difficult for the vaulters.

The crosswind kept the final from being a true jump-off between the strong field, with Kennedy clearing the bar only three times from seven attempts and 2016 Olympic bronze medallist Eliza McCartney winning on countback.

The top clearance of 4.65 metres by the gold and silver medallists was 30 centimetres lower than both of their personal bests.

Nina Kennedy came to Glasgow for gold. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Kennedy topped by 1-centimetre McCartney's eight-year-old Oceania record of 4.94m just a couple of weeks before the Commonwealth Games began.

So, despite sporting a pretty gnarly scar from last year's hamstring surgery, there's no question Kennedy was fit and in form.

She carried her typical energy into the final, sitting out the early heights and waiting in the tall grass for her chance to pounce once half her competitors had already X'd out.

Why no other runner embraced the 200m gold medallist A doping scandal dating back to 2024 was the backdrop of the women's 200m final in Glasgow, and the frosty post-race scenes.

By the time she got out of her thick coat and stood at the top of the runway, piercing blue eyes fixed on her first attempt at 4.45m, half the eight-woman field was already gone.

She got over on her first go, but not with the sort of convincing clearance over the bar we were used to seeing.

Conserving energy? Shaking off the cold? No, as it turned out. Just a tricky competition.

New Zealander Olivia McTaggart stumbled at that hurdle three times, assuring Kennedy of a medal — and most likely silver at least after 2022 bronze medallist Imogen Ayris took three tries to clear 4.30m — but minor medals are not what Kennedy came here for.

Kennedy cleared 4.65m as her top vault. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The 29-year-old has been in Glasgow as long as any of Australia's 255-strong team, having arrived early to carry the flag in the opening ceremony.

She has been so ever-present around the team that her success feels even more inevitable than usual, especially for folks who may have only watched her jump at Commonwealth Games, worlds and Olympics.

In those competitions, she had gone gold, gold, gold since her breakthrough win in Birmingham.

But so many things have to go right for an athlete to consistently catapult themselves 5 metres into the air with the accuracy and control required, and sometimes the pieces just don't quite fit.

Pole vault is hard enough in perfect conditions. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

By the time she was preparing for her third attempt at 4.70m, the stare no longer looked so steely.

Having missed three of her last four jumps to that point, it didn't feel like a foregone conclusion that she'd pull it out in the clutch yet again, and so it proved.

"Of course I'm disappointed, I wanted to win, and I didn't," she said, emphasising that she was "genuinely really happy" to see veteran McCartney win her first major international gold.

"I'm superhuman most of the time, but I'm also human a lot of the time, and I make mistakes, and that's OK.

"I'm a high achiever, and I push myself to be that, but I think it's also important to remember I'm human and I make mistakes. I didn't want to make mistakes out there tonight, but I did, and that's OK."

The epitome of a big-moment performer, Kennedy has now not been able to defend her 2023 world or 2022 Commonwealth Games titles.

She missed the 2025 athletics world championships because of her torn hamstring and missed the mark in Glasgow, but results aren't all that matter for a woman who has ticked off every career goal at this point.

Kennedy was thrilled for Eliza McCartney (centre) to get her first major international gold medal. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

She said before the opening ceremony that she would probably forget to soak in the moment as the team's flag-bearer, but after a long campaign and a surprisingly short time on centre stage, it seems she has figured it out.

"Sometimes sport is more than just the medals, it's about the memories made and the connections and the officials and the volunteers," she said.

"The crowd out there was so awesome. Everyone was just so happy to be here. I'm walking away with a lot of memories.

"I'm happy. Like, I'm sad, but I'm happy."

World.title: Football Australia welcomes U-turn on FIFA World Cup sell-off after backlash
World.content:
World football's governing body, FIFA, says it has scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors after widespread backlash.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino said in a statement: "Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place."

Senior FIFA advisor quits post A senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino resigned in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup.

The plan was to raise $US4.2 billion ($5.9 billion) by selling about a 20 per cent stake in a new unit that would run FIFA events, including the World Cup, valuing it at $US20 billion.

The proposal, first announced on Tuesday, was strongly opposed by European football's governing body, UEFA, which threatened a boycott and accused FIFA of putting the sport's "soul" up for sale.

Mr Infantino said in his statement: "[The] FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

"Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve."

FIFA had argued that selling the minority stake in its commercial operations would raise billions of dollars to fund global sports development, and accused the media of mischaracterising the proposal.

Mr Infantino had written to member associations to tell them they would receive $US40 million each if they agreed to FIFA's proposal by September 19.

Gianni Infantino's proposal received pushback from all corners of the football world. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

"Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support," Mr Infantino said in Friday's statement.

Football Australia welcomed FIFA's decision to withdraw the proposal, with chairman Anter Isaac saying the backlash reinforced "an important principle of good governance".

"Proposals of global significance should be developed through robust consultation, appropriate governance processes and meaningful engagement with member associations before they are presented for consideration," he said in a statement.

"Ultimately, the strength of football's institutions depends on the confidence and trust of the global football family. That trust is earned not simply through good decisions, but through the integrity of the processes that lead to them."

Opposition to the plan snowballed over the week

On Thursday, UEFA's 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments until the proposal was withdrawn, saying that the World Cup "cannot be treated as an investment product".

The 41-member federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean (CONCACAF) rejected the proposal during a meeting on Thursday.

On Friday, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which has 47 members, issued a statement saying it "stands in solidarity" with UEFA and CONCACAF.

UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC combined have 143 national associations, well over half of FIFA's 211 members. A majority of the members would have needed to vote in support of the plan for it to proceed.

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

Disagreement was also internal.

On Friday, Mr Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned with immediate effect, calling the plan "a bad deal for football", while FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff had been "deceived" by Mr Infantino, describing the proposal as a "project of one person".

Mr Infantino, 56, is up for re-election next year. North American football chief Victor Montagliani is reportedly looking to challenge him.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told reporters that Mr Infantino was "the wrong man to lead the organisation".

FIFA had proposed creating a $US20 billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and its other events.

Thrive Eternal, a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, had been slated to lead the proposed investor group, according to FIFA. Joshua is the brother of Jared Kushner, who is US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Mr Trump and Mr Infantino have developed a close relationship, with the US co-hosting the recent 2026 World Cup.

President Trump said he had not spoken with Mr Infantino about the external investment plan.

Tech.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day leak racks up millions of views
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A bootleg of Spider-Man: Brand New Day was up on X for over seven hours before eventually being pulled. During that time, it reached over 5.9 million accounts and accumulated over 143,000 likes. Other accounts have reposted the leaked film, but none have lasted particularly long, as Disney now seems to be on top of issuing takedown requests.

The leak is unlikely to slow down the box office juggernaut, which is already shattering records. It raked in $72 million in previews this week. The previous record holder was Avengers: Endgame, which grossed $60 million during its previews way back in 2019. Endgame went on to set staggering records for opening weekend, grossing over $1.2 billion worldwide and over $350 million in the US. Spider-Man: No Way Home currently holds the number two spot on the all-time US opening weekend list with $260 million.

Brand New Day could potentially usurp Endgame, though it certainly faces an uphill battle. Between previews and opening day, it’s already grossed $168 million, which puts it ahead of Endgame’s $157.4 million. Sony is keeping its estimates somewhat conservative, saying it expects the latest Spider-Man to pull in $325 million.

Tech.title: Trump blames Tim Walz for water hacks even though it’s probably Iran
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The FBI, the EPA, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) have stopped short of officially blaming Iran for a spate of cyberattacks on Minnesota’s water systems, but consensus is that Iran is likely behind them. That, of course, hasn’t stopped Donald Trump from sharing his own theory — that Governor Tim Walz is to blame and telling reporters that “I don’t think there was an Iranian cyberattack.”

Trump’s comments come shortly after the FBI issued a warning that the cyberattacks on American infrastructure were spreading to other states. In Minnesota alone, at least 30 community water systems had been targeted in what appeared to be a coordinated attack. The CISA has linked similar attacks earlier in the year to Iran, which has been the target of an on-again-off-again war waged by the US government. With limited military options, Iran has repeatedly turned to digital efforts to become a thorn in the side of the Trump administration and wage a PR war.

Trump has lashed out frequently at Minnesota and Walz during his second term and even threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act against it during a surge of ICE enforcement efforts in the state that left multiple people dead.

Tech.title: You could be taking way better photos on your phone
Tech.content:
is a technology reporter who has been covering the industry since 2007. He co-hosts the Waveform podcast with MKBHD. A former engineer, he now specializes in topics like computational photography and social media protocols.

Your smartphone photos can look way better. If you’re willing to put in a little extra work, use third party apps and spend a bit of time editing, it’s possible to take photos that — under the right circumstances — can rival dedicated digital cameras.

I post a lot of smartphone photos online, and “How do I take better photos on my phone?” is a question I get practically every day. It makes sense. As the saying goes, “The best camera is the one you have on you,” and we practically always have our phones on us these days.

Over the last few years, smartphone camera sensors have gotten bigger, with better light gathering capabilities and higher resolutions. But even though the sensors have gotten bigger and better, the straight-out-of-camera quality through default camera apps hasn’t improved much, if at all. In some respects, smartphone photos have actually gotten worse — aesthetically, at least.

iPhone 17 Pro Max iPhone 17 Pro Max iPhone 17 Pro Max iPhone 17 Pro Max

The reason driving this is what people generally use their smartphone cameras for. Smartphone cameras are mostly optimized for information transfer — sending photos of menus, signs, faces and objects that are clear and easy to see. This means phones will usually pull down highlights and pull up the shadows, creating a flatter image that makes it easier to see more information in the frame. But showing more information does not automatically make a photo better. In fact, much of our perception of aesthetics in a photo has to do with its ability to present depth. A photo with too much information in the shadows and highlights will appear washed out. Phones also introduce artifacts like over-sharpening and noise reduction to compensate for thier small sensors, which further contributes to the “muddy” smartphone camera look you’re used to seeing by now. This is less necessary now, but many smartphones still do it.

But that doesn’t mean phone cameras are bad. The sensors in modern smartphones have actually gotten so good, many of them can rival dedicated point-and-shoot options on the market today. Knowing how to utilize those sensors is the part most people don’t know how to do, and it really comes down to utilizing some third-party camera and editing apps.

The apps

Moment

There are plenty of apps available today that will give you an instantly “aesthetic” photo. Apps like Dazzcam and Hujicam try to emulate film aesthetics like light leaks and polaroid borders (and honestly, if that’s what you’re looking for, they do a fantastic job). There are also apps like Moment Pro Camera II and Halide that offer “Natural” and “Process Zero” modes, which apply far lighter processing than the default camera offers.

Those options are great if you want your pictures to look better instantly without needing to do any additional editing, but if you want the best possible photo, you’ll need to shoot RAW or DNG.

A RAW vs the edited photo

RAW files are a bundle of practically all the information your camera collects, with extremely minimal processing. In most cases, RAW photos won’t necessarily look better than photos straight from the default camera app right away, but that’s because the default camera app makes a lot of creative decisions for you. If you want the highest-quality photo, it’s best to make these creative decisions yourself.

There are tons of apps available that let you shoot RAW, but the apps I use frequently and that I recommend to other people are Moment Pro Camera II and Halide on iOS, and VWFNDR and Zerocam on Android.

I wouldn’t recommend shooting RAW on every photo you take on your phone. Your phone camera is, after all, optimized for what you are probably taking photos of every day. I generally shoot RAW when I see a nice landscape or city scene that I want to share, or if I’m trying to take a portrait of someone and don’t want all the automatic computational phone processing to apply. Really, I shoot RAW when I’m trying to take a photo for artistic purposes, not for informational purposes.

When you’re shooting, you’ll want to tap on your subject in the viewfinder to get the best possible exposure for it. If the rest of the image is a little bright, or a little dark, don’t worry too much. RAW photos retain a lot of information. I should note, though, that under extremely dark circumstances, RAW on smartphones won’t always be the best option. Physics is still physics, and sometimes it’s better to use the computational photography capabilities your phone offers, which mostly shine in low-light environments by stacking multiple frames to reduce noise.

You’ll notice that when you shoot in RAW, the apps will force you to stick to the native focal lengths your phone offers. That’s because RAW images are information straight off the sensor, and cropping applies processing. Photos from the main sensor will often be the best quality, since it usually has the biggest sensor on your phone, so I recommend shooting with it if you can. I do often shoot with the telephoto lens while traveling though, because sometimes you want a little more reach or a little more compression, and you can usually get good photos from that lens as well.

Editing

After you take your photos, you’re going to need to edit them. Most phones won’t show RAW images in the camera gallery, so in order to get them in an editing app, it’s best to use the share sheet and share directly to your editing app of choice. I suggest Snapseed, since it’s totally free and recently got a wonderful visual overhaul. If you’re an Adobe subscriber, Lightroom Mobile is also great, especially if you’re already used to Lightroom’s tools on your computer.

RAW photos don’t usually look great right away, and the magic of RAW is just how much you can tweak the files. Once I have the photo imported, I usually hit the auto button, just to see what the general boundaries are for the image. Auto mode tries to make everything a mid-tone, meaning it will pull down the highlights and pull up the shadows. This will already look better than straight-out-of-camera from your phone’s default camera app, because it isn’t applying noise reduction or sharpening, just highlight, shadow, contrast, and saturation tweaks, but it usually still needs more, or different, adjustments.

Once I see what auto mode wants to do, I’ll either edit from there, or hit the back button and edit myself. A good photo has a natural amount of contrast, with relatively deep shadows and bright highlights. You usually don’t want to go too hard on either of these things, and having a little bit of detail in both of these is usually preferred, but honestly, this is subjective. Occasionally, it’s preferable to crush the highlights and shadows completely, if you’re going for an ultra high-contrast look.

For color, RAW images are usually flatter than most people find pleasing, and you can fix this with either the saturation or vibrance sliders. I generally prefer vibrance. Saturation will increase the saturation of all colors in the image linearly, where vibrance is weighted, increasing saturation of flatter colors more than already-saturated colors. You can overdo this pretty easily, so I recommend having a light touch when it comes to saturation. You can also use white balance to color your image, and many people find a warmer white balance more pleasing, especially when taking photos outside.

RAW Edited RAW Edited

Another color tool I love to use is the color mix, or selective editing tool. This allows you to tap on a portion of the image and change some of its values. In Snapseed, you can change the brightness, contrast, saturation, and structure. If you’re in Lightroom mobile, you’ll have access to selective hue shifts, which I use all the time. This allows you to shift a yellow tone towards more orange or green, or shift a blue tone more cyan or purple.

Most editing apps also include geometry or perspective tools. These tools allow you to adjust distortion, aspect, scale, and offset. If you don’t know what that means, try hitting the auto button in the geometry or perspective setting. You might be surprised how distorted your phone captured a scene compared to what it looks like in reality, but this is image-dependent. If you want to straighten lines in your photo, some editing apps offer a guided tool that allows you to manually add guidance lines to tell the program what lines should be straight in the image.

The tools you’ll want to use are going to depend heavily on what you want the image to convey. For example, when I’m doing architectural photography, I rely a lot more heavily on the perspective tools, because the aesthetic of the image is heavily dictated by its geometry. If I’m photographing a landscape, I’m more focused on tone and color. Not every scene needs to be tweaked with every tool, and how you edit comes down to personal taste. That taste can also take a while to develop, so study the photos you like and try to figure out how they were edited.

RAW Edited RAW Edited

When you’re done with your edits, many editing apps like Snapseed and Lightroom Mobile also come with a handy tool to put a matte (or border) around your image. I think that photos look better with a white border, as it isolates the image for your eyes. You obviously don’t have to use this tool, but I really like it. Have some whimsy!

This process is a lot more work than just opening your camera app and snapping, but the results are worth it. I am continuously blown away by the quality of images I’m able to get off smartphones, and just how close they can be to a dedicated camera. If you don’t believe me, check out this video I did comparing RAW photos from the iPhone 17 Pro to the Leica M11.

Photography by David Imel / The Verge

Tech.title: The Mermaid Mask is a perfect vacation murder mystery
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

The Mermaid Mask, the next point-and-click game from Tangle Tower developer SFB Games, has everything you could ask for in a great murder mystery.

It starts with a compelling setup: The captain of a submarine is found dead in a locked room, his body next to a mysterious cauldron with blood trickling across the floor. The colorful cast of suspects stationed aboard are delightful to talk to, including a grumpy author trying to draft a sequel to his hit novel, an actor playing the lead in a movie based on that novel, a young woman who puts on elaborate illusion performances, and even a man who studies dreams. The submarine works as an excellent setting that elevates the mystery — in a vehicle that already has such a small footprint, how does a locked-door crime happen in the first place?

Image: SFB Games

Like other crime-solving games, such as the Ace Attorney series, The Mermaid Mask is essentially a visual novel. As Detective Grimoire and his partner Sally, the returning protagonists from Tangle Tower, you’re primarily talking with suspects, investigating rooms, poring over objects, and solving puzzles. But each room is packed with nooks and crannies and knickknacks to click around on, investigate, and learn about, so there’s almost always something to dig into.

The whole thing is backed by excellent voice acting; I often went out of my way to click on every detail I could find just to hear what the characters would say. The puzzles, which have you doing things like turning dials in exactly the right way or organizing skulls on a shelf, also do a good job breaking up what would otherwise be a whole lot of text conversations.

Even though I haven’t played Tangle Tower, I didn’t feel like I was missing any meaningful context. The Mermaid Mask borrows a tried-and-true model from other franchises starring a returning detective, like with Knives Out’s Benoit Blanc: You can come into this story cold without missing anything important, but Detective Grimoire and Sally are a fun hang that make a few nods to their previous work together.

Sometimes, you’ll have to puzzle together clues to form a conclusion. Image: SFB Games

Eventually, after you gather enough evidence about somebody, you’ll confront them in Ace Attorney-like sequences where you’ll be able to make observations or accusations that the suspect rather wished you wouldn’t. These were extremely satisfying; it always felt good to figure out a tiny detail that would break someone’s facade wide open. Whenever the opportunity to do another one came up, I couldn’t wait to jump in.

I had a few issues with The Mermaid Mask, but they’ll be familiar to anyone who likes playing these sorts of games. Presenting every clue to every suspect to get their reaction can be tedious. It’s not necessary, but I didn’t realize that until about halfway in my 10-hour playthrough when I spotted the hint system that suggests what you might want to show someone. Sometimes you have to make your case by presenting evidence in a specific order, even if you have already worked out where it might lead, so that the characters can talk things out as the script demands. At one point, I ran out of leads to explore and couldn’t figure where to go next until I manipulated one clue in one specific way that opened up a bunch of leads. More than once, I couldn’t figure out the exact clue that would advance things, so I just brute-forced guesses until I could move forward.

These roadblocks were frustrating. But that’s mostly because they stopped me from moving forward in a story that had me staying up way past my bedtime. When I reached the game’s finale — which begins with a classic murder mystery parlor room scene — I could hardly put my Steam Deck down because I wanted to see how all the pieces came together. When I finally finished The Mermaid Mask after a three-day tear, I felt like I had just closed the book on a satisfying murder mystery novel.

The Mermaid Mask is out now on Nintendo Switch, PC, and PS5.

I buried the lede here: The biggest new thing of the week, at least in my book, is Instapaper 10. Instapaper is one of the original read-later apps, and has continued to be among the best on the market. After some weird ownership stuff over the years, Instapaper has been in the hands of Brian Donohue, who has been steadily improving the service in lots of ways. This week’s launch comes with a really nice redesign, a way better web app, and a lot of helpful organization and reading tools. I’ve been testing it, and I think it’s back to being my go-to recommendation for reading apps. (For power users I still think Readwise is the move.)

With the new app out, I asked Brian to share his homescreen with us — I wanted to see how he organized his stuff, and if he might be working on even more cool stuff. Turns out he is! Here’s his homescreen, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:

The phone: iPhone 16 Pro. I almost always purchase iPhones every other generation. Maybe a foldable this year?

The wallpaper: My daughter, as a reminder that my apps must be good otherwise she will not have food on the table.

The apps: Safari, Google Calendar, Emerald, Google Maps, Weather, Photos, Instapaper, Kobo Books, Reddit, 1Password, Google Authenticator, Slack, Google Docs, Google Sheets, ForeFlight, Flight Circle, Claude, Linear, Phone, Sunflower, Messages, Spotify.

I’ll start with the ones not yet in the App Store: Emerald and Sunflower.

Emerald is a Markdown editor I’m working on that solves two personal pain points: native iOS / macOS client, and collaboration on markdown files. I have been a big Obsidian user the past two years, but it’s been failing me in those areas. I’ve been writing with Emerald exclusively for the past few months and it’s almost ready for beta testing. Waitlist in the link.

Sunflower is a new email client from Bobby Goodlatte and friends. It’s beautifully designed and has some tasteful AI features, like summarizing your inbox, chatting with your email, and an Autopilot feature which seems to be perpetually “Coming Soon.” I’ve been trying a few clients in the “AI email” space like Extra, and an autopilot tool called Cora, which didn’t stick.

Instapaper’s big launch this week included a new home screen widget. It fits nicely in the widget stack alongside the Apple News, Stocks, and Weather widgets.

Additionally, you have many of the usual suspects. I am doing a huge amount of my work with Claude and Linear these days, both of which have fantastic iOS apps.

I also asked Brian to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:

I’ve always been inspired by creative builders, and two come to mind right now. The first is Andrew Jones , who has been building free & open-source alternatives to paid software (e.g. Granola Wispr Flow ) — fingers crossed Instapaper is not next. The second is Q , a designer who has been building small, single-purpose websites for himself that I find inspiring. It almost reminds me of a purer, distant version of the Internet, where you built a bunch of Geocities pages for fun and without expectations of fame and fortune.

Hyper Mesh . Q has been exploring image reveal animations, and built a tool to tweak presets on the initial mask and the animation that reveals the image.

SVG Star Editor . Create a star from different settings and export to SVG.

Chess Moves . Q is learning how to play chess with his girlfriend and made this tutorial website as a companion tool.

Our phones are such a “This is water” thing in our lives now, and I really enjoy anything that makes me pay a little more attention to the object, the cultural force, and the economic engine that takes up so much of my life.
